SHIPBOARD MANUAL
Off Shore Supply/Platform Supply Vessels















































SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL










































































































































































SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL







The methodology recommended by British Standard BS 8800:2004 ―Guide to Occupational Health and Safety Management System‖ shall be applied for the purpose of risk assessment. This method is also recommended in ―The Code of Safety Working Practices for Merchant Seamen‖.

In any operation, risk towards health of the personnel, safety and environmental protection issues may be involved. Hazard to each of the factors may be considered to determine the probability and consequence of same. In case residual risk remains, same shall be mitigated in order to bring same to ALARP level. Template for risk assessment is provided in Form: RA001.

Ship-type specific Occupational Health & Safety Risk Assessment Register (PDF format) shall be provided. The registers are reviewed from time to time for validity of the risk assessments to include latest risk assessments based on the feedbacks from the vessels so as to maintain consistency of risk assessment standards across the fleet. Records of each risk assessment shall be maintained on board and forwarded to the operating division and concerned DO on quarterly basis.

Evaluation of Risk Tolerance

Introduction of Company | 
D.	Introduction of Company
The ISM Code was adopted by the IMO vide Resolution A.741(18) and became mandatory
w.e.f. 1st July, 1998 and was incorporated in SOLAS Chapter IX on Management for the Safe Operation of Ships.

Amendments were made to the ISM Code, vide —
Resolution MSC 104 (73), effective from 1st July 2002.
Resolution 273 (85) MSC, effective from 1st July 2010.
Resolution MSC.353(92), effective from 1st January 2015

The ISM Code, amended vide Resolution 273 (85) MSC, provides an international standard for safety of ships and personnel at sea and protection of environment. The amended ISM Code is provided in Appendix-1 of company SMS Procedures Manual.

The Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. was founded in the year 1961. In the year 1997, the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention (ISM Code) became mandatory to be implemented onboard all passenger ships, tankers and bulk carriers w.e.f. 01.07.1998. ISM Code was adopted by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) by resolution A.741 (18).

To comply with the procedural requirements as specified in the ISM Code, the Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. implemented the ISM Code onboard all its ships as well as in the shore offices including the Branch/Regional Offices and had same duly audited and certified in compliance with the requirements of the Code.

We have three basic manuals viz. Company SMS Policy Manual (part of shipboard SMS documentation and distributed as per the controlled circulation list), Company SMS Procedure Manual (distributed as per the controlled circulation list and not part of shipboard SMS documentation) and Shipboard SMS Manuals (Vols. 1 & 2). The Company SMS Procedure Manual details the procedure for implementation of the SMS in our officers and fleet. The Shipboard SMS Manuals are in two volumes, Vol. 1 which is generic to the whole fleet of SIRIUS (except for the OSV/MSV where there is only a single manual) and Vol. 2 which details the ship type specific procedures and it addresses the ISM Code relevant issues pertaining to particular ship-type operations, SMS feedbacks, SMS reviews and basic emergency preparedness and compliance with the statutory requirements pertaining to ships‘ certification and documentation. These manuals reflect the policy and the procedures of the Company with regard to the ISM Code to be followed.

The Shipboard SMS Manual (Vol. I) addresses all elements of the ISM Code (except elements under ship-specific maintenance and cargo work related issues) and the Shipboard SMS Manual (Vol. II) addresses all elements of the ISM Code pertaining to ship-specific operational issues, cargo work/trade related issues.

To avoid frequent changes to the SMS manuals, the DPA shall issue Temporary Instructions towards the required changes and these temporary instructions shall get included in the manual collectively during revisions. | D.	Introduction of Company

To avoid frequent changes to the SMS manuals, the DPA shall issue Temporary Instructions towards the required changes and these temporary instructions shall get included in the manual collectively during revisions. | D.	Introduction of Company
The ISM Code was adopted by the IMO vide Resolution A.741(18) and became mandatory
w.e.f. 1st July, 1998 and was incorporated in SOLAS Chapter IX on Management for the Safe Operation of Ships.

Amendments were made to the ISM Code, vide —
Resolution MSC 104 (73), effective from 1st July 2002.
Resolution 273 (85) MSC, effective from 1st July 2010.
Resolution MSC.353(92), effective from 1st January 2015

The ISM Code, amended vide Resolution 273 (85) MSC, provides an international standard for safety of ships and personnel at sea and protection of environment. The amended ISM Code is provided in Appendix-1 of company SMS Procedures Manual.

The Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. was founded in the year 1961. In the year 1997, the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention (ISM Code) became mandatory to be implemented onboard all passenger ships, tankers and bulk carriers w.e.f. 01.07.1998. ISM Code was adopted by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) by resolution A.741 (18).

To comply with the procedural requirements as specified in the ISM Code, the Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. implemented the ISM Code onboard all its ships as well as in the shore offices including the Branch/Regional Offices and had same duly audited and certified in compliance with the requirements of the Code.

We have three basic manuals viz. Company SMS Policy Manual (part of shipboard SMS documentation and distributed as per the controlled circulation list), Company SMS Procedure Manual (distributed as per the controlled circulation list and not part of shipboard SMS documentation) and Shipboard SMS Manuals (Vols. 1 & 2). The Company SMS Procedure Manual details the procedure for implementation of the SMS in our officers and fleet. The Shipboard SMS Manuals are in two volumes, Vol. 1 which is generic to the whole fleet of SIRIUS (except for the OSV/MSV where there is only a single manual) and Vol. 2 which details the ship type specific procedures and it addresses the ISM Code relevant issues pertaining to particular ship-type operations, SMS feedbacks, SMS reviews and basic emergency preparedness and compliance with the statutory requirements pertaining to ships‘ certification and documentation. These manuals reflect the policy and the procedures of the Company with regard to the ISM Code to be followed.

The Shipboard SMS Manual (Vol. I) addresses all elements of the ISM Code (except elements under ship-specific maintenance and cargo work related issues) and the Shipboard SMS Manual (Vol. II) addresses all elements of the ISM Code pertaining to ship-specific operational issues, cargo work/trade related issues.

To avoid frequent changes to the SMS manuals, the DPA shall issue Temporary Instructions towards the required changes and these temporary instructions shall get included in the manual collectively during revisions.

General
Definitions
For the sake of brevity and true meaning and context, ‗safety‘ to be interpreted and considered as ‗Safety, Occupational Health & Environment Protection‘ throughout this manual.

Part A – Definitions from the Code:
International Safety Management (ISM) Code – means the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention as adopted by the Assembly, as may be amended by the Organization.
Company – means the owner of the ship or any other organization or person such as the manager, or the bareboat charterer, who has assumed the responsibility for operation of the ship from the ship owner and who, on assuming such responsibility, has agreed to take over all duties and responsibility imposed by the Code.
Company for this manual – The SIRIUS Shipping (SIRIUS).
Administration – means the Government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly. In the case of Indian Flag vessels, it is Director General Of Shipping.
Safety Management System – means a structured and documented system enabling Company personnel to implement effectively the Company safety and environmental protection policy.
Document of Compliance (DOC) – means a document issued to a Company which complies with the requirements of the ISM Code.
Safety Management Certificate (SMC) – means a document issued to a ship which signifies that the Company and its shipboard management operate in accordance with the approved safety management system.
Objective Evidence – means quantitative or qualitative information, records or statements of fact pertaining to safety or to the existence and implementation of a safety management system element, which is based on observation, measurement or test and which can be verified.
Observation – means a statement of fact made during a safety management audit and substantiated by objective evidence.
Non-conformity – means an observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfillment of a specified requirement.
Major non-conformity – means an identifiable deviation that poses a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship or a serious risk to the environment that requires immediate corrective action or the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of this Code.
Anniversary Date – means the day and month of each year that corresponds to the date of expiry of the relevant document or certificate.
Convention – means the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, as amended. | General

Part B – Other useful definitions

Accidents – means incidents involving injury or damage to life, the environment, the ship or its cargo.
Anchor Handling Tug-cum-Supply Vessel – means a vessel constructed to handle spread mooring of drill ships and MSVs, towing of drilling rigs and Single Buoy Moorings from one location to another location. These vessels can also be utilised for transportation of various materials and men from supply base to offshore platforms and oil rigs and vice versa.
Cargo handler – means a member of ship or offshore installation handling the cargo on board the OSV at the offshore installation.
Cold Work – Work that cannot create a source of ignition.
Contractor – means organization that has responsibility for the operation of the ship.
Critical Equipment –The equipment or technical systems, the sudden operational failure of which may result in a hazardous situation.
Corrective Action – Action to eliminate the cause of a detected non-conformity or other undesirable situation.
Designated Person Ashore (DPA) – is a person ashore appointed by the Safety, Health and Environmental Committee with direct access to the highest levels of management, who has the responsibility and the authority to monitor the safety and pollution prevention aspects of the operation of each ship and to ensure that adequate resources and shore based support are applied, as required.
Designated Officer (DO) – is a person ashore appointed by the SIRIUS responsible to monitor the safety and pollution prevention aspects of the office and of each ship in the Division and assist DPA in the functions of SMS.
Dynamic Positioning System – A dynamic positioning system is defined as all the equipment necessary to provide means of controlling the position and heading of a floating installation within predetermined limits by means of vectored thrust.
Floating Hose – A Floating conduit used to export hydrocarbons from a point of storage/ production, either an SPM or ship‘s manifold to a receiving ship‘s manifold for transport.
Fire Fighter-I – Vessel built for early stage fire fighting and rescue operations close to structure on fire.
Fire Fighter-II – Vessel built for continuous fighting of large fires and for cooling of the structures on fire.
Fire Fighter-III – Vessel built for continuous fighting of large fires and for cooling of the structures on fire. These vessels have larger water pumping capacity and more comprehensive fire fighting equipment than Fire Fighter-I
Fixed Offshore Installation (or Installation) – Fixed Offshore Installation is used as a collective term to cover any construction or system, buoyant or non-buoyant, permanently supported by or fixed to the seafloor by gravity, piles or by other means and designed and built for installation at a particular offshore site. The Fixed Offshore Installation is used primarily for such functions as; drilling, production, processing, storage, loading and/or accommodation. Sub-sea production system and sub-sea pipeline systems are also covered by this term. | Part B – Other useful definitions

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
General | 
Group In Charge – means a senior superintendent who is nominated by and reports to the department head and is responsible for the day to day activities of the superintendents reporting to him.
Hazard – means a source or situation with a potential to harm in terms of injury or ill health, damage to property, damage to workplace environment or combination of these.
Hazardous Occurrences – are situations which could have led to an accident if they had developed further (i.e. near miss situations)
Incident – An unplanned sequence of events and/or condition that results, or could have reasonably resulted, in a loss event.
International Safety Management Code – means the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention, as adopted by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) by resolution A.741 (18), as may be amended by the Organisation.
Logistics Coordinator – means a person or persons based on shore or offshore, specifically designated by the operator as a focal point and having responsibility for the proper preparation of cargo for transport offshore, loading/unloading/back loading plans, sailing schedules, contingencies and other matters as required by the situation including dangerous goods.
Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) – A document identifying a substance and all its constituents. It provides the recipient with all necessary information to manage the substance safely.
Mobile Offshore Drilling Unit (MODU) – means a vessel capable of engaging in drilling operations for the exploration or exploitation of resources beneath the seabed such as liquid or gaseous hydrocarbons, sulphur or salt.
Multi Support Vessel – means a vessel constructed to handle various offshore specialized support services like sub sea structural and sub sea pipeline maintenance repairs, fire fighting operations at offshore platforms and rigs, pollution control services, crane assistance, helicopter rescue operations. These vessels maintain their position either on dynamic positioning system or on spread mooring system.
Near Miss – means sequence of events and/or conditions that could have resulted in loss.
Offshore Installations – means a structure which is, to be or has been, used while standing or stationed in water or on the foreshore or other land intermittently covered with water.
Offshore Installation Manager (OIM) – means the person responsible for all activities on offshore installation.
Offshore Supply Vessel (OSV) – means a vessel which is used for the transportation of stores, materials, equipments or personnel to, from and between offshore installations.
Operator – means the party who contracts an offshore supply vessel.
OSV Code – means Offshore Supply Vessels code to provide, safe practice for both operator and contractor, an international standard to avoid or reduce to a minimum hazards which affect offshore supply vessels in their daily operation of carrying cargo and persons to, from and between offshore installation.
Preventive Action – Action to eliminate the cause of a potential non-conformity or other undesirable potential situation.

Hazard – means a source or situation with a potential to harm in terms of injury or ill health, damage to property, damage to workplace environment or combination of these.
Hazardous Occurrences – are situations which could have led to an accident if they had developed further (i.e. near miss situations)
Incident – An unplanned sequence of events and/or condition that results, or could have reasonably resulted, in a loss event.
International Safety Management Code – means the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention, as adopted by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) by resolution A.741 (18), as may be amended by the Organisation.
Logistics Coordinator – means a person or persons based on shore or offshore, specifically designated by the operator as a focal point and having responsibility for the proper preparation of cargo for transport offshore, loading/unloading/back loading plans, sailing schedules, contingencies and other matters as required by the situation including dangerous goods.
Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) – A document identifying a substance and all its constituents. It provides the recipient with all necessary information to manage the substance safely.
Mobile Offshore Drilling Unit (MODU) – means a vessel capable of engaging in drilling operations for the exploration or exploitation of resources beneath the seabed such as liquid or gaseous hydrocarbons, sulphur or salt.

Riser – A sub-sea rigid or flexible pipe which connects the surface facilities with the sea floor and thus the conduit for fulfilling the desired function of conveying fluids, gas, electrical power, etc.
Risk – Combination of the likelihood and consequence(s) of a specified hazardous event occurring.
Risk Assessment – Overall process of estimating the magnitude of risk and deciding whether or not the risk is tolerable.
Safety Management Audit – means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether the SMS activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives.
External SMS Audit – means an audit carried out by a third party such as Classification Society, Administration or any authorised body.
Internal SMS Audit – means an audit carried out by the Company personnel.
Seismic Survey Vessel – Vessel engaged in seismic survey activities.
SOHSP – A Shipboard Occupational Health & Safety Programme (SOHSP) is a systematic plan to identify and control occupational hazards and respond to shipboard emergencies.
Spread Mooring – A system having multiple catenary mooring lines or drag anchors at the seabed; with the other end of each line individually attached to winches or stoppers on vessel through fairleads as necessary.
Sub-sea System – A flexible/articulated piping system providing a conduit for the hydrocarbons from the sub-sea pipelines to the surface components. It includes sub-sea pipelines, sub-sea well system and risers.
Superintendent – Means Sr. Manager or GM or Vice President or Sr. Vice President, who is assigned the technical management responsibilities of the vessel by the Company.
Tension Leg Platform (TLP) – is defined as a buoyant installation connected to a fixed foundation by pre-tensioned tendons. The tendons are normally parallel, near vertical elements, acting in tension, which restrain the motions of the platform in heave, pitch and roll. The platform is compliant in surge, sway and yaw.
Verify – means to investigate and confirm that an activity or operation is in accordance with a specified requirement. (Examples of verification activities include inspections, tests and operational checks on ships and their equipment prior to departing port, at sea or before entering port or closing with the land. A system audit is also an example of a verification activity.)
Well Stimulation Vessel – means a vessel constructed to hold position close to the oil wells and carry out well activation by way of water injection/acidising to improve the flow of oil thereby enhance the oil production. Shipboard Organisation
The shipboard organization is constituted as per the organization chart documented herein. The Shipboard Organization in general will conform to the requirements of minimum safe manning, and shall consist of the following departments with departmental heads:
Engine Department	–	Chief Engineer Officer
Deck Department	–	Chief Officer
Catering Department	–	Catering Officer/Person deputed by Master
The responsibility of the overall safety of the ship and of those on board rests with the Master. Under him each individual member of the ship‘s staff has a duty to ensure safety in those matters within his own control whether supervising or carrying out a task or in reporting non-conformities, which might impair safety.
In order to ensure that personnel onboard are familiar with the structure of the Safety Management System, the following charts shall be posted conspicuously onboard:
Shipboard Organization
Ship-Shore Communication
Safety Management Team
Safety, Occupational Health & Environmental Committee
Master and senior Officers onboard should be able to identify DPA and his role in Company‘s Safety Management System. | Technical & Offshore Services Division Organisation Chart

Under him each individual member of the ship‘s staff has a duty to ensure safety in those matters within his own control whether supervising or carrying out a task or in reporting non-conformities, which might impair safety.
In order to ensure that personnel onboard are familiar with the structure of the Safety Management System, the following charts shall be posted conspicuously onboard:
Shipboard Organization
Ship-Shore Communication
Safety Management Team
Safety, Occupational Health & Environmental Committee
Master and senior Officers onboard should be able to identify DPA and his role in Company‘s Safety Management System.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Organization | 
The departmental heads are responsible to the Master for the administration, maintenance, upkeep, supervision and safe, economical operation of their respective departments in accordance with procedures of Company‘s Safety Management System and applicable National and International Rules and Regulations. They must keep the Master fully informed with regard to departmental activities, equipment condition and staff conduct.
Shipboard personnel are organized in three levels namely:
Management Level – Officers serving as Master, Chief Engineer Officer, Chief Officer and Second Engineer Officer on board a seagoing ship, and ensuring that all functions within the designated area of responsibility are properly performed.
Operation Level – Officers serving as in charge of a navigational or engineering watch or as designated engineer officer, electrical Officer for periodically unmanned/manned machinery spaces or as radio operator on board a seagoing ship, and maintaining direct control over the performance of all functions within the designated area of responsibility in accordance with proper procedures and under the direction of an individual serving in the management level for that area of responsibility.
Support Level – Personnel whose level of responsibility associated with performing assigned tasks, duties or responsibilities on board a seagoing ship under the direction of an individual serving in the operation or management level.

Safety Management Team (SMT)

Master



Chief Eng.Off.
(Safety Off.)


Chief Off.	2nd Eng. Off.
(Safety Off.)	(Member)

Shipboard Management Team shall consist of the Officers whose responsibilities include a supervising role for all aspects of effective Safety Management System on board. Safety Management Team shall comprise of the Master and other Officers on board belonging to the management level. This team shall meet whenever necessitated by any non-conformities, accidents (Form: AR001), near miss/hazardous occurrences (Form: NMHO001), else once a month. Role of the Safety Management Team —
make safety and pollution prevention a key issue in all management decisions;
keep to the guidelines set out in ship‘s manuals;
make out an action plan for all Safety, Health and Environmental Committee recommendations;
supplement where required instructions and procedures provided in Shipboard SMS Manual with ship specific procedures;
follow up any incident with a prompt and thorough investigation;
plan and carry out unscheduled and planned maintenance on board;
make or encourage regular routine inspections;
Maintain records of the meeting on board.
The Chief Engineer Officer and the Chief Officer act as Safety Officers (SO) for their respective departments and will assist and advise the Master in implementation of the Shipboard SMS. The task of the safety officers will be as follows:
The functioning of the ship‘s Safety, Health and Environmental Committee.
Enforce all safety and pollution prevention rules and regulations.
Encourage ship‘s staff to submit ideas and suggestions for improving safety and environment protection.
Endeavour to anticipate safety problems in their respective areas of responsibility.
Take corrective action to eliminate unsafe practices.
Ensure all ship‘s personnel are provided safety and task familiarisation.
Stop any work they reasonably believe may cause a serious accident and immediately inform the Master, who will decide when work can be safely resumed.
Investigate accidents and near misses/hazardous occurrences occurring on board and recommend proposals to Master to prevent recurrence of same or to remove the hazard.
Investigate all complaints made by shipboard personnel concerning safety. | Safety Management Team (SMT)

In addition to the SMT, there is a Safety, Health and Environmental Committee (SHEC) on board each vessel which comprises of the following members:
Master		Chairman
Chief Engineer Officer		Secretary

Deck Crew	  Member
Engine Crew	  Member
(In addition to the above members, the Chairman may encourage other members of the ship‘s staff on rotational basis to attend the meetings as invitee members).
The Safety, Health and Environmental Committee (SHEC) will be the safety forum on board and will make all efforts to create a safe and healthy working environment on board. The Safety, Health and Environmental Committee will assist the Safety Officers to investigate accidents and near miss/hazardous occurrences occurring on board, with a view to prevent recurrence.

Vessel shall record Nil where no accidents, near misses/hazardous occurrences have occurred during the month

signed by the Master and forwarded to the superintendent of the vessel with copies sent to the concerned Group In-charge and DO of the Division. Follow up action on the Safety, Health and Environmental Committee Meeting report shall be initiated by Company wherever required. Records of such follow ups shall be maintained by the Master for verification.
The SHEC shall meet every month and special SHEC meeting shall be called immediately after any serious incident or accident within fleet and the following points will form the agenda of the meeting:
To read and approve the minutes of the last meeting.
Follow up actions arising from previous meetings.
Findings of inspections of work places, with a view to eradicate unsafe, unhygienic practices and propose corrective measures.
Investigation of causes of accidents, near miss/hazardous occurrences and unsafe practices with proposal for preventive action to be taken.
Actions taken or required to be taken for bringing about consciousness among ship staff regarding safety, health and environmental protection.
Rectification of any safety, health and environmental protection related shortcomings in the ship or her equipment.
Risk assessments undertaken.
Deviations from rest hours, if any.
Suggestions received from ship staff to improve Safety, Health & Environment Protection standards and awareness on board.
Implementation of corrective action on non-conformities/deficiencies.
Discussion of fleet circulars issued by the Company.
Discussion of information received from the Company pertaining to the accidents/near misses within the industry. | signed by the Master and forwarded to the superintendent of the vessel with copies sent to the concerned Group In-charge and DO of the Division. *  Those damages which pose immediate threat to life, safety of the vessel and environment protection.
(All other routine accident, near misses/hazardous occurrences shall be reported as per SMS procedures) #  P&S Department comprises of Bunker Cell, Victualling & Stores, Insurance, Agency Services.
¶ Subjects pertaining to 75/100/150 Pax (A&N) ships (Port Blair controlled vessels), shall be reported to A&N Administration/DSS, instead of ED/SVP (FP) and/or P&S Department, since manning and stores/provisions are provided by A&N Administration.
Subjects pertaining to passenger vessels of A&N Administration, controlled by Chennai Regional Office shall be reported to A&N Administration/DSS, instead of ED/SVP (FP) and/or P&S Department, since officers are recruited by FPD and crew are posted by A&N Administration under their pay roll.
Note:
Master shall route all communication and reporting to the company through the concerned superintendent. In case of emergencies, delays affecting safety and commercial aspects and urgencies, he is also required to inform the Group In-charge by quickest means. The Master can inform the Director, ED/SVP, DPA or the top management directly, if required to do so.
Upon receipt of report/information from the vessel, the superintendent shall take necessary action and bring the same to notice of concerned Group In-charge or the Departmental head. The Group In-charge or the Departmental head shall initiate followed up action. He shall also ensure that all concerned are duly informed.
For all matters of safety of life, property at sea and pollution prevention, environmental protection aspects, he shall ensure that the concerned DO and DPA are always kept informed. | *  Those damages which pose immediate threat to life, safety of the vessel and environment protection.

(All other routine accident, near misses/hazardous occurrences shall be reported as per SMS procedures) #  P&S Department comprises of Bunker Cell, Victualling & Stores, Insurance, Agency Services.
¶ Subjects pertaining to 75/100/150 Pax (A&N) ships (Port Blair controlled vessels), shall be reported to A&N Administration/DSS, instead of ED/SVP (FP) and/or P&S Department, since manning and stores/provisions are provided by A&N Administration.
Subjects pertaining to passenger vessels of A&N Administration, controlled by Chennai Regional Office shall be reported to A&N Administration/DSS, instead of ED/SVP (FP) and/or P&S Department, since officers are recruited by FPD and crew are posted by A&N Administration under their pay roll.
Note:
Master shall route all communication and reporting to the company through the concerned superintendent. Responsibility and Authority of Group I/C (Technical) Member of Safety Review Committee of the concerned division Reports to: ED/SVP

Safety Management Responsibility and Authority
The Group I/C is assigned the responsibility of supervising the technical management of a group of vessels. Safety Management responsibility and authority of the Group I/C include, but are not limited to, the following:
Supervise day to day work of superintendents of the group.
Verify that vessels of the group are maintained in a seaworthy and cargoworthy condition.
Be directly responsible for the emergency organization ashore, in any emergency relating to vessels of his respective group.
Verify that vessels of the group comply with all statutory, national, international, port authority and classification rules and regulations.
Verify that vessels of the group have valid statutory and Class certificates on board at all times.
Plan repairs of the vessels of the group.
Ensure that superintendents provide shore-based technical support and plan repairs of the vessels of the group.
Ensure that superintendents of the group provide resources to vessels for compliance with the SMS.
Advise superintendents regarding corrective action for non-conformities, accidents, near misses/hazardous occurrences reported by the vessels of the group.
Discuss with superintendents SHEC Reports, Master‘s Verification Reports, Master‘s Review Reports and other reports/suggestions received from vessels of the group.
Co-ordinate the risk assessments activities, for reasonably foreseeable risks and review/approve same, in consultation with Superintendent, as and when received from the ships under his charge and maintain records.
In the event of there being any regulatory/operational/manufacturer required changes of PMS, same to be initiated by Group I/C for uploading the changes in the DANAOS PMS. Accordingly, the Group I/C shall co-ordinate with the IT Department towards uploading the required changes in the DANAOS (for vessels having computerized maintenance system). The DPA shall be kept duly informed.
Send the Reviewed Risk Assessment to DO for analyzing the trends.
Monitor technical performance and ensure effective implementation of SMS of the vessels of the group under his charge. | Responsibility and Authority of Group I/C (Technical) Member of Safety Review Committee of the concerned division Reports to: ED/SVP

Responsibility and Authority of Superintendent
Reports to: Group I/C
Safety Management Responsibility and Authority
The superintendent is assigned the responsibility of technical management of a number of ships within a group and ensuring that the vessels are operated and maintained in a safe and economical manner. Safety Management responsibility and authority of the Superintendent/ Base Manager include, but are not limited to, the following:
Supervise the Master and Chief Engineer Officer of assigned ships.
Ensure that vessels under his charge are maintained in a seaworthy and cargo worthy condition.
Ensure that vessels under his charge comply with all statutory, national, international, port authority and classification rules and regulations.
Ensure that vessels under his charge have valid statutory and class certificates on board at all times.
Assess condition of hull, shipboard equipment and performance of ships assigned to him through ships returns and also through visits to vessels, at least once in six months.
Plan and supervise repairs of the vessels under his charge.
Provide shore-based technical support to vessel under his charge.
Provide resources to vessels under his charge for compliance with the SMS.
Brief management level officers regarding the SIRIUS SMS and related matters at the time of joining vessels.
Advise corrective action for non-conformities, accidents, near miss/hazardous occurrences reported by the vessels under his charge and follow up on non-conformities, in consultation with Group In-charge.
Discuss with Group In-charge and follow up SHEC Reports, Master‘s Verification Reports, Master‘s Review Reports and other reports/suggestions received from vessels under his charge.
Co-ordinate the risk assessments activities, for reasonably foreseeable risks and review/approve same, in consultation with Group I/C, as and when received from the ships under his charge and maintain records.
Monitor technical performance and ensure timely external audits for obtaining SMC of the vessel under his charge and compliance with the SMS.
Keep close liaison with vessels under his charge.
Co-ordinate activities between Head Office, Regional Offices, Owner‘s/Charterer‘s Agents and vessels for technical operations of vessels under his charge.
Carry out root cause analysis (wherever applicable), in consultation with ship personnel, for deficiencies identified during FSI/GI/PSC inspections and NCs raised during SMS audits.
Conduct Safety Health and Environmental Committee (SHEC) meeting during Ships visit and maintain records (applicable only on tankers).
Be a part of emergency response team in any emergency relating to vessel‘s safety and shall function under instructions of the Group I/C. | Responsibility and Authority of Superintendent

3.10	Safety Management Responsibilities of Chief Officer
Member of the safety management team, member of Safety, Health and Environmental Committee and belongs to management level.
Reports to	:  Master
Supervises	: Operation level Officers, junior operation level personnel and support level ratings connected to the deck department or deck operations.
Responsibilities : The Chief Officer is the principal executive officer in-charge of the deck department and is the designated officer in charge in the absence of the Master.
The safety management responsibilities of Chief Officer include, but are not limited to, the following:
Familiarize himself with the procedures of safety management system and comply with same.
Administration, supervision and delegation of duties to the operation level officers and support level ratings connected to the deck department.
Maintenance and supervision of safe working practices during deck operations.
Understanding of the Safety, Occupational Health & Environment Protection Policy of the Company and enforcement of same on board the vessel.
Indenting and safe keeping of all deck stores, equipment and spares.
Monitor the requirement of fresh water for the vessel.
Testing and thorough examination of cargo gear and deck lifting appliances.
Preparing of work specifications for repairs and dry docking and supervision of repairs.
Ensure safe ballasting/de ballasting operations
Maintenance of all LSA and FFA.
Maintenance of hull and deck equipments.
Prepare vessel for classification and statutory surveys.
Watch keeping duties at sea and at anchor. In-charge of cargo operations in port.
Maintenance of hygiene, housekeeping and sanitation on board the vessel.
Implementing Garbage Management Plan on board.
Calculation and monitoring of stability and trim of vessel prior departure and on voyage.
Ensure testing of controls for navigation and communication means before departure port.
Safe stowage of cargo, safety and security of cargo on board.
Sounding of all tanks every day.
All navigational charts and hydrographic publications for the intended voyage to be fully corrected uptodate from the current Notices to Mariners, navigational warnings and other sources.
To act as a Medical Officer and treat the ship‘s crew under the directions of the Master, and upkeep of Medical Locker.
Acting as Spill Co-ordinator under SOPEP, upkeep and maintenance of SOPEP equipment.
Complying with Master‘s Standing and Night Orders.
Compliance with applicable port, terminal and dock safety regulations.
Compliance with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
Carry out emergency duties as per emergency response procedures. | 3.10	Safety Management Responsibilities of Chief Officer

3.11	Safety Management Responsibilities of NWKO/Second Off./Third Off.

Reports to	:  The Master for all Navigational Watchkeeping duties.
Chief Officer for all Deck Watchkeeping and Maintenance work.
Supervises	:  Junior operation level and support level functions
Responsibilities  :  NWKO/2nd Off./3rd Off. is an executive officer designated as the
―Navigating Officer‖ and belongs to operational level of the vessel.
The safety management responsibilities of the NWKO/2nd Off./3rd Off. include, but are not limited to, the following:
Familiarise himself with the procedures of safety management system and comply with same.
Prepare a passage plan for the intended voyage under the directions of Master.
All navigational equipment on the vessel to be kept in good order and regularly serviced and maintained. Indenting and safe keeping of required spares for the navigational equipment on board.
All navigational charts and hydrographic publications for the intended voyage to be fully corrected uptodate from the current Notices to Mariners, navigational warnings and other sources, under supervision of Chief Officer.
A noon position to be fixed on the chart daily.
An abstract of navigational logs to be maintained.
Preparing reports and returns as per company‘s procedure.
To keep a navigational watch at sea and at anchor.
Keep a cargo watch in port as per directions of the Chief Officer and applicable rules and regulations.
Assist Chief Officer in preparing vessel for classification and statutory surveys and ship‘s operational routine duties and day to day work.
To act as a Medical Officer (in ships without doctors) and treat the ship‘s crew under the directions of the Master, and upkeep of Medical Locker.
Compliance with applicable port, terminal and dock safety regulations.
Assistant to spill co-ordinator (Chief Officer) on the scene as per SOPEP.
Compliance with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
Carry out emergency duties as per emergency response procedures and as directed by command and control.
Incharge of a life-boat during rescue operations and while abandoning ship.
To comply with applicable rules of STCW Convention.
To prepare handing over notes along with report while signing off the vessel.
To acquaint himself and prepare for the rank above.
Has the authority to identify and report non-conformities and near misses/hazardous occurrences, as per procedures defined within this Safety Management System. | 3.11	Safety Management Responsibilities of NWKO/Second Off./Third Off.

3.12	Safety Management Responsibilities of Chief Engineer Officer
Member of the Safety Management Team and belongs to management level. Secretary of the Safety, Health and Environmental Committee on board.
Safety Officer for the Engine Department.
Reports to	: Master and communicates through Superintendent for all technical matters
Supervises	: 2nd Engineer Officer, 3rd Engineer Officer, Electrical Officer, junior operation level personnel and Engine ratings of support level.
Responsibilities :  The Chief Engineer Officer is in charge of the Engine Room Department and is responsible for the efficient and safe operation and maintenance of all machinery and cargo systems on board. He is the first watch keeping Engineer.
The safety management responsibilities of Chief Engineer Officer include, but are not limited to, the following:
Familiarise himself with the procedures of Safety Management System and comply with same.
Maintenance of M/E or Thrusters, auxiliaries, steering system, air-conditioning, mechanical blowers, refrigeration plant, all cranes, winches, windlass, mooring winches, and electrical and hydraulic systems pertaining thereto.
Maintain the Engine Room and other spaces under his charge clean at all times.
Responsible for indenting and safe keeping of all engine stores, spares, tools and instruments and maintaining proper records of same.
Advise Master promptly of any occurrence in the Engine Room, which might affect the navigation or other essential services.
Aim at achieving maximum economy in consumption of fuel, lubricating oils and use of stores/spares.
Administration, supervision and delegation of duties to the Engineer Officers and crew, in order to ensure efficient running of the Engine Room Department at sea and in port.
Ensure Schedules of planned maintenance system are implemented on board.
Make a round of the machinery spaces before the main engine/thruster is required.
Be readily available for emergency call from engine room during manoeuvring.
Ensure availability of windlass and mooring winches and other deck machinery for use whenever required.
Obtain approval from Master for any planned stoppage of main engine for inspection or maintenance.
Ensure all Engineer Officers are familiar with emergency procedures and Code of Safe Working Practices.
Ensure safety and testing of all tackle and lifting gear in Engine Room.
Ensure classification & statutory surveys status maintained up to date.
Supervision of bunkering operations and ensuring that correct quantity and quality of bunkers received.
Preparation of work specification for Engine Department/Deck machineries for repairs/dry docking and to supervise.
Issue standing instructions for efficient and effective performance for engine department personnel. | 3.12	Safety Management Responsibilities of Chief Engineer Officer

3.13	Safety Management Responsibilities of Second Engineer Officer
Member of the Safety Management Team, Safety, Health and Environmental Committee and belongs to management level.
Reports to	:	The Chief Engineer Officer.
Supervises	:	3rd Engineer Officer, Electrical Officer, junior operation level, ratings of support level.
Responsibilities	:	The 2nd Engineer Officer is the second watch-keeping engineer.
The safety management responsibilities of Second Engineer Officer include, but are not limited to, the following:
Familiarise himself with the procedures of safety management system and comply with same.
Comply with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
Directly responsible to the Chief Engineer Officer for efficient and safe operation and maintenance of all machinery on deck, in the Engine Room.
Watch keeping duties at sea.
To plan, allocate and supervise the work of all Engineers, Electrical Officer and Engine Room crew.
Preparation of work specifications for engine department repairs and dry-docking and supervision of repairs.
To maintain all Engine Room fire fighting and Safety equipment in working condition.
Advise Chief Engineer Officer fully of all details of Engine Room maintenance and operation on a day to day basis.
Maintain cleanliness of all machinery spaces.
To test all controls in engine room/thruster room and steering gear before departure and arrival in port or anchorage.
To carry out the manoeuvring of the main engine, if required.
Indenting, safe-keeping and inventory control of instruments and tools, stores and spares required for use.
To operate various machinery and equipment as per instructions of the spill co-ordinator under SOPEP.
Compliance with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
Carry out emergency duties as per emergency response procedures.
Assist Chief Engineer Officer for preparing reports and returns as per company‘s procedure and maintenance of records.
To comply with applicable rules of STCW Convention/MLC.
To prepare handing over notes along with handing over report while signing off the vessel.
Carry out risk assessment in compliance with SMS.
To acquaint himself and prepare for the rank above.
Has the authority to identify and report non-conformities and near misses/hazardous occurrences, as per procedures defined within this Safety Management System. | 3.13	Safety Management Responsibilities of Second Engineer Officer

3.14	Safety Management Responsibilities of Third/Fourth Engineer Officer

Reports to	:	2nd Engineer Officer.
Chief Engineer Officer when required.
Supervises	:	Junior Operation level & Support level functions
Responsibilities	:	The 3rd/4th Engineer Officer is the second watch-keeping engineer on board and belongs to operation level.
The safety management responsibilities of Third/Fourth Engineer Officer include, but are not limited to, the following:
Familiarise himself with the procedures of safety management system and comply with same.
Watch keeping duties at sea.
Engine Room watches in port.
Carry out repairs and maintenance as instructed by 2nd Engineer Officer in particular of the main engine, aux. engines, purifiers, rescue boat engine, emergency air compressor and all fire extinguishers/fire fighting installations or any other work.
To assist Chief Engineer Officer during bunkering.
To assist 2nd Engineer Officer in his day to day work and in indenting stores/spare parts.
Carry out maintenance for the machineries and equipments as per planned maintenance system as delegated by Chief Engineer Officer and maintain records of maintenance and repairs carried out, and inventory of stores and spares for such machineries and equipments.
Compliance with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
Carry out emergency duties as per emergency response procedures and as directed by command and control.
To assist spill co-ordinator on the scene under SOPEP.
To comply with applicable rules of STCW Convention.
To prepare handing over notes along with handing over report while signing off the vessel.
To acquaint himself and prepare for the rank above.
Has the authority to identify and report non-conformities and near misses/hazardous occurrences, as per procedures defined within this Safety Management System. | 3.14	Safety Management Responsibilities of Third/Fourth Engineer Officer

3.16	Safety Management Responsibilities of Radio Officer (when & if on board)

Reports to	:  Master
Responsibilities :  The Radio Officer belongs to operation level and is in-charge and of ship‘s radio communication centre and is responsible for its proper maintenance and operation.
When Radio Officer is not posted, the duties shall be carried out by any other officer designated by Master.

The safety management responsibilities of Radio Officer include, but are not limited to, the following:
Carry out radio watch keeping duties as per applicable rules and regulations and also Master‘s instructions.
To assist bridge team during manoeuvring operations while mooring/unmooring, approaching installations and during cargo operations as per the Masters instructions
Familiarise himself with the procedures of safety management system and comply with the same.
Ensure ship‘s radio communication centre and all ancillary equipment kept in good working order at all times.
Maintain proper and up-to-date record of all radio communication/GMDSS installations spares, tools, instruments and publications.
Maintain	record	of	all	maintenance	carried	out	radio	communication/GMDSS installations and equipment.
Assist with maintenance and repairs of navigational electronic equipment, distress and life saving appliances such as on the bridge.
Operate and maintain the ship‘s broadcasting system.
Ensure that all messages are approved by the Master before despatch/distribution.
Maintain in good working order all GMDSS equipment.
Maintain and record communications as per instructions of Master under SOPEP and other emergencies.
Compliance with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
To comply with applicable rules of the STCW Convention.
Assist Master with regard to secretarial job.
To prepare handing over notes along with the report while signing off the vessel.
Has the authority to identify and report non-conformities and near misses/hazardous occurrences, as per procedures defined within this Safety Management System. | 3.16	Safety Management Responsibilities of Radio Officer (when & if on board)

3.18	Safety Management Responsibilities of all Shipboard Personnel serving at Support Level (TMEs, TNOCs and Deck, Engine & Catering Crew)

Reports to	:	Master through respective Departmental Heads.
Responsibilities	:
The safety management responsibilities of all shipboard personnel include, but are not limited to, the following:
Familiarise himself with the procedures of Safety Management System and comply with the procedures emphasising on emergency procedures and arrangements on board in accordance with Safety Management System.
Familiarise himself and comply with environment protection procedures, safe operating procedures for machinery/equipment, shipboard operations, emergency response systems and arrangements on board in accordance with safety management system.
Carry out duties with regard to ship‘s operational routine duties as directed by the Management level under the supervision of operation level.
Comply with safe working practices, personnel protective equipment and clothing according to appropriate instructions.
Be able to communicate with other persons on board on elementary safety matters and understand safety information symbols, signs and alarm signals.
Promptly report unsafe machinery, equipment, conditions or operations.
Familiarise himself with and always follow the general safety rules which apply to the particular job and/or ship.
Know what to do if:
A person falls overboard,
Fire or smoke is detected, or
The fire or abandon ship alarm is sounded.
Locate their lifejackets and be able to don it.
Raise the alarm and have basic knowledge of the use of portable fire extinguishers.
Be able to close and open the fire, weathertight and watertight doors fitted on the particular ship other than those for hull openings.
Comply with lawful command.
Comply with applicable rules of the STCW Convention.
Comply with the Company‘s documented safety and security procedures.
Carry out emergency duties as per emergency response procedures.
All shipboard personnel have the authority to identify non-conformities and near miss/ hazardous occurrences, as per procedures defined within the Safety Management System. | 3.18	Safety Management Responsibilities of all Shipboard Personnel serving at Support Level (TMEs, TNOCs and Deck, Engine & Catering Crew)

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Designated Person Ashore | 
Designated Person Ashore (DPA)
Qualification, Duties & Responsibility of DPA
In order to ensure the safe operation of each ship and to provide a link between the Company and those onboard, the Company has appointed a Designated Person Ashore considering the following qualifications required as per MS Notice No.09 of 2014 dated 15.05.2014.
At least two years of shipboard sailing (as Master or Chief Engineer Officer)/shore experience at the management level.
Knowledge and understanding of ISM Code, mandatory rules and regulations, applicable codes, guidelines and standards as appropriate.
Knowledge on assessment, technique of examining, questioning, evaluating and reporting, technical or operational aspects of safety management.
Appropriate knowledge of shipping and shipboard operations.
Experience of participation in at least one marine related management system, audit and effective communication with shipboard staff and senior management and should be able to determine the effectiveness of SMS by using internal audit, management review, assess effectiveness of SMS and able to gather and analyse data from hazardous occurrences, hazardous situations, near misses, incidents and accidents and apply the lessons learnt to improve the SMS within the Company and its ships.

Responsibility and Authority of Designated Person Ashore (DPA)
Member of Safety Review Committee of the Operating Divisions and Management Safety Policy Committee
Reports to: Chairman & Managing Director

Safety Management Responsibility and Authority of DPA
The Designated Person Ashore (DPA) is in charge of the ISM Cell. He monitors the safety, occupational health and pollution prevention aspects of the operation of each ship and ensures that adequate resources and shore-based support are provided for the SMS. He reports all the Occupational Health and Safety related issues to the top management (C&MD) on a regular basis from time to time. Safety Management responsibility and authority of the DPA include, but are not limited to, the following:
Examine and approve all documents related to the SMS.
Examine and approve all revisions to the SMS.
Prepare annual budget for the ISM Cell.
Prepare an annual audit plan for the fleet and the offices ashore.
Verify through regular audits that SMS on board, as well as, ashore function according to documented procedures.
Convene and chair the CSMC meetings every month (except for the month when SRC meeting is conducted).
Analyse and maintain records of non-conformity, accident and near miss/hazardous occurrence reports.
Issue instructions, as necessary, for effective functioning of SMS.
Periodically review and update all safety management instructions sent to the fleet.
Report major non-conformities to the Chairman & Managing Director and ensure appropriate corrective action. | Designated Person Ashore (DPA)

4.1.3    Alternate Designated Person Ashore (ADPA)
Company has appointed Alternate Designated Person Ashore (ADPA) to discharge the functions of DPA in latter‘s absence or in similar emergency situations whose qualifications meet the requirements as per IMO Circular MSC-MEPC.7/Circ.6.

Designated Officer(s) (DO)
The Company has appointed Designated Officer(s) for each Operating Division, who is responsible to monitor the safety and pollution prevention aspect of the office and of each ship in the Division. He is responsible to keep DPA apprised regarding the activities pertaining to SMS.

Responsibility and Authority of Designated Officer(s) (DO)
Member of Management Safety Policy Committee and Safety Review Committee of the concerned division
Reports to: Designated Person Ashore (DPA)

Safety Management Responsibility and Authority of DO
The Designated Officer (DO) assists the DPA to monitor the safety and pollution prevention aspects of the operation of each ship within the Division and ensures that adequate resources and shore-based support are provided. Safety Management responsibility and authority of the DO include, but are not limited to, the following:
Monitor the implementation of the SMS on board ships and in the Division.
Arrange to carry out periodical internal Safety Management System audits on board the ships and liaise with the superintendent and Group I/C to ensure that external audits are carried out in time.
Ensure that ships are provided proper follow up for efficient functioning of the SMS i.e. reports on Accidents, Near Misses, Non-conformities, FSI/PSC inspection deficiencies and risk assessment reviews etc.
Arrange meetings of the SRC within the division, maintain its records.
Report non-conformities and corrective actions taken on ships of the division and at the Division office to the DPA and maintain records.
Report accidents, near misses/hazardous occurrences on ships of the division to the DPA and assist in analysing such reports and maintain records.
Comply with procedures for SMS document control.
Submit periodical reports as desired by C&MD/DPA in respect of ISM implementation onboard vessels.
Assisting DPA towards Company‘s DOC audits and corrective action for the findings.
Note: He shall keep the C&MD/DPA updated on the issues under ISM as and when instructed to do so. | Ensure that essential safety and occupational health issues are communicated to the Management and decisions regarding such issues are communicated back to ships.
Ensure compliance with procedures for SMS document control.
Planning DOC Audits of the Company and maintaining validity of Company‘s DOC.

Master‘s Responsibility | 
Responsibility and Authority of Master
Safety Management Responsibilities and Authority of Master
Member of the Safety Management Team and belongs to Management level. Chairman of the Safety, Health and Environmental Committee on board.
Reports to	:  The Company through the superintendent.
Responsibilities  : The Master is appointed by the Company and acts as its representative in matters related to ship, crew and cargo. He takes on authority and responsibilities as laid down in the Indian Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (as amended) and mandatory rules and regulations, applicable codes, guidelines and standards recommended by the IMO, Administration and other authorized bodies.
The Master has the authority and overall responsibility for the safe operation of the ship, safety of the crew, passengers (on passenger vessels) and protection of the environment at all times.
The safety management responsibilities of Master include, but are not limited to, the following:

implement the Safety, Occupational Health & Environment Protection Policy of the Company;
motivate the crew in the observation of that policy;
issue appropriate orders and instructions in a clear and simple manner;
Verify from time to time during his contract on board that the requirements of SMS are being fulfilled on board the vessel which could be an informal review of records of the Chief Officer and Chief engineer to see if the SMS system is being followed by the departments.
review the SMS and report its deficiencies to the Company Once at least in 12 months or if the master has served on board for more than 90 days once during his Contract period;

In addition the following but not limited shall be his responsibility
familiarize himself with the procedures of safety management system and comply with same
ensure that the ship is fully equipped, well maintained and in all respects seaworthy and cargo worthy;
ensure that the ship‘s Officers and crew are trained and made familiar with the safety requirements and environmental protection policy with a view of achieving higher productivity.
conduct appraisal of Officers and crew;
ensure that procedures and instructions regarding the SMS and internal audits are implemented;
prepare watch keeping schedule for sea and port watches establishing rest period for watch keeping personnel;
comply with applicable rules of STCW Convention. | Responsibility and Authority of Master

Master shall ensure that the following functions are conducted safely and professionally, in accordance with the standard operating procedures of the Company:
navigation and machinery operation;
deck operations
loading, including serving of relevant notices and signing of cargo documents;
unloading;
dry docking and repairs,
ballasting/de ballasting;
bunkering;
tank /Hold cleaning;
port departure, readiness for sea.
serving note of protest as required.
communication and reporting to shore offices as per Company‘s procedure.
Master along with Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that sufficient time and resources are allocated to execute the following activities effectively:
maintenance and repairs of ship, machinery and equipment, an adequate stock of essential stores and spare parts;
maintenance of classification and statutory certificates;
safety training and drills, including handling of dangerous cargo;
separation, segregation and proper discharging of waste such as sediments, slop, garbage and sludge; and
maintenance of health, welfare, hygiene and housekeeping on board; and
close attention for the economical and commercial operation of the ship to safeguard the interest of the Company, charterer, cargo interest and other concerned parties connected with the ship‘s business.

5.2	Master‘s Over-riding Authority
The Master is empowered in all situations with overriding authority to act decisively and according to his best judgment to prevent injury to crewmembers and other persons; protect the vessel and other vessels or property from damage; and prevent pollution from the vessel.
The Master may request assistance from any person of The Company any time in order to fulfill these responsibilities.

This overriding authority has been incorporated in the ISM code by IMO resolution A443
(XI) that deals with the decision of the shipmaster with regards to maritime safety and maritime environment protection. | carry out routine inspection of the ship in accordance with the verification procedures of SMS; and

Master‖ discretion for Ships safety & security has been incorporated in SOLAS Chapter XI- 2 Regulation 8 and same shall be used by Master when required.

5.3	Master‘s Decision Authority
Further to stated above under SOLAS chapter V regulation 34-1 Master‘s Discretion Authority is defined as under:

The owner, the charterer, the company operating the ship as defined in regulation IX/1, or any other person shall not prevent or restrict the master of the ship from taking or executing any decision which, in the master‘s professional judgment, is necessary for safety of life at sea and protection of the marine environment. | Master‖ discretion for Ships safety & security has been incorporated in SOLAS Chapter XI- 2 Regulation 8 and same shall be used by Master when required.

5.3	Master‘s Decision Authority
Further to stated above under SOLAS chapter V regulation 34-1 Master‘s Discretion Authority is defined as under:

The owner, the charterer, the company operating the ship as defined in regulation IX/1, or any other person shall not prevent or restrict the master of the ship from taking or executing any decision which, in the master‘s professional judgment, is necessary for safety of life at sea and protection of the marine environment. | Master‖ discretion for Ships safety & security has been incorporated in SOLAS Chapter XI- 2 Regulation 8 and same shall be used by Master when required.

5.3	Master‘s Decision Authority
Further to stated above under SOLAS chapter V regulation 34-1 Master‘s Discretion Authority is defined as under:

The owner, the charterer, the company operating the ship as defined in regulation IX/1, or any other person shall not prevent or restrict the master of the ship from taking or executing any decision which, in the master‘s professional judgment, is necessary for safety of life at sea and protection of the marine environment.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Resource & Personnel | 
Personnel

Manning Requirements
Company shall ensure that each ship is —
manned with qualified, certified and medically fit seafarers in accordance with national and international requirements, and
appropriately manned in order to encompass all aspects of maintaining safe operations onboard (refer to the principles of Minimum safe manning adopted by the IMO by Resolution A.1047(27).

Company also uses its discretion to have additional manning to suit the operational requirements. Also, to comply with the safe manning requirements on some offshore vessels, additional hands are posted on the vessel when the vessels are proceeding from one coast to another as per the requirement of the Operator.
Relevant documents and data pertaining to all floating staff personnel engaged on the vessels are maintained by Fleet Personnel Department.
Master shall ensure that all joining personnel assigned with shipboard duties hold appropriate certificates, as required by the STCW Convention, proving their qualification and medical fitness. The Master shall not sign on an officer or crew member who is not certified as per the STCW convention and relevant DGS/Flag Administration circulars nor shall he release the outgoing officer until remedial action has been taken in consultation with the head office. These certificates shall be kept in custody of the Master on board and presented to the authorities during inspections on demand. These certificates shall be handed over back to the respective personnel when they are signed off from the vessel.
In the offshore industry, all the ratings are generally referred to as ‗OSV Seamen‘. As per the requirement, the OSV Seamen are posted as Deck Ratings or as Engine Ratings. Additionally, OSV Seamen holding watchkeeping certificates are posted and form part of the Bridge or Engine Room watchkeeping team, to meet the safe manning requirements.

Familiarisation and Training
The Company has established various methods of familiarisation to ensure that new personnel assigned or transferred on board for duties are given proper familiarisation with their duties. The Company adopts the means of familiarisation from the following methods, which suit the circumstances and conditions and as far as practicable to comply with the requirements of ISM Code and STCW Convention:

For Officers
Briefing with respect to SMS and operational functions in particular senior officers‘ prior joining.
Familiarisation course on ISM-STCW, in particular senior officers.
Rotating personnel on similar type of vessels.
Induction familiarisation on the ship after joining, its specific equipment as documented under Shipboard SMS Manual section – Ship Operations.
Safety Familiarisation upon joining as documented under section ‗Safety & Security‘. | Personnel

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Resource & Personnel | 
For Crew
Allow a brief hand-over discussion and rounds on board between crew joining and leaving ships.
Induction familiarisation after joining ship, its specific equipment as documented under section – Ship Operations.
Safety Familiarisation upon joining as documented under section ‗Safety & Security‘.
Master shall ensure that all newly employed personnel on board are given reasonable opportunity to become familiar with the shipboard equipment, operating procedures and other arrangements needed for the proper performance of their duties, before being assigned to those duties. It is recommended that whenever conditions permit, Master should train Chief Officer and other navigating officers in practical ship-handling.

Officers and crew members have responsibility for ensuring that the obligations set out in STCW are given full effect and that such other measure taken to ensure that each individual makes a knowledgeable and informed contribution to the safe operation of the ship.

Familiarisation and basic safety training
Company ensures that all persons employed or engaged in any capacity on ships other than passengers, receive approved shore based basic safety training, which complies with the relevant provisions of STCW as applicable:
Personal Survival Techniques (or advanced training as applicable)
Fire Prevention and Fire Fighting (or advanced training as applicable)
Elementary First Aid (or advanced training as applicable)
Personal Safety and Social Responsibilities
STSDSD (Security training for seafarers with Designated Security Duties)
The ratings, forming part of navigational and engineering watch, have required training for carrying out watch specific duties and comply with the provisions of the STCW Convention.

Special Training Requirements for Personnel on Certain Types of Ships
To meet Operator‘s requirements, the seafarers are given additional training, such as Hydrogen Sulphide Evacuation training on certain types of offshore vessels, Dynamic Positioning training course for Masters/Chief Officers on vessels fitted with D.P. System.

6.3	Safety & Task/Job Familiarisation on Board Safety Familiarisation
This is carried out for all personnel joining vessels for assigned duties. A model checklist [Form: SS006(OS)] is included in this section to assist the Master to ensure that all personnel receive adequate familiarisation upon joining and while on board.
The Safety Familiarisation is done in two parts. Upon joining every individual is given the familiarisation on basic safety requirements. Then, within seven days, the individual is made familiar with the various safety equipment on board, as appropriate. The Chief Engineer Officer and Chief Officer supervise such familiarisation programmes as designated Safety Officers on board. Records of all such safety familiarisations are maintained on board. | For Crew

To meet Operator‘s requirements, the seafarers are given additional training, such as Hydrogen Sulphide Evacuation training on certain types of offshore vessels, Dynamic Positioning training course for Masters/Chief Officers on vessels fitted with D.P. System.

6.3	Safety & Task/Job Familiarisation on Board Safety Familiarisation
This is carried out for all personnel joining vessels for assigned duties. A model checklist [Form: SS006(OS)] is included in this section to assist the Master to ensure that all personnel receive adequate familiarisation upon joining and while on board.
The Safety Familiarisation is done in two parts. Upon joining every individual is given the familiarisation on basic safety requirements. Then, within seven days, the individual is made familiar with the various safety equipment on board, as appropriate. The Chief Engineer Officer and Chief Officer supervise such familiarisation programmes as designated Safety Officers on board. Records of all such safety familiarisations are maintained on board.

Safety Familiarisation emphasises upon:
Communication with other persons on board on safety matters and understand safety information symbols, signs and alarm signals
Know what to do if:
a person falls overboard
fire or smoke detected, or
fire or abandon ship alarm is sounded
identify muster and embarkation stations and emergency escape routes
locate and don life jackets
raise the alarm and have basic knowledge of the use of portable fire extinguishers
take immediate action upon encountering an accident or other medical emergency before seeking further medical assistance on board
close and open the fire dampers, vent flaps, weathertight and watertight doors fitted in the particular ship other than those for hull openings.
Familiarization with procedures involving helicopter/ship operations.
familiarisation with the relevant procedures of Company‘s SMS.

Task/Job Familiarisation
This familiarisation is provided to assist enjoining personnel to familiarise themselves with all procedures and equipment relating to their areas of responsibilities. Master ensures that all crewmembers take full advantage of every opportunity provided to become familiar with the shipboard equipment, operating procedures and other arrangements needed for the proper performance of their duties. Immediately upon arriving on board for the first time, each seafarer has the responsibility to become acquainted with the ship‘s working environment, particularly with respect to new or unfamiliar equipment, procedures or arrangements. Procedure for Task/Job Familiarisation, along with model checklist (Form: SO001), is included herein for guidance and appropriate use in enforcing the procedure. Chief Engineer Officer and Chief Officer shall supervise the familiarisation procedures for Engine and Deck/ catering personnel, respectively. Records of all such Task/Job Familiarisation are maintained on board.
For crew members the shipboard task/job familiarisation normally consists of:
visit the spaces in which their primary duties will be performed
get acquainted with the location, controls and display features of equipment they will be operating or using
activate the equipment when possible and perform functions using the controls on the equipment (as appropriate)
observe and ask questions of someone, who is already familiar with the equipment, procedures and other arrangements and
providing for a suitable period of supervision when there is any doubt that a newly employed seafarer is unfamiliar with the shipboard equipment, operating procedures and other arrangements needed for the proper performance of his or her duties.

This familiarisation is given as soon as practicable upon joining, or during handing over process but not later than seven days. Period may be extended by the Master, if required to do so; however, it should not exceed one month after joining. | Safety Familiarisation emphasises upon:

Training Assessment Record (TAR) Book for Trainee Officers
Company also provides training to TNOC and TME for obtaining Certificate of Competency, as officer in charge of navigational watch or engineering watch, in accordance with the provision of the STCW Convention, approved by the Administration. The training programme ensures:
That during the required period of seagoing service, the Trainee Officer receives systematic practical training in the tasks, duties and responsibilities of an officer in charge of navigational or engineering watch.
Close supervision and monitoring by qualified officers such as Chief Engineer Officer, Chief Officer aboard the ships, in which the approved seagoing service is performed.
Adequate documentation in the Training Assessment Record book held by the concerned Trainee Officers.

Carriage of Transit Passengers, Charterer‘s Representatives & Repair Squads
Supernumeraries such as transit passengers, charterer‘s representatives and service engineers of manufacturer of ship specific machinery/equipment, upon their joining, are required to be imparted elementary safety familiarisation by the safety officer. This elementary safety familiarisation training shall include, but not be limited to, the following:
Fire/Emergency/Abandon Ship alarms, safety signs and signals
Their emergency muster stations and routes to such stations
Location and donning of lifejackets
Other supernumeraries, such as generic repair personnel/squads etc., are required to undergo following basic familiarization courses as per Paragraph 1 of Section A-VI/1 of the STCW Code and should be in possession of valid certificates, prior joining the ship:
Personal Survival Techniques
Fire Prevention and Fire Fighting
Elementary First Aid
Personal Safety & Social Responsibility

Section ‗A‘ of Form: SS006(OS) shall be used, as applicable for Safety Familiarisation. Master shall ensure that the total number of individuals (souls) onboard the vessel does not exceed (a) LSA capacity and (b) certified accommodation. Names, age and passport numbers of supernumeraries shall be recorded in the ship‘s ‗Crew List‘ (IMO Crew List — Form: PER006).

6.7	Handing Over/Taking Over Procedure, Change of Officers
Whenever Master, Chief Engineer Officer and other officers are being disengaged from the ship, the outgoing personnel shall prepare an appropriate report, including filling up of prescribed forms (included under this section), as documented by the Company‘s procedure. The handing over report and notes shall include the details of all ship‘s equipment, stores, spares, tools and instruments, publications, files/records, documents, drawings, manuals for which he was responsible. The note may contain pertinent details of the assigned duties, ship specific problems encountered during service on board, major repairs, surveys, etc. and information, which will assist the incoming officer in the performance of such duties.
As far as practicable, no officer should leave the ship until the relieving officer has been made duly familiarised by the outgoing officer. The departmental heads shall verify that the handing over reports and notes are having correct information.

In cases of emergency, an officer may have to leave the ship without reliever, which will only be effected as deemed by the Company, in consultation with the vessel. In such cases the outgoing officer shall prepare such reports and notes and hand over to the departmental head or to the responsible officer authorised to do so.

The outgoing officer, when time permits, shall take a round of the workplace along with the relieving officer and familiarise him. The recommended checklist can be used for such procedure, under the supervision of the departmental heads and verified by the Master. | Carriage of Transit Passengers, Charterer‘s Representatives & Repair Squads
