Working Language
Effective communication on board a ship is of paramount importance to ensure safety of the ship and ship‘s personnel. Shipboard personnel are expected to understand and relay commonly used terminology and orders, especially during operations such as conning, mooring, watch-keeping, emergency stations, etc. In compliance with Chapter V of SOLAS, as amended, the Company has established English as working language for use on board ships, owned, as well as, operated by the Company. Master shall make following entry on the instruction page of the Deck Log Book, as required by SOLAS regulation:
―The Company has established English as a working language on board‖.
On Board Communication Phrases – IMO resolution A.918(22)
IMO Standard Marine Communication Phrases (IMO-SMCP) has been compiled:
to assist in the greater safety of navigation and of the conduct of the ship
to standardise the language used in communication for navigation at sea, in port approaches, waterways and harbours and on board vessels with multilingual crews
A copy of IMO-SMCP has been provided to the ship. Its usage is recommended and it should be available on the Bridge for use.
6.9	Standards Regarding Watch keeping — Hours of Rest
As per STCW Code Ch. VIII Section A-VIII/1(2)/MLC 2006 —
Rest Hours for all personnel on board to be maintained and recorded.
All seafarers on board shall be provided a minimum of 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period.
The hours of rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours. The Interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.
The requirements for rest periods laid down in above paragraphs need not be maintained in the case of an emergency or drill or in other overriding operational conditions.
Musters, fire-fighting and lifeboat drills, and drills prescribed by national laws and regulations and by international instruments, shall be conducted in a manner that minimizes the disturbance of rest periods and does not induce fatigue.
Notwithstanding the above provisions, the minimum period of ten hours may be reduced to not less than 6 consecutive hours provided that any such reduction shall not extend beyond two days and not less than 77 hours of rest are provided each seven-day period.
Time spent for drills and time spend by engineers attending UMS alarms to be recorded as working hours.
Any deviation from rest hours to be reported to office through SHEC and Master/Seafarer shall suitably be compensated by giving additional rest.
Master shall request company for additional man power in case of projected non- compliance of Rest hours due to trading pattern, dry-docking etc.
Fatigue
The management and operational level personnel onboard the ship should be aware of the factors that can contribute to fatigue and accordingly take appropriate measures to reduce the potential for fatigue when planning and managing the activities and working times of ship‘s personnel. The most effective means of preventing fatigue is to ensure compliance with seafarers‘ hours of rest regulations.
Records of hours of work/rest of seafarer (Form: PER005) shall be maintained on board. | Working Language

Drug and Alcohol Policy & Procedures
Drug and Alcohol Policy
The Company shall maintain safeguards against drug and alcohol abuse on board its ships as a part of its commitment to the health and welfare of its employees, operational safety and the environment.

Responsibilities/Implementation of Policy
Master shall be responsible to ensure that the Company‘s Drug & Alcohol Policy and Procedures are understood and complied with by all personnel on board.
Each individual is responsible to ensure that he is at all times in full compliance with the requirements of the Company‘s Drug Policy.

Drug and Alcohol Procedures
Drug and Alcohol Abuse
Drug and Alcohol abuse can be defined as the intermittent or continual use of drugs and/or alcohol which causes harm to the employees‘ health and/or work performance, affecting efficiency, productivity, safety, attendance or behaviour at work. If these problems are not treated on observing the symptoms at the initial stages, progressive physical and social deterioration takes place accompanied by mental disturbance that can lead to premature death. Drug abuse can additionally be defined as the deliberate use of illegal drugs for the purpose of intoxication or for any reason other than a genuine medical one, which affects a person‘s work performance.
Offshore regulations do not permit carriage/storage of alcohol on board any offshore vessel. Accordingly, people joining offshore vessels either through ONGC helibase or through ONGC Nhava base have to pass through strict security check. Hence carriage of alcohol on offshore vessel is nil and consequently alcohol abuse, which can be defined as the intermittent or continual use of alcohol causing detriment to the employee‘s health and/or work performance, does not happen on any offshore vessel. Moreover, Master shall use breath analyser for random alcohol test on board and maintain records towards compliance of Alcohol Policy.

Impact of Drug Abuse
Abuse of drug on board the ship has a serious adverse impact on the health and safety of the personnel on board. It impairs job performance, particularly the safe operation of ships and the ability of individual(s) to respond at any time to any emergency situation leading to accidents. Further, drug abuse by any person on board can lead not only to his prosecution involving severe penalty but also can lead to confiscation of the ship and severe penalties on the shipowner in many countries. The Company recognises the need to combat drug abuse on board ships.

Drug Testing
The Company recognises the contentious nature of drug testing and the various procedures involved therein and do not feel that shipboard personnel are sufficiently trained to carry out such testing. The Company, therefore, does not intend to arrange for drug testing to be carried out by shipboard personnel. | Drug and Alcohol Policy & Procedures
Drug and Alcohol Policy
The Company shall maintain safeguards against drug and alcohol abuse on board its ships as a part of its commitment to the health and welfare of its employees, operational safety and the environment.

Responsibilities/Implementation of Policy
Master shall be responsible to ensure that the Company‘s Drug & Alcohol Policy and Procedures are understood and complied with by all personnel on board.
Each individual is responsible to ensure that he is at all times in full compliance with the requirements of the Company‘s Drug Policy.

Drug and Alcohol Procedures
Drug and Alcohol Abuse
Drug and Alcohol abuse can be defined as the intermittent or continual use of drugs and/or alcohol which causes harm to the employees‘ health and/or work performance, affecting efficiency, productivity, safety, attendance or behaviour at work. If these problems are not treated on observing the symptoms at the initial stages, progressive physical and social deterioration takes place accompanied by mental disturbance that can lead to premature death. Drug abuse can additionally be defined as the deliberate use of illegal drugs for the purpose of intoxication or for any reason other than a genuine medical one, which affects a person‘s work performance.
Offshore regulations do not permit carriage/storage of alcohol on board any offshore vessel. Accordingly, people joining offshore vessels either through ONGC helibase or through ONGC Nhava base have to pass through strict security check. Hence carriage of alcohol on offshore vessel is nil and consequently alcohol abuse, which can be defined as the intermittent or continual use of alcohol causing detriment to the employee‘s health and/or work performance, does not happen on any offshore vessel. Moreover, Master shall use breath analyser for random alcohol test on board and maintain records towards compliance of Alcohol Policy.

Impact of Drug Abuse
Abuse of drug on board the ship has a serious adverse impact on the health and safety of the personnel on board. It impairs job performance, particularly the safe operation of ships and the ability of individual(s) to respond at any time to any emergency situation leading to accidents. Further, drug abuse by any person on board can lead not only to his prosecution involving severe penalty but also can lead to confiscation of the ship and severe penalties on the shipowner in many countries. The Company recognises the need to combat drug abuse on board ships.

Drug Testing
The Company recognises the contentious nature of drug testing and the various procedures involved therein and do not feel that shipboard personnel are sufficiently trained to carry out such testing. The Company, therefore, does not intend to arrange for drug testing to be carried out by shipboard personnel. | Drug and Alcohol Policy & Procedures

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Resource & Personnel | 
Medical Examination
All shipboard personnel shall be required to undergo the medical examination by the Administration approved Medical Officer prior joining the vessel.
As per STCW, the medical examination report is valid for two years for ship‘s crew up to 40 years of age and one year for the crew above 40 years of age.
Master may also request any shipboard personnel to undergo a renewed medical examination when he considers that there are valid reasons for this to be done. During medical examination, the Company Medical Officer shall arrange for a test to be carried out for the drug and alcohol abuse.

Permitted Drugs carried on board
Most vessels today carry medical supplies for treatment of illness during a voyage as well as
‗Emergency‘ lifeboat medical stores. Vessels within territorial waters are subject to the provisions of the appropriate national legislation and any regulations relating to storage and supply of listed drugs will need to be observed. These are generally common rules based on international agreement.

Each vessel shall provide a list, with quantities, of all controlled drugs (e.g. morphine sulphate, diazepam, Phenobarbital tablets etc.) to the boarding customs officer together with the ship‘s report on arrival at the port where required. Provided the quantities being carried are for ship‘s medical use, no licence will generally be required.

Instructions to Ship‘s Staff
It is the joint responsibility of shipboard personnel to comply with the Company‘s Drug and Alcohol Policy and Procedures. Non-compliance of the Drug & Alcohol Policy and Procedures by the ship staff shall be viewed as an offence and dealt with by the Master in accordance with the Merchant Shipping Act. Master shall have the authority to sign off anyone found to have violated the Company‘s Drug & Alcohol Policy and Procedures. The matter shall be promptly reported by the Master to Fleet Personnel Department, operating division and ISM Cell. | Medical Examination

Shipboard Operations | 
Shipboard Operations

Key Shipboard Operations
This section provides procedures for the preparation of plans and instructions including checklists for Key Shipboard Operations concerning safety of ship, protection of environment and safety of personnel.

Definitions
Key Shipboard Operations are Special Shipboard Operations and Critical Shipboard Operations.
Special Shipboard Operations are those where errors may become apparent only after they have created hazardous situations or when accidents have occurred.

Critical Shipboard Operations are those where an error may immediately cause an accident or a situation which could threaten people, the environment or the ship.

Development of plans and instructions including checklists for Key Shipboard Operations
In order to develop plans for Key Shipboard Operations, the Company undertakes the following activities:
The DPA convenes meetings of a group generally comprising of Department Heads/Group Incharge, DOs and technical personnel responsible for the Company‘s Safety Management System. Key shipboard operations are identified in these meetings taking into account the following:
review results;
relevant international and national rules and regulations;
industry guidelines;
accident/casualty reports;
existing Company fleet circulars (Guidelines and Case-Studies);
various ship inspection and audit reports;
various performance reports from vessels of the fleet;
operational experience.
Protection of the environment
Safety of personnel
These personnel, who are responsible for the Company‘s Safety Management System, shall ensure that plans and instructions including checklists for Key Shipboard Operations, concerning safety of ship, protection of environment and safety of personnel are prepared in accordance with the method described under section ‗Documentation‘ of the Shipboard SMS Manual. These plans and instructions, including checklists for Key Shipboard Operations, form Section 7 — Ship Operations, of the Shipboard SMS Manual.

Section 7 — Ship Operations of the Shipboard SMS Manual contains the following ship- specific sub-sections, as applicable: | Shipboard Operations

and/or
there is a need for corrections/amendments to Section 7 — Ship Operations of the Shipboard SMS manual.

Shipboard Operations | 
During Master‘s review and verification of the Shipboard Safety Management System, the Master shall consult and examine carefully with the Safety Management Team on board and establish whether:
there is a need for inclusion of procedures for any newly identified Key Shipboard Operations in Section 7 — Ship Operations of the Shipboard SMS Manual;
and/or
there is a need for corrections/amendments to Section 7 — Ship Operations of the Shipboard SMS Manual.
In case addition/amendment/correction to Section 7 — Ship Operations of the Shipboard SMS manual is deemed necessary to be effected immediately related to ship-specific procedure, the Master or the Chief Engineer Officer may develop the same upon discussion in the Safety Management Team Meeting. The procedure to be documented and effected immediately on board in case it is required to do so for safe key shipboard operations. The Master shall send such procedure to the Group In-charge, Superintendent and DO for further review and necessary amendments, if any and for records. These ship-specific procedures may be further effected after being vetted and agreed by the Group In-charge and Superintendent under temporary instructions from DO, in consultation with DPA, or by DPA himself as required. However, these temporary instructions and procedures will be reviewed in accordance with the Company‘s review procedures and necessary inclusion or exclusion will be carried out in the Safety Management System manuals. The DPA shall issue the correction/amendments in the manner as described under section ‗Documentation‘ and as per his authority.

Shipboard suggestions and feedback can also form a part of Master‘s Verification and Review report.

All temporary instructions related to SMS, issued as described above, are to be placed along with the records of Verification and Review maintained on board and in the respective division.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Navigation

General Introduction
Attention of Master and officers in-charge of the navigational watch is drawn to the STCW and the STCW Code, regarding regulations, standards and guidance on watchkeeping.
Master and officers in-charge of the navigational watch shall at all times comply with regulations and standards contained in the STCW and STCW Code Part A.
Master and officers in-charge of the navigational watch shall take guidance on watchkeeping from STCW Code Part B.
Navigational watchkeeping procedures provided in this section shall be read and complied in conjunction with regulations, standards and guidelines provided in the following publications:
Collision regulations, (as amended)
SOLAS (as amended)
STCW (as amended)
Bridge Procedures Guide
These procedures shall also be read and complied in conjunction with the instructions contained in:
Company's Fleet Circulars (Guidelines)
Deck Logbook
Master's Night Order Book
Bridge/ER Movement Book
The objective of these procedures is SAFETY of:
life
environment
vessel and
cargo and third party property.
These procedures:
intend to establish the basic standards of ship operations on board all vessels of the Company;
are to remain the basis on which the watch keeping officer and the Master will take decisions relating to navigation;
are in no way meant to restrict or constrain the Master or watch keeping officer's authority or contradict International, National or local regulations;
shall be supplemented by the Master's Standing Orders, Night Orders and other instruction pertaining to specific navigational situations, in the Master's Bridge/Night Order Book.
Master‘s Standing Orders should be read by all officers as soon as they join the vessel and signed accordingly. A copy of the orders should be available on the Bridge for reference. | Navigation

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Master‘s Standing Orders
Master‘s standing orders shall include, but not be limited to, the matters such as:
calling the Master;
reducing speed in the event of restricted visibility or other circumstances (distances shall be specified);
making landfall/port;
posting lookouts;
manning the wheel;
the use and correction of charts;
the use of echo sounder, radar and other navigational aids;
an established drill for changing over from automatic to manual steering;
provision of additional watchkeeping personnel in special circumstances, e.g. heavy traffic, narrow passages or restricted visibility;
the need for checking information in order to reduce to a minimum the risk of 'one- man' errors;
radio communications;
boarding/disembarking arrangements for pilots.
Navigational warnings shall be received throughout the sea passage and while the vessel is at anchor. On vessels with a Radio Officer, the Radio Officer shall be responsible for taking navigational warnings at least 24 hours in advance prior entering an area.
Long range navigational warnings shall be taken regularly by the officer performing radio duties. Navtex reports shall be monitored and filed.
The Master shall ensure that the requirements in terms of frequency of position fixing, safety precautions, monitoring of pilot instructions and other navigational demands are fully understood by officers in charge of the navigational watch and they shall be fully listed in the Master's bridge/night order book. It is suggested that while navigating in congested waters vessel's position be fixed every 15 minutes (more frequently, if deemed necessary).
The officer in charge of the navigational watch at noon shall ensure that the daily tests and checks listed in Form: NAV003 are conducted.
Masters and officers in charge of the navigational watch are reminded of the obligation under SOLAS Chapter V to participate in vessel reporting systems, where applicable.
All vessels should, as far as possible, send voluntary weather observation reports. Vessels chosen to participate in voluntary IMD Weather Reporting system shall forward weather reports as required.
During his watch, each officer in charge of the navigational watch shall comply with Form: NAV007 or Form: NAV008, as appropriate.
The officer in charge of the navigational watch shall continue to be responsible for the navigational watch, despite the presence of the Master on the bridge, unless the Master specifically takes over. Whenever the Master takes over navigational watch, he shall clearly inform the officer in charge of the navigational watch.
Though the Master is overall responsible, officers in charge of the navigational watch are, as a team, responsible for the continued safe navigation of the vessel. Any attempt at risky navigation is to be abhorred and shall be avoided. The usage of the four 'Ls' viz. Lead, Log, Lookout & Latitude shall not to be neglected. | Master‘s Standing Orders

calling the Master;
reducing speed in the event of restricted visibility or other circumstances (distances shall be specified);
making landfall/port;
posting lookouts;
manning the wheel;
the use and correction of charts;
the use of echo sounder, radar and other navigational aids;

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Guidance to prevent distraction on bridge
To prevent distraction on bridge during navigation, the master shall ensure that —
Use of mobile phones is prohibited on bridge when navigation requirements demand the utmost focus of the Bridge team for safe navigation.
Use of satellite phone by shipstaff/visitors shall be restricted during pilotage, Narrow Channel, restricted visibility, high traffic density or navigational requirements demand the utmost focus of the bridge team.
Wheel house shall remain out of bounds for all unauthorised persons, viz. Agents, cargo representatives, suppliers, officers‘ family, contractors and off duty personnel.
Any noise (any sound disturbance above 40 db) is prohibited in or near wheelhouse when the vessel is underway.

Checklists
Generic checklists have been provided in this section to aid safe and efficient navigation of the vessel. Master shall ensure that various checks, as detailed in these checklists (as applicable to specific ship type), are carried out and verified while conducting respective operations. After satisfactory compliance of the checklist, proper entry shall be made in the Deck Log Book, confirming that the applicable actions in the checklist for a particular operation are complied with.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Bridge Procedures
Attention of Master and navigating officers is drawn to the contents of ‗Bridge Procedures Guide – ICS‘, as amended with respect to safe bridge resource management.

Bridge Organisation
The Master shall regulate the watch arrangement to suit the service of the vessel and any special circumstances of the case and eliminate the risk that an error on the part of one person could pose to the ship. Special emphasis has to be put on the necessity of maintaining lookouts and carrying out collision avoidance routines.
Whilst at sea, normally, the conventional watch system at sea shall be followed on board. This consists of six four-hour watches in a day.
The officer in-charge of the navigational watch:
is directly responsible to the Master for the safe navigation of the ship;
shall be assisted by a seaman/helmsman during each watch;
shall not leave the bridge until relieved by another navigating officer or the Master of the vessel.
shall use all means of establishing ship‘s position, so that in case one method becomes unreliable, others are immediately available.
ensure that all instrument errors are known and correctly applied.
The Master may increase number of persons in each navigational watch, taking into account:
weather conditions, visibility;
dense traffic areas;
proximity of navigational hazards;
operational condition of navigational aids;
whether automatic steering is available;
whether radio duties are to be performed;
Master is responsible to ensure that newly-joined officers, who are to undertake duties of the officer in-charge of navigational watch, make themselves thoroughly familiar with standing orders and any other directives before taking over watch and that they know how to set up and operate all appropriate bridge equipment. Form: NAV001 shall be used when familiarising with bridge equipment. Soon on joining the vessel, Master may hold briefing/debriefing meetings with the navigating officers in order to overcome any communication gap or understanding of the laid down standing instructions.
All navigational charts and publications for the intended voyage and for possible ports of refuge on the passage shall be on board and corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners (relevant authorities) available on board.
Admiralty List of Radio Signals shall be corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners (relevant authorities) available on board by the Radio Officer or a navigating officer assigned such duties by the Master.
Admiralty List of Lights shall be corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners (relevant authorities) available on board by navigating officer assigned such duties by the Master.
All other navigational charts and publications shall be corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners (relevant authorities) available on board by the navigating officer assigned such duties by the Master.
Note: Wherever charts issued by national authorities are required to be carried and used, the charts should be corrected to the latest notices of the authorities. | Bridge Procedures

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Taking over the navigational watch
The relieving officer in-charge of the navigational watch shall use the checklist provided in Form: NAV002 and Form: NAV020 (if applicable); when taking over a navigational watch.
Lookout
The importance of maintaining proper lookout and posting additional lookouts cannot be over emphasised. To ensure the effectiveness of the navigational watch and prevent potential dangerous close quarter situations, it is recommended that the Master should make rounds of the Bridge especially when the officer of the watch is new, during change of watch, during major course alterations and when navigating during periods of heavy weather/restricted visibility, in areas of coastal waters/traffic convergence and dense traffic areas.
The relevant regulation from COLREGs (Rule 5) states:
Quote
Every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing, as well as by all available means appropriate in the prevailing circumstances and conditions, so as to make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.
Unquote
While interpreting the COLREG, following should be taken into consideration:
The phrase ‗at all times‘ includes while vessel is at anchor
Lookout by Sight
The lookout should be able to give full attention and should not be tasked with any other duties which could interfere with lookout duties
Lookout duties and Helmsman duties are separate.
By Hearing
Lookout personnel to be stationed outside the wheel house and bridge doors to be kept open
All noisy work on board be stopped during poor visibility (heavy rainfall etc.) so that the officer of the watch/look out would be able to hear other vessel‘s sound signals
By all available means
This would include use of —
Radar – Properly functional radar must be utilised, particularly during restricted visibility. Whether keeping a lookout by radar or not, visual lookout must be maintained.
Binoculars – these must be used. There have been instances where during formal investigations, ship‘s officers have been faulted for not using binoculars in instances of collisions.
Listening watch on VHF – the warnings or intentions must be given consideration to make a full appraisal of the situation. However, while doing so, use of VHF for collision avoidance can be dangerous, if —
identification of vessels is not positive
too much time is spent in communicating with other ship instead of taking action
action agreed by the concerned ships is contrary to COLREGS
Undue communication pertaining to other operational activities need not get routed through the bridge in order to provide an undisturbed atmosphere required for safe navigation. The Master shall apprise the ship‘s personnel regarding above requirement. | Taking over the navigational watch

Binoculars – these must be used. There have been instances where during formal investigations, ship‘s officers have been faulted for not using binoculars in instances of collisions.
Listening watch on VHF – the warnings or intentions must be given consideration to make a full appraisal of the situation. However, while doing so, use of VHF for collision avoidance can be dangerous, if —
identification of vessels is not positive
too much time is spent in communicating with other ship instead of taking action
action agreed by the concerned ships is contrary to COLREGS
Undue communication pertaining to other operational activities need not get routed through the bridge in order to provide an undisturbed atmosphere required for safe navigation. The Master shall apprise the ship‘s personnel regarding above requirement. | Taking over the navigational watch
The relieving officer in-charge of the navigational watch shall use the checklist provided in Form: NAV002 and Form: NAV020 (if applicable); when taking over a navigational watch.
Lookout
The importance of maintaining proper lookout and posting additional lookouts cannot be over emphasised. To ensure the effectiveness of the navigational watch and prevent potential dangerous close quarter situations, it is recommended that the Master should make rounds of the Bridge especially when the officer of the watch is new, during change of watch, during major course alterations and when navigating during periods of heavy weather/restricted visibility, in areas of coastal waters/traffic convergence and dense traffic areas.
The relevant regulation from COLREGs (Rule 5) states:
Quote
Every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing, as well as by all available means appropriate in the prevailing circumstances and conditions, so as to make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.
Unquote
While interpreting the COLREG, following should be taken into consideration:
The phrase ‗at all times‘ includes while vessel is at anchor
Lookout by Sight
The lookout should be able to give full attention and should not be tasked with any other duties which could interfere with lookout duties
Lookout duties and Helmsman duties are separate.
By Hearing
Lookout personnel to be stationed outside the wheel house and bridge doors to be kept open
All noisy work on board be stopped during poor visibility (heavy rainfall etc.) so that the officer of the watch/look out would be able to hear other vessel‘s sound signals
By all available means
This would include use of —
Radar – Properly functional radar must be utilised, particularly during restricted visibility. Whether keeping a lookout by radar or not, visual lookout must be maintained.
Binoculars – these must be used. There have been instances where during formal investigations, ship‘s officers have been faulted for not using binoculars in instances of collisions.
Listening watch on VHF – the warnings or intentions must be given consideration to make a full appraisal of the situation. However, while doing so, use of VHF for collision avoidance can be dangerous, if —
identification of vessels is not positive
too much time is spent in communicating with other ship instead of taking action
action agreed by the concerned ships is contrary to COLREGS
Undue communication pertaining to other operational activities need not get routed through the bridge in order to provide an undisturbed atmosphere required for safe navigation. The Master shall apprise the ship‘s personnel regarding above requirement.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Voyage Planning General
The offshore supply vessels are normally deployed in the oil fields around the Indian coast. Vessels usually ply between base port set up by the operator, depending on the location of the oil field and supply various consumables e.g. fuel oil, pot/drill water, barite, cement, materials required for offshore operations, food containers etc. to offshore installations, as per the requirements. Vessels come back to base port for replenishment of stock, as planned by the operator. The vessels are required to report to base port two times a day i.e. 1000 and 1500 hrs. Instructions regarding their next operation/destination are communicated to the vessel by the base port. Accordingly, Master plans the passage and communicates same to the base port. The passage plan can be changed with the consent of the Logistics coordinator at the base port.
Master shall ensure that the vessel is seaworthy with sufficient stores, provision, bunkers and lubricants on board for the contemplated voyage. The Master shall inform Chief Officer and Chief Engineer Officer regarding the forthcoming voyage to enable them to make necessary preparations. Master shall ensure that there are updated charts and navigational publications on board for the intended voyage. Prior to commencement of voyage, the Chief Officer or a navigating officer, assigned such duties by the Master, shall draw all courses on the most suitable charts. Such courses shall be checked and approved by the Master and are not to be altered without the Master‘s approval. The Master shall ensure that watch keeping personnel who perform duties during departure from port and immediately thereafter have adequate rest prior sailing.

The Chief Engineer Officer shall, in consultation with the Master, determine the requirements of fuel, water for machinery operations, sufficient lubricants, chemicals, expendable and other spare parts, tools, supplies etc. for the intended voyage. In determining the requirements of fuel and lubricants for the intended voyage, the Chief Engineer Officer shall follow guidelines provided in section 7.2. The Chief Officer shall, in consultation with the Master, determine the requirements of water for domestic consumption, expendable and other spare parts, tools, supplies etc. for the intended voyage.

Passage Planning
For offshore vessels voyages are short and limited to the oil fields, located in close proximity of the base port and are usually repetitive nature. At times, the vessels are required to sail from east coast to west coast of India or vice-e-versa or to another port other than the base port. Passage Planning requirements available in checklists (Form: NAV014 and Form: NAV015) shall be complied with. The publication, Bridge Procedures Guide, provided on board, shall also be referred. The Master is responsible to ensure that the vessel is navigated safely at all times. He shall depute the navigating officer(s) for making the standard passage plan as per Form: NAV017.
In the events ECDIS is the primary means of navigation, the above should be taken into account.
The appraisal stage of the passage planning shall be commenced as soon as instructions for the next voyage are received (Checklist Form: NAV014 shall be used for passage plan appraisal). | Voyage Planning General

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Requisition for charts and publications shall be made in advance to ensure that if charts etc. are not available locally, they can be arranged in good time from outside sources.
In an emergency, Master has full authority to buy charts or publications required for the voyage through local Agents, and advise the Gp. I/C regarding the same.
As soon as practicable, after the voyage instructions are received and an appraisal has been made, the Master shall discuss the general routes to be taken with the navigating officer (Second Officer) and other officers in-charge of the navigational watch (if assisting in the making of the passage plan). He shall advise his requirements regarding the passage. The planned route shall embrace the whole passage, from berth to berth, and include all waters where a pilot will be on board the vessel. When planning routes, the following are some of the facts which shall be taken into consideration:
Depth of water relative to draft, making due allowance for squat, pitch, roll, swell, predicted tidal height and possible increase of draft due to heel/trim.
Transverse Stability
Established traffic separation and routing Schemes, where applicable.
Availability and reliability of navigational aids, both conventional and electronic.
Capability and conditions of the vessel and equipment including vessel‘s own manoeuvring ability.
Situation in event of break-down (particularly in relation to the possibility of such occurrence on a lee shore).
Currents and tides. The use of tidal diamonds and tidal effect of turning point shall be indicated on chart.
Traffic conditions.
Weather conditions including areas where reduced visibility may be expected.
Advice and recommendation given in the Sailing Directions.
Navigational Warnings, temporary/preliminary notices affecting the area.
Visibility of lights, rising/dipping distances, arcs and colour of light sectors.
Safe distance of dangers, allowing for weather, tidal stream, anticipated traffic, availability of safe water and navigational system in use.
Alter course positions, which can be monitored conveniently by means of Radar or by visual bearing.
Management of chart changes, which shall not occur at critical points of the passage.
Indicate planned ETA(s), speed.
To show reporting points, VHF frequencies, VTIS/VTMS requirements, areas of special concern and pilot boarding stations.
To mark out "NO-GO" areas.
The track shall be planned to:
Provide the maximum relevant clearances away from any obstructions or hazard.
Facilitate transit to the starboard side of a fairway for collision avoidance.
Provide sufficient margins for corrections with respect to the ship's manoeuvring ability, bearing in mind weather conditions, current and squat.
When the route plan is completed, taking into consideration all pertinent information, the planned route shall be clearly laid on the relevant navigational charts. Such route information shall be continuously available to the officer in-charge of the navigational watch and the Master during the voyage. The planned route is to be clearly established so that it is fully understood by all the officer in-charge of the navigational watch.
Checklist – Form: NAV015 shall be used for preparing the passage plan. | Requisition for charts and publications shall be made in advance to ensure that if charts etc. are not available locally, they can be arranged in good time from outside sources.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) |  | 
The officer in-charge of the navigational watch shall check the progress of the vessel against the plan and advise the Master of any discrepancies. Checklists – Form: NAV007, Form: NAV008 shall be used, as applicable to execute and monitor the passage plan.
When using radar for parallel indexing, target shall be:
Safe and easy to identify;
Radar conspicuous;
Located outside the clutter field;
Limited to a number sufficient for safe navigation.
The parallel indexing technique shall be practiced and must be used frequently.
Positions obtained by one method shall be counter-checked by another position fixing system.
If a decision is made, during a voyage to change the next port of call of the planned route, or if it is necessary for the ship to deviate substantially from the planned route for other reasons, then an amended route shall be planned prior to deviating from the route originally planned.
Record of passage planned and courses laid with position or co-ordinates shall be maintained in a register (Passage Plan Register) for verification. Records shall be maintained for the current year and for the past three calendar years.
After each navigation watch duty officer shall take fire rounds and same will be recorded in deck log book.
Time of changing steering to hand or auto pilot shall be recorded in deck log book.
Timings of taking over and handing over the watch by the master shall also be recorded.

Under Keel Clearance (UKC) Policy
During ocean passages (depths more than 50 m or more than 7 times the draft), the vessel shall keep clear of localized shallow areas.
In open coastal waters (depth ranging from 2 to 7 times the draft), the minimum UKC of 20% of the maximum static draft shall be maintained. Accordingly, ‗NO-GO‘ areas shall be marked on the chart.
While approaching port, a minimum UKC of 10% of the maximum static draft shall be maintained.
When underway, the squat effect shall be taken into account to maintain sufficient UKC. Vessel-specific information on squat for loaded as well as ballast passages shall be readily available in the wheelhouse for reference.
In port (alongside or at moorings), the minimum UKC required to be maintained shall be as under: | The officer in-charge of the navigational watch shall check the progress of the vessel against the plan and advise the Master of any discrepancies. In port (alongside or at moorings), the minimum UKC required to be maintained shall be as under:
 | Ship‘s Maximum Draft | Ship‘s Maximum Draft | Minimum UKC | Minimum UKC | 
 | Less than 10 m | Less than 10 m | 0.30 m | 0.30 m | 
 | Between 10 m and 17 m | Between 10 m and 17 m | 0.60 m | 0.60 m | 
 | Greater than 17 m | Greater than 17 m | 0.90 m | 0.90 m | 
However, the permissible draft stipulated by the port shall not be exceeded notwithstanding the Company‘s UKC Policy. Precautions shall be taken to ensure that ship remains afloat at all times, especially in tidal ports.
When in doubt that sufficient UKC cannot be maintained during any part of the voyage, the Master shall inform the Company seeking for guidance. Information regarding the soundings and nature of the bottom shall be obtained from the port/terminal authorities. | However, the permissible draft stipulated by the port shall not be exceeded notwithstanding the Company‘s UKC Policy. Precautions shall be taken to ensure that ship remains afloat at all times, especially in tidal ports.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Heavy Weather and Tropical Storms (refer Form: NAV012) General
Master shall observe present and forecast weather condition closely and shall, if necessary, alter course and reduce speed to avoid heavy weather that might damage the vessel or endanger persons on board. The safety of the personnel, vessel, cargo and environment always takes priority over any other consideration.
Master shall require Radio Officer or the officer performing radio duties to obtain all pertinent weather reports. A close study of this information shall be made in connection with local weather conditions as observed on the vessel in order that the track of approaching storm or dangerous conditions may be determined and avoided. Vessels fitted with weather facsimile plotters can receive the weather charts/synopsis.
Whilst the risk of damage in heavy weather cannot be totally eliminated, such risk can be substantially reduced by the exercise of prudent seamanship.

Precautions to be taken before approaching/during heavy weather
Inform Master, Engine Room and the crew of approaching weather conditions.
Secure all movable objects on Deck and below Deck. Pay particular attention to securing of cranes.
Re-check and secure container lashings and anchor lashings.
Close all WT doors and portholes.
Secure air pipes, booby hatch covers, ventilator flaps and openings in closed position.
Check that vessel has adequate GM. Slack tanks to be avoided.
Obtain weather reports and check/record barometer readings at regular intervals.
Transmit weather reports to the appropriate authorities, especially in circumstances required by SOLAS 1974 Chapter V.
Adjust speed and course as necessary.
Warn crew to avoid exposed Deck areas.
Check and ensure all bilge pumping arrangements are in working order so that in case of accidental flooding of stores, peak tanks, cofferdams, chain lockers, etc. same can be pumped out without difficulty.

Ice and Cold Weather Procedures (refer Form: NAV013)
Vessels encountering ice conditions at sea shall observe the following procedures:

General
Non-ice strengthened vessels now frequently trade to areas closed for normal navigation in winter months because of:
improved ice-breaker assistance;
improved ice observation;
an improved advisory service in programming vessels through ice-affected areas.
The risk of damage to the ship is substantially reduced provided that the Master acts in accordance with sound operating practice, in relation to:
speed in ice conditions;
manoeuvring;
ice convoy procedures;
drift ice, pack ice and consolidated pack ice; | Heavy Weather and Tropical Storms (refer Form: NAV012) General

manoeuvring;
ice convoy procedures;
drift ice, pack ice and consolidated pack ice;

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
The Master shall consult Sailing Directions and the Mariner's Handbook or equivalent publication, before entering areas where ice may be encountered, in order to be fully briefed about dangers, and how best to deal with them.

Recommended Cold weather procedures
Bring vessel down in the water to a draught at which the sea suctions and propeller are well below the level of any ice. Ensure there is adequate under keel clearance in this condition.
Restrict trim (1-3 meters) to avoid the possibility of ice sliding under the vessel and blocking up the sea suctions.
Take in cargo prior to discharging ballast to maintain the maximum safe draught (in relation to the level of the ice).
If unloading cargo, reverse the procedure outlined in previous point. Maintain maximum safe draught by taking ballast simultaneously with discharge.
Bow shall stem the heaviest ice flow when moored, during periods of heavy ice.
Except in an emergency, avoid anchoring during periods of heavy ice.
When manoeuvring in heavy ice, restrict speed to maintain only safe steerage and headway, to prevent bow plating damage. Minimize astern propulsion.
Hard contacts with ice, docks and fenders may result in structural failure at a significantly lower impact level, at temperatures below freezing. A close examination of possible contact areas shall be done.
Immediately on clearing heavy ice, or areas where cold weather procedures are in force, an inspection shall be made of all safely accessible cargo compartments, void spaces, forepeak, forward deep tanks, cofferdams and (pump rooms in case of a tanker) to verify the integrity of the hull.
Special precautions such as air/steam blow shall be taken to prevent the blocking of sea inlets by ice.
Maintain a small flow of water through the sanitary system and soil drains. Add a small amount of antifreeze or salt to unused drain traps and toilets. Put heating on in the sanitary holding tank and overboard line (if fitted), if the space temperature falls below 5°C (41°F).
Ensure Deck system hydraulic oil is free of impurities.
When possible, or if time permits, air or steam purges all wash water outlets that do not drain to a level well below the water line.
Reduce the flow of outside air into the engine spaces by closing down the vent fans and throttling the dampers. However, ensure that no vacuum is created in machinery spaces. Re-circulation of air in the Engine Room shall be avoided, as this will result in a hydrocarbon and noxious gases.
Circulate freshwater systems continuously to eliminate the possibility of freezing.
If the emergency generator fuel tank is not provided with heaters, and the pour and cloud points of the fuel are not known, then:
maintain the tank at least 90 percent full to avoid condensation;
if the tank is placed on or above the main deck in a ventilated space, add flow improver; | The Master shall consult Sailing Directions and the Mariner's Handbook or equivalent publication, before entering areas where ice may be encountered, in order to be fully briefed about dangers, and how best to deal with them.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
have in stock 2-3 barrels of kerosene, which may be added to storage tank if the temperature is expected to drop below -20°C (-4°F) (a normal cloud point for winter diesel);
add antifreeze to the radiator and jacket system of the diesel generator, if not air cooled.
Change fresh or brackish ballast water with sea water prior to arrival in the cold water zone.
If the sea water temperature falls or is expected to fall below 0°C (32°F) all tanks adjacent to the vessel's shell plating (double bottom tanks, fore/after peaks, deep tanks etc.) shall be reduced to 90% capacity to allow for expansion if freezing takes place.
Keep moisture-absorbing material away from cold areas. If this is not possible, move it away from the ship's side where moisture collects.
Keep all doors closed as much as possible.
Keep accommodation and storerooms warm.
Attend to hold ventilation to avoid cargo sweat.
Be alert to the possibility of flooding from frozen and burst water pipes. Burst water pipes normally become evident when the vessel returns to warmer waters or experiences a substantial rise in the ambient temperature. As a general precaution all piping that has been blocked by a frozen liquid shall be treated as suspect. The pipe section shall be isolated and thoroughly examined and tested before being returned to normal water or other liquid service. If pipe-work is fastened to the steel structure of the accommodation, the panel over the pipes shall be removed when testing for leakage.
Keep the deck and alleyways as ice-free as possible to reduce the danger of slipping. Apply a generous amount of salt to the deck, to prevent ice forming in areas where there is the most traffic.
Avoid carrying bunkers in the deep tanks forward. If leakage occurs from a tank as a result of ice damage, lowering the level will prevent oil pollution. This is because the water head outside will be higher than that inside the tank. This action shall be consistent with the recommended stern trim and well within the allowed stress level.
Check that all crew members are wearing clothing and shoes that are suitable for the weather. Be aware of and check for the possibility of frostbite when personnel are exposed to the cold. Vessels that are to enter cold weather zones shall have an adequate supply of cold weather clothing on board.
In subzero temperature conditions, using quick start spray on air filters may be considered before starting lifeboat engines.

Navigation with Pilot Embarked (refer Form: NAV005, Form: NAV006)
The presence of a pilot does not relieve the Master or the officer in charge of the navigational watch of their duties and obligations.
The Master shall inform the pilot of the ship's characteristics using a pilot card. A format of the pilot card is reproduced in this section (Form: NAV016). This card shall be completed as directed by the Master and handed to the pilot on boarding.
The Master shall request information from the pilot regarding local conditions and his navigational intentions. This information shall be in a form to enable the Master or officer in charge of the navigational watch to monitor the planned passage. | have in stock 2-3 barrels of kerosene, which may be added to storage tank if the temperature is expected to drop below -20°C (-4°F) (a normal cloud point for winter diesel);

The officer in charge of navigational watch shall co-operate closely with the pilot to assist him where possible and to maintain an accurate check on ship's position and movements.

Restricted Visibility (refer Form: NAV011)
When restricted visibility is encountered or expected, the officer in-charge of the navigational watch shall:
comply with the relevant rules of the International Regulations for Preventing Collision at Sea, 1972.
inform the Master.
exhibit appropriate navigation lights, sound fog signals.
operate and use the radar.
proceed at a safe speed.
post additional lookouts.
steer the vessel on manual mode.
record all actions taken in the Logbook.

Coastal and Confined Waters (refer Form: NAV008) General
By comparison with open waters, margins of safety in coastal or confined waters can be critical, as the time available to take corrective action is likely to be limited.
The manoeuvring characteristics of the ship and any limitations or peculiarities that the ship may have, including reliability problems with its propulsion and steering systems, may influence the route selected through coastal waters. In shallow water, particularly if the ship is operated at speed, ship squat can reduce under keel clearances.

Ships‘ routeing schemes and reporting systems along the route, as well as vessel traffic services, should be taken into account.

Coastal weather bulletins, including gale/storm warnings and coastal navigation warnings broadcast by coast radio stations and NAVTEX, may require changes to be made to the route plan.

Monitoring
It is important that when a route is planned through coastal and confined waters, due consideration is given to ensuring that the progress of the ship can be effectively monitored, especially when approaching the wheel over position at the end of a track, and checking that the ship is safely on the new track after alteration of the course. Distinctive chart features should be used for monitoring the ship‘s position visually, by radar and by echo sounder.
Monitoring by visual and radar techniques may be undertaken as follows:
Visual Monitoring
Ahead, transits can provide a leading line along which a ship can safely steer.
Abeam, transits provide a ready check for use when altering course.
Bearing lines can also be effectively used. | The officer in charge of navigational watch shall co-operate closely with the pilot to assist him where possible and to maintain an accurate check on ship's position and movements.
Pilot ladder and other embarkation arrangements shall be in accordance with SOLAS'74 - Chapter V. (Refer illustration in Bridge Procedures Guide).

proceed at a safe speed.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
  A head mark, or a bearing line of a conspicuous object lying ahead on the track line can be used to steer the ship, while clearing bearings can be used to check that a ship is remaining within the safe area.
Radar Monitoring
When radar conspicuous targets are available, effective use can be made of radar clearing bearings and ranges.
Ships with good athwartship track control can use clearing bearings to monitor the advance of a ship towards the wheel over position, while parallel indexing can be used to check that the ship is maintaining track and not drifting to port or starboard. (Also refer Section 6.2.3 of Bridge Procedures Guide).

The Master shall have considered the points enumerated in Bridge Organisation and issue appropriate instructions in Master‘s night order book.

The officer in charge of the navigational watch shall:
Follow Master‘s standing orders and instructions in the Master‘s night order book;
Appraise the Master of the progress/action taken;
Proceed at a safe speed;
Have the vessel steered on manual mode, if necessary;
Effectively monitor the progress of the ship using monitoring techniques; and
Record all actions taken in the bridge note book/movement book, thereafter transfer all important entries using his own discretion in the Logbook before going off the watch.

7.1.2.9	Gyro Compass Failure
Procedure to be followed in case of Gyro Compass failure:
Change over to Hand Steering immediately; select second Gyro Compass (if provided).
Steer with Magnetic Compass.
Change over Radar to Head up/Relative mode.
Follow the Planned and charted track.
Monitor Course made good on GPS.
Verify magnetic compass error on each heading and adjust course steered accordingly.
If in congested water, reduce speed, if needed.
Investigate the cause of Gyro Compass failure and try to rectify/re-start.
Inform Technical Department.

7.1.2.10  Electronic Chart Display & Information System (ECDIS)
It is an electronic navigational chart with information on position fixing and additional information on navigation towards assisting in safe navigation. Although ECDIS reduces navigational workload, simplifies chart correcting procedures, simplifies voyage planning, track monitoring and position fixing etc., it has its own limitations.

ENC Procurement & Corrections
Master to raise indent in DANAOS for obtaining permit for the trading area.
Corrections are supplied in CD regularly to vessel through agent. Vessel to update the data on regular basis. |   A head mark, or a bearing line of a conspicuous object lying ahead on the track line can be used to steer the ship, while clearing bearings can be used to check that a ship is remaining within the safe area.
Radar Monitoring
When radar conspicuous targets are available, effective use can be made of radar clearing bearings and ranges.
Ships with good athwartship track control can use clearing bearings to monitor the advance of a ship towards the wheel over position, while parallel indexing can be used to check that the ship is maintaining track and not drifting to port or starboard. (Also refer Section 6.2.3 of Bridge Procedures Guide).

The Master shall have considered the points enumerated in Bridge Organisation and issue appropriate instructions in Master‘s night order book.

The officer in charge of the navigational watch shall:
Follow Master‘s standing orders and instructions in the Master‘s night order book;
Appraise the Master of the progress/action taken;
Proceed at a safe speed;
Have the vessel steered on manual mode, if necessary;
Effectively monitor the progress of the ship using monitoring techniques; and
Record all actions taken in the bridge note book/movement book, thereafter transfer all important entries using his own discretion in the Logbook before going off the watch.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Ships using ECDIS for navigation must carry Electronic Navigational Charts (ENC), the Official Vector Charts and should be corrected by obtaining current weekly Notices to Mariners.
T&P notices correction and management are to be done as per maker and service provider. A clear system must be in place to ensure TNP notices are incorporated.
Navigational warnings are to be incorporated manually as and when required.
The Hydrographic offices of various countries process official charts and take on the responsibility of maintaining their accuracy. However, corrections made by these offices might only be available at certain fixed intervals and reliability/margin of error of a position-fix must be borne in mind.

Checks prior using ECDIS for Appraisal and Route planning
The following checks shall be carried out by the Navigating Officer:
The vessel's controlling operational parameters (maximum draft, air draft, turning data, minimum under keel clearance required, 'look ahead' distance etc.) should be entered.
The GPS position system should be set to WGS 84 datum.
The alarm functions of the ECDIS should be fully operational; they will alert the operator of any danger exposed in good time during the voyage.
The electronic chart coverage for the voyage must be adequate and all relevant charts must be fully corrected. Kindly ensure expired cell permits are deleted and valid cell permits are imported.

Planning using Electronic Chart Display Systems
Passage planning can be undertaken either on paper charts or using an electronic chart display and information system (ECDIS) displaying electronic navigational charts (ENC). While planning passage using ECDIS, the navigating officer shall consider following:
Screen into ―large‖ or ―planning‟ screen format.
Orientate the chart to show the beginning and end of the route to get a ―big handful‖ feel for the route.
Create a blank canvas by hiding all old routes, constructs etc.
Begin with waypoint plotting in the general area of the start and end of the route.
Select either Rhumb Line or Great Circle route etc.
Zoom in to a more appropriate scale to modify the start and finish waypoints and ‗click here ―massage‖ waypoints to account for TSS etc.
Ensure that you have adequate XTD for the various legs of your route to take into account the nature of the environment and expected possible deviations, lateral separation from the route and collision avoidance.
Check Zones of Confidence (ZOC) or Source Data Diagrams and amend the route or highlight as necessary.
Set Safety Depth and Safety Contour values.
Conduct a system check of the route at an appropriate XTD to allow for deviations, collision avoidance etc.
Once all alarms have been checked and verified, check the route in its entirety on 1:1 scale by manually scrolling along it.
Add relevant additional information and manual corrections.
Double check Distance/ETD/ETA and Tidal Constraints. | Ships using ECDIS for navigation must carry Electronic Navigational Charts (ENC), the Official Vector Charts and should be corrected by obtaining current weekly Notices to Mariners.

Protect the route as necessary and save a back up.
If updates are installed prior to sailing or during the execution of the route, ensure that the route is checked again, as updates may affect it.

Execution & Monitoring – Interpretation & Cross-check
When passage planning, using a combination of electronic and paper charts, particular care needs to be taken at transition points between areas of electronic and paper chart coverage. The passage reflects distinct pilotage, coastal and ocean water phases. Planning within any one phase of the voyage should be undertaken using either all electronic or all paper charts rather than a mix of chart types. Where a passage is planned using paper charts, care should be taken when transferring the details of the plan to an electronic chart display system. In particular, the navigating officer should ensure that:
Positions are transferred to, and are verified on, electronic charts of an equivalent scale to that of the paper chart on which the position was originally plotted;
Any known difference in chart datum between that used by the paper chart and that used by the electronic chart display system is applied to the transferred positions;
The complete passage plan as displayed on the electronic chart display system is checked for accuracy and completeness before it is used.

Secondary ECDIS must have the ENC chart database and voyage plan loaded before commencement of the voyage and must be operational at all times when the ship is in coastal waters.

When paper charts serve as the only back-up arrangements, the charts shall include the planned route and, when navigating within restricted waters, the ship‘s position is to be regularly updated to ensure a safe take-over of ECDIS functions, should the need arise.

Vessel Specific ECDIS Setup Requirements
The Master shall supplement this document by outlining vessel specific ECDIS setup requirements in 'Master's Standing Orders'. A copy of this document shall be kept readily available at ECDIS units.

Amending the Safety Parameters
The Safety Parameters as required by the Master‘s order must not be changed by OOW. Under no circumstances are these to be altered without the express concurrence of Master. Should the safety parameters stipulated by the Master in the Passage Plan be amended during the voyage on the Master‘s request, then it must be recorded in the deck log book as well.
During the change of watch the oncoming OOW shall verify the below settings before taking over the watch.
Contour Settings (to check and enter correct settings):
Safe Depth: Draft + Squat + Heeling Effect + UKC
Safety Contour: Same as safe Depth
Shallow Contour: Same as Draft
Deep Contour: Twice the draft | Protect the route as necessary and save a back up.
If updates are installed prior to sailing or during the execution of the route, ensure that the route is checked again, as updates may affect it.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Category of Zone of Confidence
Unlike paper charts where source data diagrams are mostly provided, ENCs (Electronic Navigation Charts) do not provide this information. Instead they provide the navigator with a facility to examine reliability and quality of source data by means of CATZOCs (Category of Zone of Confidence). This gives an estimate of the reliability of data related to five quality categories for assessed data (CATZOC A1, A2, B, C and D) and a sixth category for data which has not yet been assessed. It is also recommended to consider these CATZOC features while determining a 'Ship Safety Settings'. Adequate margin to be applied while navigating in shallow waters.
Data Presentation & Performance Check as required by International Hydrographic Organisation.
Master shall ensure IHO Data Presentation & Performance checks of ECDIS are carried out to comply with the chart carriage requirements as per SOLAS V Regulation 19.2.1.4 as follows:
Prior to using a newly installed ECDIS,
After any software update,
Once every three months,
The relevant report shall be forwarded to IHO, under due intimation to Technical Department, SIRIUS HO.

Checks during passage planning
Marking and highlighting of electronic charts should be carried out in a similar way to paper charts. Such marking should identify radar conspicuous targets, no-go areas, parallel index lines, transit marks, clearing bearings, etc.
It is prudent for a simulated passage to be run prior to the vessel's departure to ensure that the route does not enter any alarm preset danger areas that may have been overlooked;
Estimated positions should be marked on the chart for each watch, in advance.
List of safety alarms to be set and monitored on ECDIS
Safety depths and safety contours
Depth/UKC alarms
Dangerous targets alarms
Cross track distance alarms
Ahead sector (distance/time)
Bridge alarms (alarm from other navigational equipments) Gyro, GPS, Log error alarms.
Checks during watch
Form: NAV019 to be complied with and following to be checked:
Data input from the gyro compass, speed log, echo sounder and other electronic equipment to the ECDIS should be periodically monitored to ensure accuracy.
Secondary ECDIS must be operational at all times when the ship is in coastal waters.
Check back up ECDIS.
Check safety alarms settings and their functioning.

Ahead sector (distance/time)
Bridge alarms (alarm from other navigational equipments) Gyro, GPS, Log error alarms.

Form: NAV019 to be complied with and following to be checked:
Data input from the gyro compass, speed log, echo sounder and other electronic equipment to the ECDIS should be periodically monitored to ensure accuracy.
Secondary ECDIS must be operational at all times when the ship is in coastal waters.
Check back up ECDIS.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Parallel indexing and use of clearing bearings
Visual cross bearings
Use of radar to check the accuracy of the charted position
The Risks of ECDIS
It should be noted that the ECDIS is only a tool that helps a mariner navigate a ship safely and effectively. One of the biggest risks with the transition to ECDIS is an over reliance on the information provided.
Limitation of ECDIS
There are some limitations of the ECDIS as followings:
Chart Accuracy: ECDIS provides the navigator with a tactical tool which incorporates a high accuracy positioning device. The navigator can "zoom" in on an ECDIS chart to a scale beyond the intended accuracy of the charted information.
Familiarization of ECDIS: A mariner must invest time and effort to mastering the device prior to his first navigational watch. This will be crucial to the navigation safety of the vessel in the event paper charts are not required or available on the vessel.
ENC charts do not cover all sea areas.
Caution should be exercised whenever information layers are removed or information level is reduced from an ENC and must be reviewed by the Master. All members of the Bridge Team must be advised whenever such changes are carried out.
Positions are primarily derived from the GPS. Therefore any GPS alarms must be immediately investigated in order to avoid error in position and the possibility of the vessel running into danger.
There is a risk of running too close to danger with a zoomed-in chart scale. The Navigating Officer should alternatively switch smaller chart scale to appraise of the situation.
Positions of other vessels and targets displayed on the ECDIS might be obscured because of improperly tuned radars or improperly set anti-clutter on either the radar or ECDIS.
AIS displays target course and speed over ground as well as heading. However, AIS does not calculate target course/speed based on 'Speed over Ground'.
An ECDIS equipped with a radar overlay shall only be used as a situational awareness tool during anti-collision manoeuvres and not for primary anti-collision purposes. The ship's ARPA radars will be used for this purpose.
Navigating officers must not become over-reliant on ECDIS. Frequent checks should be made of the ECDIS position fixing system (normally GPS) by the use of some other means like parallel indexing, radar fix, visual cross bearings.
If display is zoomed beyond intended scale accuracy, the chartered information could be erroneous.
Independent position fixing system input and must be in operational mode in confined water.
Actions in the Event of Complete ECDIS Failure
The Officer of the Navigations Watch (OOW) shall immediately
Change over to other Back up (ECDIS or Paper Chart)
Inform the Master. & call additional OOW
Carry out trouble shooting as per Manufacturer instruction | Parallel indexing and use of clearing bearings
Visual cross bearings
Use of radar to check the accuracy of the charted position

7.1.2.11	Procedures for Corrections and Upkeep of Charts and Nautical Publications The Navigating Officer shall be responsible to the Master for ensuring that all charts and publications are maintained in good order and, where relevant, corrected up-to-date. Chart correction Log and Folio Index – BA shall be used to record the corrections made.
Correction applicable to charts and nautical publications shall be obtained from Notices to Mariners. The Company has arrangements with their approved charts vendors to provide weekly (BA charts) and fortnightly (Indian Charts) Notices to Mariners to Company‘s vessels.
Additionally, the Company has arrangements with the approved chart vendors to provide online Digital Notices to Mariners and Correction Tracings for Charts and Publications through E-Mariner on weekly basis to all vessels, in order to keep the Charts and Publications updated promptly.
Only current editions of Charts and Publications are to be used. Cancelled editions must be clearly marked so, in pen, and removed from the confines (territory) of the wheelhouse.
Temporary (T) & Preliminary (P) notice numbers are to be recorded in Chart Correction Record. Such information is readily available in weekly notices to mariners or from the E- Mariner system as well as from the monthly E-Mariner update CDs (containing complete Notices to Mariners with corrections for all Charts & Publications).
Applicable T & P corrections shall then be made in Pencil on all charts to be used for the current voyage. After correcting affected voyage charts for applicable T & P corrections, the correction number shall be entered in Pencil at the location of correction as well as on the bottom of chart.
After making such correction, suitable annotation shall be made in the Chart Correction Record to indicate that the correction has been physically made on the chart. Any cancelled T&P notices should be struck out in the Chart Correction Record and erased from the corresponding charts.
A copy of the current In-Force list (usually published monthly) shall be filed along with the Chart Correction Record and used for monitoring and verification of current T & P notices in force.
Navigational Warnings promulgated through Notices to Mariners (Navareas/Hydrolant/ Hydropac) should be filed area wise as long as valid (removed when cancelled), in a dedicated file, and relevant ones marked on voyage charts. | Report to Technical Superintendent and if defect not rectified, OEM service engineer to be arranged at next port.

7.1.2.12	Guidance for use of Bridge Navigational Watch Alarm System (BNWAS) at Sea
BNWAS must be switched on at SBE departure & Switched off only after all Fast by Master; as it requires password.
The BNWAS should be operational whenever the ship‘s heading or track control system is engaged, unless inhibited by the Master. BNWAS should be operational when vessel is at anchor.
Record shall be maintained whenever BNWAS is Switched ON or OFF.
Ensure BNWAS is powered ―ON‖ and Power indication LED is Lit at all times when ever bridge is manned. System should be kept on ―Manual‖ or ―Manual ON‖ mode ONLY. And Never on "Auto" mode.
At Night BNWAS Reset Button inside Chart enclosure or on the GMDSS Console shall not be used, Reset Buttons on Front Console in the Wheel House shall be used to reset Timer.
On a weekly basis BNWAS be tried out on both A.C. and D.C. power supply.
All 1st, 2nd & 3rd stage Visual Indication and Audible Alarm shall be tried out monthly.
7.1.2.13	Guidance for Bridge Control Failure
Inform to the duty in E/R and C/E, and then switch to Engine Room Control
Inform Master
Establish Emergency Communication with E/R
E/R to be in Manned condition
If unable rectify, to advise to the office for arranging repair.
Guidance for Bridge Black-Out
Inform to the duty in E/R and C/E, and then switch to Engine Room Control
Inform Master
Establish Emergency Communication with E/R
E/R to be in Manned condition
Reduce speed to minimum and change over to Emergency steering
Inform vessel in vicinity, Display appropriate signal
Steer the vessel away from any Dangers existing in the area/away from Traffic.
If in anchorable Depths, Call Anchor Party forward to Stand By and anchor if required
Send Emergency Initial Report to H.O.
When Power/Engine restored, check all equipments working properly, resume voyage and inform H.O. (send Status Report/Final Report).
If fault is not fully rectified, ask for shore assistance from office. | Navigation warnings received through EGC or Navtex should also be marked by OOW as and when received.

Arrival/Departure
The checklist, Preparation for Arrival in Port, Form: NAV009 and Form: NAV005 (if applicable) shall be complied with — when preparing the vessel for arrival in port.
The checklist, Preparation for Sea, Form: NAV004 and Form: NAV005 (if applicable) shall be complied with — when preparing the vessel for departure from port.
Prior to departure Master shall obtain sailing schedule, cargo manifest and other relevant items from the Logistic co-ordinator. Prior to arrival, port shall be informed regarding vessel‘s ETA, cargo and any special circumstances of the vessel.
Prior to departure, Master to ensure that the Flush hatch located at the main deck between frame 75-79 is kept closed at sea at all time & same has been marked at the location and weather tightness maintained at all times (Applicable to PSV SIRIUS Nalanda & SIRIUS Yamuna).
On departure from one installation, the Master shall communicate the departure time and the ETA at the next installation to the Oil Installation Manager/Logistic Coordinator of the Base Port. | Arrival/Departure

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Mooring Operations

Guidelines
Since mooring operations are potentially dangerous and the hazards are inseparable from operation, risk assessment shall be made of all mooring areas onboard.
The crew shall be called for mooring stations well in advance of arrival at the dock, or other mooring operations to complete all preparations.
When Pilot is on board, he shall be consulted regarding the anticipated mooring operation. A diagram showing the mooring arrangements and indicating the mooring lines shall be used.
The Pilot shall be informed of any deficiencies in the vessel‘s mooring equipment.
Adequate personnel shall be available for mooring operations to ensure the efficient handling of lines.
The mooring plan developed by the Master and pilot shall address the minimum requirements of the berth, anticipated weather, passing traffic and tidal currents.
A mooring team for mooring stations shall consist of Deck Crew distributed forward and aft to ensure safe mooring.
Efficient communication between bridge and mooring stations shall be provided.
A clear set of hand signals shall be agreed between the officer and his crew so that the winches can be operated safely without the use of voice commands.
Long leads shall be preferred for mooring lines, both to reduce the amount of line tending required and because the holding power of the brakes is inversely related to the amount of wire on the winch drum (i.e. more wire on the drum equals less brake holding power).
Mooring lines shall not be heaved tight until all persons, both ashore and on board, have moved clear of the line and the mooring point.
Mooring ropes shall not be secured on warping drums.
Mooring ropes shall as far as practicable not be secured on single bitts; they shall be secured on twin bollard in a figure-of eight fashion.
If the anchor has been backed out ready for letting go while approaching the berth and mooring, it shall be brought home and secured after the ship is all fast.
Heaving lines and messenger lines shall be retrieved and properly stowed.
Highlighting hazards should help the new crew, cadets and even experienced crew if they become complacent.
The winch operator should have clear view of the active operations that are going on and the winch operator shall refrain from ropes handling operation. Fixing a lanyard to an operating liver and pulling on it is an unsafe practice which shall be avoided.
Personal Protective Equipment i.e. helmet, safety footwear and boiler suit shall be worn during mooring operation. Proper fitting hand gloves shall be used. Loose hand gloves can be dangerous while handling the ropes on a windlass drum.
Only personnel involved in the mooring operation should be present at stations during mooring operations and cadets should be supervised by experienced seafarers.

Emergency Departure Procedures
On completion of mooring, procedures for emergency departure arrangement from the berth shall be discussed with the shore authorities. | Mooring Operations

Highlighting hazards should help the new crew, cadets and even experienced crew if they become complacent.
The winch operator should have clear view of the active operations that are going on and the winch operator shall refrain from ropes handling operation. Fixing a lanyard to an operating liver and pulling on it is an unsafe practice which shall be avoided.
Personal Protective Equipment i.e. helmet, safety footwear and boiler suit shall be worn during mooring operation. Proper fitting hand gloves shall be used. Loose hand gloves can be dangerous while handling the ropes on a windlass drum.
Only personnel involved in the mooring operation should be present at stations during mooring operations and cadets should be supervised by experienced seafarers.

Emergency Departure Procedures
On completion of mooring, procedures for emergency departure arrangement from the berth shall be discussed with the shore authorities.
