Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Anchoring and Anchor Watch (refer Form: NAV010)
While approaching the anchoring area, all precautions shall be taken in observance to sound seamanship practice and navigational requirements. Navigational checklist Form: NAV010 shall be complied with while preparing for anchoring and during the anchor watch.

Anchoring
These vessels usually operate in offshore development areas where submarine pipelines/ cables and other underwater obstructions are likely to exist. Hence, special precautions shall be taken to ensure vessel anchors well clear of such obstructions.
Vessel shall anchor clear of:
main shipping routes, traffic lanes and fairways.
prohibited anchorage.
submarine pipelines or cables.
other vessels.
Wreck, foul ground/other submerged objects.
When in deep waters, it may be prudent to avoid anchoring to prevent risk of difficulty in retrieving the anchor. If due to some reason it becomes unavoidable to slip the cable, the end shall be marked with an anchor marker buoy and attached with a wire pendant of suitable length to facilitate retrieval using the anchor handling winch at a later stage.

Anchor Watch
The officer in charge of the navigational watch shall verify that anchor is holding and the cable is not slipping by close observation of anchor bearings. If there is doubt that the vessel is not maintaining position, the officer in charge of the navigational watch shall:
Inform the Master.
Inform the E/R.
Call anchor stations.
Inform the port control.
Under heavy weather conditions or when threatened by a storm, the Master shall consider picking up the anchor in good time and clear the anchorage area. It would be safer to head into the sea and swell in open waters.
Ship's position circle, showing maximum reach of the vessel as she swings around at change of tide and exact position of the anchor is to be charted on the largest scale chart available.
Officer in-charge of the navigation watch shall observe weather, tidal and sea conditions and record same in the Deck Logbook.
Ships in the vicinity shall be plotted on the chart.
In the event if another vessel is anchored in the vicinity and is found dragging her anchor or other vessel navigating in the vicinity and coming close to own vessel, officer in- charge of the navigation watch shall ensure safety of own vessel and take following action immediately:
Inform the dragging vessel or vessel navigating in the vicinity by any means of communication,
Inform Master and port authorities, | Anchoring and Anchor Watch (refer Form: NAV010)

Have the engines ready,
Call anchor stations,
Keep adequate number of fenders ready and rigged on the side vessel is expected to come closer.
If danger appears to be increasing, arrange to heave up the anchor and clear the area.
Make use of helm/Engines to cant vessel away.
A continuous listening watch shall be maintained on VHF, on the appropriate working channel for the area and on channel 16.

Anchors heaved up and housed in the hawse pipe
Hawse pipe cover put in place

General Instructions to Vessels working at an Offshore Location
All vessels engaged in the oil fields are required to have a valid Naval Security Clearance Certificate (NSC) issued by Offshore Development Advisory Group (ODAG) in order to ensure safety and security of the Offshore Development Area (ODA).
Marine Procedure for Offshore Supply Vessels and Multi-Support Offshore Vessels, documented by the Operators (ONGC) is provided on board all offshore vessels for guidance of Masters. These guidelines shall be complied with for safe approach and operations, prior to entering 500 mtrs. and within 500 mtrs. of any installation in the offshore field.

Approaching Installation
Masters of all offshore vessels approaching an installation must satisfy themselves that they are in possession of the latest marine information which should include, lights and signals displayed by the installations and or support vessels, names of such vessels, VHF Channels in use and positions of any buoy or underwater obstructions.

Procedure for approaching Offshore Installation
Obtain following information from the installation
Obtain prior permission from OIM before entering 500m zone of installation.
Any projection from the installation e.g. Mud mats that may hamper cargo operations or reduce under keel clearance when in shallow water
Which side the installation proposes to have the OSV for working
Compass Heading of the rig/drill ship
Details regarding the anchor patters and marker buoys used by the drill ship
Any other vessel working in the proximity to the installation or any obstructions within 100 meter radius of the installation
VHF working channel
Vessels best ETA should be conveyed to the installation in advance at least one hour before arrival so that they are ready with appropriate slings, ropes etc to commence operations on arrival.
After taking in to consideration all information obtained as above and having factored in weather information, including under keel clearance, shallow water effects and tidal conditions, Master must plan the most suitable final approach and heading on which to station the vessels close to the installation for cargo operation.
Master should ensure that all hazards, accidents or incidents affecting safety of the vessel is reported to the operator in his initial reporting.
Any defect occurring after initial reporting must be immediately reported to the installation as they occur. Continuity of operations shall be subject to agreement between master and OIM.
The Master is solely responsible for the safety of the vessel, crew and cargo. If the conditions do not permit safe approach to the installation, he must postpone the operation and inform the OIM regarding the difficulty. No operations must take place without the total agreement of the Master, OIM and the crane operator.
It must be remembered that vessels will be subjected to forces such as wind, swell, current, and tidal conditions varying strengths. The ideal heading would be in line with the resultant of all the above force. However, this may not be always possible. Master | General Instructions to Vessels working at an Offshore Location

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
should then plan the most suitable safe working heading depending on the prevailing conditions.
A good method of assessing the most suitable and safe working heading would be to stop (dead stop) when about 2-3 cables from the installation and observe the direction of drift in relation to the installation. Navigational aids such as GPS and radar shall be used to get a good idea of the direction of the resultant force and the rate of drift.
As a further precaution, Masters should take up the planned heading about one ship‘s length from the installation and watch the station keeping capability of the vessels on that heading for some time. Only when satisfied that the ship will be safe on this heading should he start moving closer, within the reach of the crane for cargo operation.
Sufficient sea room must always be kept between installation and vessels so that the vessel can pull out safely in case of emergency.
It is recommended that the working heading be so chosen that sufficient angle is made with installation‘s working side and vessel can pull out to safety easily in an emergency.
Internal and external communication must be checked before entering the 500 meters safety zone.
All controls in wheelhouse must be tested before final approach is made. Ensure bow thruster is ‗ON‘ and ready for instant use. Steering shall be changed over to hand steering.
At night, search lights must be ‗ON‘ and trained on installations to improve safety.
In shallow waters, echo sounder and echo watch must be ‗ON‘ and under keel clearance continuously monitored.
Safe speed must be kept for final approach. If necessary, all the way may be taken off for a better assessment for the set and drift.

If the ship is making final approach with the resultant force following her, care must be taken to make the turn into the intended working heading well in advance to prevent the ship from drifting in to the installation while making the turn. Continuous watch on the station holding capability of the vessel must be kept. Operations must be aborted and ship pulled out into safety well before the limits are reached. If there are any restrictions on the use of the ME‘s and/or bow thruster power, same must be taken in to account when deciding the station keeping capability. Continuous watch on weather parameters must be kept.

In bad weather, if required to work on the weather side of the installation, vessel should take up position, at a minimum safe distance off the installation of 50 meters, such that the vessel would drift clear in the event of engine failure, but close enough to give visual position referencing prior to coming alongside. The vessel should also adopt the heading which would be assumed when working alongside. During this period it will soon become apparent how much power is required to maintain position. This should assist the Master in deciding whether it is safe to work on the weather side of the installation.

The Master has overall authority to terminate operation or refuse cargo when it is felt unsafe to continue with the operation in hand. Although OIM is responsible for operations within 500 meter zone of the installation, if the Master finds that conditions are unsafe, he can discontinue/suspend any operation with intimation to OIM. | should then plan the most suitable safe working heading depending on the prevailing conditions.

Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
When working with the installation, if the installation alarm is heard, and if not connected by hoses, the Master shall inform the crane driver and pull clear, stand off and await instructions. If connected by hoses, then the vessel should cease pumping, inform crane driver and await instruction.

Communications while approaching Offshore Installation
One hour before arrival OSV shall contact installation and provide ETA.
At all times when on location at an installation and especially when operating within 500 metre zone, the vessel should monitor the working channel of the installation. The vessel must also monitor VHF Ch.16 at all times.
Before a vessel is positioned, radio communication between the vessel and the appropriate platform station (control room, radio room, cranes, deck foreman, bulk cargo supervisor etc.) must be established and tested as satisfactory.
Mobile phones must be switched off at all times within the 500 metre zone.
Weather must be monitored at all times through EGC and Navtex reports.

Responsibility and Authority of OIM
OIM is in charge of the installation and responsible (on behalf of installation owner & operator) for the safety of installation and those on board.
Responsible for operation to be carried out within 500m zone/radius of installation.
Shall appraise Master regarding the configuration of the side being approached and nature of operation to be undertaken.
Shall instruct the vessel to approach the installation on the side he considers safe for operation, as well as, for vessel‘s movement.
OIM has the authority to refuse permission to any vessel entering the 500m of installation on the following grounds:
In case any other operation is taking place that may endanger the platform safety.
Bad weather.
He can modify or terminate any vessels activity which is considered hazardous.
Status Report to OIM
Any limitations or working procedures which could impose restrictions on the vessel or other vessels in the area and defects, if any, particularly in relation to Main Engines, Thrusters, Steering Gear, Windlass, Mooring Equipment, Cargo Stowage, Cargo Stowage, Bulk Pumps, Lifting Gear, Navigational and Radio equipment etc., shall be informed to the OIM prior getting permission for approaching the installation. Defects noticed after the initial report shall be reported to OIM promptly.

Information to OIM
Master shall inform OIM to promulgate the information regarding the ship operation. OIM, in turn, will advise and update the units under his control in the vicinity i.e. rigs, platforms etc.

Unnecessary use of communications equipment
Unnecessary use of VHF communications on an oil field or work boat site is to be avoided. Conversations shall be limited to operational matters only and be as brief as possible. | When working with the installation, if the installation alarm is heard, and if not connected by hoses, the Master shall inform the crane driver and pull clear, stand off and await instructions. Unnecessary use of VHF communications on an oil field or work boat site is to be avoided. Conversations shall be limited to operational matters only and be as brief as possible.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Navigation) | 
Contact between Vessel and Platform
Physical contact between a vessel and an offshore installation shall be avoided. Any such contact shall be immediately reported to OIM.

Offshore Installation‘s Radio Silence Periods
Periods of Radio Silence are imposed on installations from time to time to reduce the risk of premature triggering of explosive charges used for perforating. Normally one hour‘s notice will be given by OIM before imposition of a Radio Silence Period. Immediately prior to such periods, all vessels which are able will be ordered to withdraw and remain outside the 500 metre zone and they shall maintain a listening watch on both VHF Channel 16 and whichever other channel is designated until further instructions are given by OIM. Vessels, which for any reason are unable to withdraw to a position outside the 500 metre zone, are required to cease all radio, radar and beacon transmissions during the silence period. To guarantee total compliance, the Master shall recall all portable radios prior to the start of the silence period and ensure that they are in a non-operative state for the duration of the silence period. Radio calls to an installation from approaching vessels will usually be acknowledged by the standby vessel, which will relay whatever instructions are necessary. A vessel approaching an installation, which is in radio silence, shall not proceed into the 500 metre zone.
In an emergency situation, the installations will usually have a low power (1 watt) portable radio which can, if the incharge of marine control gives permission, be used to answer calls directly during radio silence periods.

Standby Vessel Procedures
Standby vessels are required to remain within 5 miles of the assigned installation.

The standard operating procedure for OSVs provided by the Operator shall be followed.

Operational Control
Standby vessels are functionally managed by the OIM of the assigned installation. In case of a fixed installation, this management is generally delegated to the OIM who has overall control of vessel movements within the field development area. Master shall comply with the advice of the OIM consistent with safety.

Normal duties while on station
To remain within 1 mile of the installation unless otherwise instructed by OIM.
To maintain a continuous VHF radio watch on Channel 16 and the appropriate working Channel.
To keep round the clock watch with radar on.
To be underway close to installation during helicopter operation.
To warn all approaching vessels well in advance, of the presence of installation.
To carry out firefighting drills periodically (once/fortnightly) near the platform for functional test of the firefighting system.
To respond to calls from vessels to the installation during periods of radio silence passing on to them whatever instructions may be necessary.
To keep in regular contact with the installation, the frequency of the contact to be increased in inclement weather. | Contact between Vessel and Platform

To be ready in all respects to save life. If for any reason the Standby vessel is unable to maintain station or operational readiness, OIM is to be informed immediately.
To keep radar watch for other vessel likely to pass within 2 miles of the platform and report same to OIM, in case of poor visibility.
To report any oil slicks to the OIM.
To report any object seen falling from the platform to OIM.
Should at any time a ship be detected on a collision course with the platform, or attempting to penetrate the 500 metre zone, the standby vessel shall:
Report the situation immediately to OIM.
Try by all available means to warn the vessel concerned to keep clear.

7.1.6.12	Operational Limitations
During adverse weather conditions, Master, with due regard to the capability of the vessel and safety of personnel working on deck, shall suspend any operations in due time.
When approaching a platform the vessel should be in a safe position before transferring control to the after conning position.

During heavy/monsoonic weather, while ship handling, appropriate care must be exercised in approaching platform/rigs in the field if required to do so for urgent support. Vessels should avoid anchoring to the extent possible and heave to/proceed at slow speed with due consideration to safety and keep OIMs, owners/managers informed of the situation.

Extreme Weather
During adverse weather conditions, the Master shall seek shelter or steam into the wind, for safety. This may take the vessel away from an installation beyond the statutory distance. It shall be recognised that at such times, standby cover could be reduced or non-existent and emergency helicopter cover is likely to be similarly effected. | To be ready in all respects to save life. Tests and Checks
Tests and checks detailed in Checklist Form: NAV003 shall be complied with, every noon at sea, by the officer in charge of the navigational watch.
If the vessel is on auto pilot, every watch the officer in charge of the navigational watch shall change over steering controls to manual for a brief period of time.
Weather and visibility permitting, the standard compass course shall be established at least once a watch, and after any major course alteration.
Weather and visibility permitting, the standard compass error shall be checked at least once in 24 hours during normal offshore operations. However, when on a sea passage of more than 24 hours, the error shall be checked once in 12 hours.
Standard and gyro compass shall be compared once every watch and after any major alteration of course.
Where practicable, positions obtained by one navigational system shall be cross-checked utilising another navigational system. | Tests and Checks

Management of Navigational Equipment
The Chief Officer shall be responsible to the Master for ensuring that all navigational instruments, navigational aids, navigational publications and charts are kept in good order.
Navigational Equipment Maintenance Register shall be maintained by the Chief Officer. This register shall contain an index of all navigational instrument/equipment. The entry pages for each instrument/item shall contain its particulars, viz. maker, serial number, type, model, when installed, any major overhaul, defects and details of repairs done, list of spares required and in stock. The Chief Officer shall present this register to the Master every month for his inspection and signature.
When required by the Master, the Radio Officer or officer assigned such responsibility, shall assist with the maintenance, repairs and maintenance of various electronic navigational equipment on board.
Maintenance routines detailed in section 10 shall be complied with. | Management of Navigational Equipment

7.1.9    Records
The following navigational records shall be maintained on board, in the wheelhouse. Records of the current year and past three calendar years shall be retained in the other registers and logs named below:

Sr.	Name of Record	Maintained by No.
Deck Logbook	Officer in charge of navigational watch
Bridge Note Book/Movement Book	Officer in charge of navigational watch
Navigational Equipment Maintenance Register	Chief Officer
Chart Correction Log	Chief Officer
Master's Bridge/Night Order Book	Master
Compass Error Book	Officer in charge of navigational watch
Radar Log	Officer in charge of navigational watch
GPS Log	Officer in charge of navigational watch
Echo Sounder Log	Officer in charge of navigational watch
Passage Plan Register	Chief Officer
GMDSS Logbook	Radio Officer or general operator

Master shall sight, review and sign all the above records at least once a month. The Deck Logbook and GMDSS Logbook shall be sighted and reviewed once every day.

Position Reporting
Various types of position reporting schemes exist, namely INSPIRES, INDSAR (Search & Rescue) Oceanic Schemes in the Indian Ocean. These schemes were initiated to assist in the location of vessels in difficulty and to facilitate the organisation of assistance from the knowledge of location of other vessels in the same area.
Indian Ship Position & Information Reporting System (INSPIRES) is operated by Indian Navy for open ocean vessel management for security of all vessels within the assigned INSPIRES area i.e. Arabian Sea/Bay of Bengal. Indian Naval communication centre (COMCENs) at Mumbai and Vizag are functioning as shore stations for receiving INSPIRES messages.
Indian Ship Reporting System (INDSAR) is operated by Indian Coast Guard under SAR Convention. For providing the effective search and rescue operation in the event of marine casualty. The system is maintained by Indian Coast Guard through their MRCC at Mumbai.
Reporting through INDSAR and INSPIRES is mandatory for all Indian Flag Vessels within their coverage area.
Master and officers in charge of the navigational watches shall ensure that the vessel participates in such position reporting schemes.
Details of such position reporting schemes are available in the Annual Notices to Mariners and DGS Circulars. | 7.1.9    Records

Daily Position Reporting by Ships on International Voyages to the Company
When voyage duration between two successive ports is more than 24 hours, daily position report shall be forwarded to the Company. The report shall contain the following:
ship‘s position;
ship‘s course and speed; and
details of any external or internal conditions that are affecting the ship‘s voyage or the normal safe operation of the ship. | Daily Position Reporting by Ships on International Voyages to the Company

Shipboard Operations (Machinery) | 
Machinery

General
Attention of Chief Engineer Officer and officer in charge of the engineering watch is drawn to the STCW and the STCW Code, regarding regulations, standard and guidance on watchkeeping. The Chief Engineer Officer and the officer in charge of the engineering watch shall at all times comply with regulations and standards contained in the STCW and STCW Code Part A. The Chief Engineer Officer and the officer in charge of the engineering watch shall take guidance on watch keeping from STCW Code Part B.
Engineering watch keeping procedures and machinery operations procedures provided in this section, Section 7.2, shall be read and complied in conjunction with regulation, standards and guide lines provided in the following publications:
STCW (as amended)
SOLAS 74 (as amended)
MARPOL 73/78 (as amended)
These procedures shall be read and complied in conjunction with the instructions and guidelines contained in:
Fleet Circulars Guidelines
Engine Log Book
Chief Engineer Officer‘s Night Order Book
Bridge/ER Movement Book
Manufacturer‘s Manual of Machinery Items
The objective of these procedures is Safety of Life, Environment, Vessel and Machinery. These procedures:
intend to establish the basic standards of engineering watch keeping and machinery
operations on board all vessels of the Company;
form the basis on which the officer in charge of engineering watch and Chief Engineer Officer will take decisions relating to engineering watch and machinery operations;
are in no way meant to restrict or constrain the Chief Engineer Officer or watch keeping officer‘s authority or contradict applicable rules and regulations;
shall be supplemented by the Chief Engineer Officer‘s Standing Orders, Night Orders and other instruction, pertaining to specific situation during engineering watch. | Machinery

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Machinery) | 
Procedures

Familiarisation with Machinery and Machinery Operations
All Engineer Officers upon joining the vessel shall familiarise themselves with emergency procedures, lay out of machinery spaces, systems, escape routes, water tight doors, location and operation of all emergency, safety and fire fighting equipment. A ship specific checklist shall be prepared and used to complete the familiarisation and the duly filled in checklist shall be filed in File No.306 with Chief Engineer Officer. For preparation of this checklist guidance may be taken from the sample checklist Form: E12 (Sample).

Stand-by Arrangements
Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure regular trying/testing out of all stand-by arrangements and machinery, provided on board, in order to promote reliability of such equipment and systems. All stand-by machinery available on board shall be identified and their change-over intervals shall be specified and ship personnel shall be made aware of these change-over intervals. All efforts shall be made to rectify defects, if any, and attending superintendent informed immediately for arranging spares, if required, and defective machinery made operational at the earliest.

Chief Engineer Officer‘s Standing Orders
Chief Engineer Officer shall issue standing orders, clearly detailing the various aspects for safe and efficient running of machinery. The incumbent Chief Engineer Officer shall sign these standing orders. All officers in charge of the engineering watch and other Engineer Officers (where applicable) shall read and acknowledge these standing orders by duly signing the same. A copy of Chief Engineer Officer‘s standing orders shall be placed in the engine control room.
The standing orders may vary in scope but shall include, and not be limited to, the matters such as:
Relieving officer in charge of the engineering watch shall be in the Engine Room 15 minutes before commencement of his watch and apprise himself about operating conditions of all the running engine room machinery and systems.
Prior coming to Engine Room, the relieving officer in charge of the engineering watch shall visit and inspect other machinery spaces located outside ER, check the condition of exhaust from the funnel and vents on main deck.
All officers in charge of the engineering watch shall understand operating procedures of important machinery and systems and their respective duties in case of fire and black out.
Engine Room bilges shall be monitored and kept dry at all times. Engine Room bilges shall be pumped out either to bilge holding tank/slop tank or overboard through 15 ppm separator with strict adherence to MARPOL regulations and Coastal State/Port State regulations. Entries required by MARPOL regulations shall be made in the Oil Record Book — Part I.
Engine Room Log Book shall be preserved neatly and in orderly manner. All entries shall be accurate. In case of any wrong entry, a line must be drawn across wrong entry and correction shall be entered above or alongside with the initial of the concerned engineer. | Procedures

All efforts shall be made to rectify defects, if any, and attending superintendent informed immediately for arranging spares, if required, and defective machinery made operational at the earliest.

Chief Engineer Officer‘s Standing Orders
Chief Engineer Officer shall issue standing orders, clearly detailing the various aspects for safe and efficient running of machinery. The incumbent Chief Engineer Officer shall sign these standing orders. All officers in charge of the engineering watch and other Engineer Officers (where applicable) shall read and acknowledge these standing orders by duly signing the same. A copy of Chief Engineer Officer‘s standing orders shall be placed in the engine control room.
The standing orders may vary in scope but shall include, and not be limited to, the matters such as:
Relieving officer in charge of the engineering watch shall be in the Engine Room 15 minutes before commencement of his watch and apprise himself about operating conditions of all the running engine room machinery and systems.
Prior coming to Engine Room, the relieving officer in charge of the engineering watch shall visit and inspect other machinery spaces located outside ER, check the condition of exhaust from the funnel and vents on main deck.
All officers in charge of the engineering watch shall understand operating procedures of important machinery and systems and their respective duties in case of fire and black out.
Engine Room bilges shall be monitored and kept dry at all times. Engine Room bilges shall be pumped out either to bilge holding tank/slop tank or overboard through 15 ppm separator with strict adherence to MARPOL regulations and Coastal State/Port State regulations. Entries required by MARPOL regulations shall be made in the Oil Record Book — Part I.
Engine Room Log Book shall be preserved neatly and in orderly manner. All entries shall be accurate. In case of any wrong entry, a line must be drawn across wrong entry and correction shall be entered above or alongside with the initial of the concerned engineer. | Procedures

Familiarisation with Machinery and Machinery Operations
All Engineer Officers upon joining the vessel shall familiarise themselves with emergency procedures, lay out of machinery spaces, systems, escape routes, water tight doors, location and operation of all emergency, safety and fire fighting equipment. A ship specific checklist shall be prepared and used to complete the familiarisation and the duly filled in checklist shall be filed in File No.306 with Chief Engineer Officer. For preparation of this checklist guidance may be taken from the sample checklist Form: E12 (Sample).

Stand-by Arrangements
Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure regular trying/testing out of all stand-by arrangements and machinery, provided on board, in order to promote reliability of such equipment and systems. All stand-by machinery available on board shall be identified and their change-over intervals shall be specified and ship personnel shall be made aware of these change-over intervals. Special emphasis shall be given to the overall cleanliness of Engine Room and other machinery spaces in order to minimise the risk of fire. Combustible material like oily rags and waste, which are generated during maintenance and repairs, shall not be allowed to accumulate and shall be periodically disposed of through the incinerator. All drip trays and gutters for various machinery and tanks etc. shall be kept clean and drains from these areas to be kept clear. Flammable stores shall be stored in a safe and secured space. Paints shall be stored only in the designated lockers, fitted with fire fighting arrangement.
Chemicals shall be handled with care and stored in a safe and well-ventilated space. Proper instructions for handling the chemicals shall be displayed in the vicinity.
No smoking is allowed outside the specified areas.
All engineer officers shall read and understand Shipboard SMS Manual and related documents and clarify doubts with Chief Engineer Officer.
Officers in charge of the engineering watch and engineer officers forming a part of the watch shall acknowledge all alarms and take remedial measures immediately in consultation with the Chief Engineer Officer.
Change of any setting of alarms, controllers, etc. is not allowed without permission of Chief Engineer Officer.
Presence of Chief Engineer Officer or Second Engineer Officer in E/R does not relieve the officer in charge of the engineering watch of his responsibilities unless specified.
No hot work is permitted inside or outside Engine Room, without prior permission from the Chief Engineer Officer. No hot work is permitted during F.O. loading/discharging/ bunkering operations.
All watertight doors shall be kept closed at sea. Entry into enclosed space shall be made only with the permission of Chief Engineer Officer.
Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that all loose heavy objects are secured in E/R.
The Bridge and Chief Engineer Officer shall be immediately informed in case of any abnormal situation, which requires reduction of pitch (CPP)/stopping the Main Engine and of steering failure (loss of steering). However, as far as possible, the Bridge and Chief Engineer Officer shall be alerted prior to aforesaid action as this would afford maximum time to navigating personnel to take appropriate action.
The Chief Engineer Officer shall be immediately contacted upon receiving notice for arrival location/port.
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall notify the Chief Engineer Officer without delay
When engine damage or a malfunction occurs which may be such as to endanger the safe operation of the ship;
When any malfunction occurs which, it is believed, may cause damage or breakdown of propulsion machinery, auxiliary machinery or monitoring and governing systems; In any emergency or if in any doubts as to what decision or measures to take.
Despite the requirement to notify the Chief Engineer Officer in the foregoing circumstances, the officer in charge of the engineering watch shall not hesitate to take immediate action for the safety of the ship, its machinery and crew where circumstances require.
All Engine Room personnel while in Engine Room and other machinery spaces shall wear protective equipment such as eye, ear and head protection depending on the area of work. They shall also wear proper fitting boiler suits and safety shoes. | Special emphasis shall be given to the overall cleanliness of Engine Room and other machinery spaces in order to minimise the risk of fire. Shipboard Operations (Machinery) | 
Principles to be observed in keeping an engineering watch
The term ‗Engineering Watch‘ as used in the Shipboard SMS Manual means either a person or a group of personnel comprising the watch.
The officer in charge of the engineering watch is the Chief Engineer Officer‘s representative and is primarily responsible, at all times, for the safe and efficient operation and upkeep of machinery affecting the safety of the ship and is responsible for the inspection, operation and testing, as required, of all machinery and equipment under the responsibility of the engineering watch.

Watch arrangements at sea
The composition of the engineering watch shall, at all times, be adequate to ensure the safe operation of all machinery affecting the operation of the ship, in either automated or manual mode, and be appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions.
When deciding the composition of the engineering watch, which may include appropriately qualified ratings, the following criteria, inter-alia, shall be taken into account:
The type of ship and the type and condition of the machinery;
Adequate supervision, at all times, of machinery affecting the safe operation of the ship;
Any special modes of operation dictated by conditions such as weather, shallow waters, emergency conditions, damage containment or pollution abatement;
The qualifications and experience of the engineering watch;
The safety of life, ship, cargo and port and protection of the environment;
The observance of applicable rules and regulations; and
Maintaining the normal operations of the ship.

Taking Over Watch at Sea
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall not hand over the watch to the relieving officer if there is reason to believe that the latter is not capable of carrying out the watch keeping duties effectively, in which case the Chief Engineer Officer shall be notified. The relieving officer of the engineering watch shall ensure that the members of the relieving engineering watch are fully capable of performing their duties effectively.
Prior to taking over the engineering watch, relieving officers shall satisfy themselves regarding at least the following:
The standing orders and special instructions of the Chief Engineer Officer relating to the operation of the ship‘s systems and machinery;
The nature of all work being performed on machinery and systems, the personnel involved and potential hazards;
The level and, where applicable, the condition of water or residues in bilges, ballast tanks, slop tanks, reserve tanks, fresh water tanks, sewage tanks and any special requirements for use or disposal of the contents thereof;
The condition and level of fuel in the reserve tanks, settling tank, day tank and other fuel storage facilities;
Any special requirements relating to sanitary system disposals; | Principles to be observed in keeping an engineering watch

Condition and mode of operation of the various main and auxiliary systems, including the electrical power distribution system;
Where applicable, the condition of monitoring and control console equipment, and which equipment is being operated manually;
Any potentially adverse conditions resulting from bad weather or shallow water;
Any special modes of operation dictated by equipment failure or adverse ship conditions;
The reports of Engine-Room ratings relating to their assigned duties;
The availability of fire-fighting appliances;
The status of Engine Room log; and
Operations relating to ballasting/deballasting.

Performing Engineering Watch at Sea
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that the established watch keeping arrangements are maintained and that, under direction, engine-room ratings, if forming part of the engineering watch, assist in the safe and efficient operation of the propulsion machinery and auxiliary equipment. The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall continue to be responsible for machinery-space operations, despite the presence of the Chief Engineer Officer in the machinery spaces, until specifically informed that the Chief Engineer Officer has assumed that responsibility and this is mutually understood.
All members of the engineering watch shall be familiar with their assigned watch keeping duties. In addition, every member shall, with respect to the ship they are serving in, have knowledge of:
The use of appropriate internal communication system;
The escape routes from machinery spaces;
The Engine Room alarm systems and be able to distinguish between the various alarms, with special reference to the fire-extinguishing media alarm; and
Number, location and types of firefighting equipment and damage control gear in machinery spaces, together with their use and various safety precautions to be observed.

Any machinery not functioning properly, expected to malfunction or requiring special service shall be noted along with any action already taken. Plans shall be made for any further action if required.

When the machinery spaces are in the manned condition, the officer in charge of the engineering watch shall at all times be readily capable of operating the propulsion equipment in response to needs for changes in direction or speed.

All bridge orders shall be promptly executed. The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that the main propulsion unit controls, when in the manual mode of operation, are continuously attended under stand-by or manoeuvring conditions.

Due attention shall be paid to the ongoing maintenance and support of all machinery, including mechanical, electrical, electronic, hydraulic and pneumatic systems, their control apparatus and associated safety equipment, all accommodation service systems equipment and the recording of stores and spare gear usage. | Condition and mode of operation of the various main and auxiliary systems, including the electrical power distribution system;

Shipboard Operations (Machinery) | 
The Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that the officer in charge of the engineering watch is informed of all preventive maintenance, damage control, or repair operations to be performed during the engineering watch. The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall be responsible for the isolation, bypassing and adjustment of all machinery under the responsibility of the engineering watch that is to be worked on, and shall record all work carried out.

When the Engine Room is put in a stand-by condition, the officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that all machinery and equipment, which may be used during manoeuvring is in a state of immediate readiness and that an adequate reserve of power is available for steering gear and other requirements.

Officers in charge of an engineering watch shall not be assigned or undertake any duties which would interfere with their supervisory duties in respect of the main propulsion system and ancillary equipment. They shall keep the main propulsion plant and auxiliary systems under constant supervision until properly relieved, and shall periodically inspect the machinery under their charge. They shall also ensure that adequate rounds of the machinery and steering-gear spaces are made for the purpose of observing and reporting equipment malfunctions or breakdowns, performing or directing routine adjustments, required upkeep and any other necessary tasks.

Officers in charge of an engineering watch shall direct any other member of the engineering watch to inform them potentially hazardous conditions that may adversely affect the machinery or jeopardize the safety of life or of the ship.

The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that the machinery space watch is supervised, and shall arrange for substitute personnel in the event of the incapacity of any engineering watch personnel. The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall not leave the machinery space unsupervised in a manner that would prevent the manual operation of the Engine Room plant or throttles.

The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall take the action necessary to contain the effects of damage resulting from equipment breakdown, fire, flooding, rupture, collision, stranding, or other cause.

Before going off duty, the officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that all events related to the main and auxiliary machinery, which have occurred during the engineering watch, are suitably recorded.

The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall co-operate with any engineer in charge of maintenance work during all preventive maintenance, damage control or repairs. This shall include but not necessarily be limited to:
Isolating and bypassing machinery to be worked on;
Adjusting the remaining plant to function adequately and safely during the maintenance period; | The Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that the officer in charge of the engineering watch is informed of all preventive maintenance, damage control, or repair operations to be performed during the engineering watch. Recording, in the engine-room log or other suitable document, the equipment worked on and the personnel involved, and which safety steps have been taken and by whom, for the benefit of relieving officers and for record purpose; and
Testing and putting into service, when necessary, the repaired machinery or equipment.
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that any Engine Room ratings that perform maintenance duties are available to assist in the manual operation of machinery in the event of automatic equipment failure.
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall bear in mind that changes in speed, resulting from machinery malfunction, or any loss of steering, may imperil the safety of the ship and life at sea. The Bridge shall be immediately notified, in the event of fire, and of any impending action in machinery spaces that may cause reduction in the ship‘s speed, imminent steering failure, stoppage of the ship‘s propulsion system or any alteration in the generation of electric power or similar threat to safety. This notification, where possible, shall be accomplished before changes are made, in order to afford the Bridge the maximum available time to take whatever action is possible to avoid a potential marine casualty.

The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall give the watch keeping personnel all appropriate instructions and information, which will ensure the keeping of a safe engineering watch. Routine machinery upkeep, performed as incidental tasks as a part of keeping a safe watch, shall be set up as an integral part of the watch routine. Detailed repair maintenance involving repairs to electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic or applicable electronic equipment throughout the ship shall be performed with the cognisance of the officer in charge of the engineering watch and Chief Engineer Officer. These repairs shall be recorded.
7.2.2.6 Engineering Watchkeeping in different conditions and areas Restricted Visibility/Heavy Traffic
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that sufficient air pressure is available for sound signals and that the auxiliary machinery, used for manoeuvring, is readily available.

Coastal and Congested Waters
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that all machinery involved with the manoeuvring of the ship can immediately be placed in the manual mode of operation when notified that the ship is in congested waters. The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall also ensure that an adequate reserve of power is available for steering and other manoeuvring requirements. Emergency steering and other auxiliary equipment shall be ready for immediate operation.

Ship at Anchor
At an unsheltered anchorage the Chief Engineer Officer shall consult with the Master whether or not to maintain the same engineering watch as when under way.
When a ship is at anchor in an open roadstead or any other virtually ―at-sea‖ condition, the engineer officer in charge of the engineering watch shall ensure that: | Recording, in the engine-room log or other suitable document, the equipment worked on and the personnel involved, and which safety steps have been taken and by whom, for the benefit of relieving officers and for record purpose; and

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Machinery) | 
Proper engineering watch is kept;
Periodic inspection is made of all operating and stand-by machinery;
Main and auxiliary machinery is maintained in a state of readiness in accordance with orders from the bridge;
Measures are taken to protect the environment from pollution by the ship; and that applicable pollution-prevention regulations are complied with; and
All damage control and fire-fighting systems are in readiness.

Watch Arrangements in Port
The Chief Engineer Officer, in consultation with the Master, shall ensure that engineering watch keeping arrangements are adequate to maintain a safe engineering watch while in port. When deciding the composition of the engineering watch that may include appropriate Engine Room ratings, the following points are among those to be taken into account:
on all ships of 3000 kW propulsion power and over there shall always be an officer in charge of the engineering watch;
on ships of less than 3000 kW propulsion power there may be, at the Master‘s discretion and in consultation with the Chief Engineer Officer, no officer in charge of the engineering watch;
officers, while in charge of an engineering watch, shall not be assigned or undertake any task or duty which would interfere with there supervisory duty in respect of the ship‘s machinery system;
maintaining the normal operations of the ship; and
comply with applicable rules and regulations.

Taking Over Engineering Watch in Port
The officer in charge of the engineering watch shall not hand over the watch to the relieving officer if there is reason to believe that the latter is obviously not capable of carrying out the watch keeping duties effectively, in which case the Chief Engineer Officer shall be notified.
The relieving officer of the engineering watch shall ensure that the members of the relieving engineering watch are fully capable of performing their duties effectively.

Prior taking over the engineering watch in port, the relieving officer shall be informed by the officer in charge of the engineering watch as to:
The standing orders of the day, any special orders relating to the ship operations, maintenance functions, repairs to the ship‘s machinery or control equipment;
The nature of all work being performed on machinery and systems on board ship, personnel involved and potential hazards;
The level and condition, where applicable, of water or residue in bilges, ballast tanks, slop tanks, sewage tanks, reserve tanks and special requirements for the use or disposal of the contents thereof;
Any special requirements relating to sanitary system disposals;
The condition and state of readiness of portable fire-extinguishing equipment and fixed fire-fighting installations and fire-detection systems;
Authorised repair personnel on board engaged in engineering activities, their work locations and repair functions and other authorised persons on board and required crew; | Proper engineering watch is kept;

Any port regulations pertaining to ship effluents, fire-fighting requirements and ship readiness, particularly during potential bad weather conditions;

Unloading/loading of cargo machinery operations and ballasting/deballasting.
Relieving officers, before assuming charge of the engineering watch, shall satisfy themselves that they are fully informed by the officer being relieved, as outlined above, and:
Be familiar with existing and potential sources of power, heat and lighting and their distribution;
Know the availability and condition of ship‘s fuel, lubricants and all water supplies; and
Be ready to prepare the ship and its machinery, as far as is possible, for stand-by or emergency conditions, as required.

7.2.2.9	Performing Engineering Watch in Port
Officers in charge of the engineering watch shall pay particular attention to:
The observance of all orders, special operating procedures and regulations concerning hazardous conditions and their prevention in all areas in their charge;
The instrumentation and control system, monitoring of all power supplies, components and system in operation;
The techniques, methods and procedures necessary to prevent violation of the pollution regulations of the local authorities; and
The state of the bilges.
Officers in charge of the engineering watch shall:
In emergencies, raise the alarm when in their opinion the situation so demands, and take all possible measures to prevent damage to the ship, persons on board and cargo;
Be aware of the deck officer‘s needs relating to the equipment required in the loading or unloading of the cargo and the additional requirements of the ballast and other ship stability control systems;
Make frequent rounds of inspection to determine possible equipment malfunction or failure, and take immediate remedial action to ensure the safety of the ship, of cargo operations, of the port and the environment.
Ensure that the necessary precautions are taken, within their area of responsibility, to prevent accidents or damage to the various electrical, electronic, hydraulic, pneumatic and mechanical systems of the ship;
Ensure that all important events affecting the operation, adjustment or repair of the ship‘s machinery is satisfactorily recorded. | Any port regulations pertaining to ship effluents, fire-fighting requirements and ship readiness, particularly during potential bad weather conditions;
The lines of communication available between the ship and shore personnel, including port authorities, in the event of an emergency arising or assistance being required;
Any other circumstances of importance to the safety of the ship, its crew, cargo or the protection of the environment from pollution;

Operating Instructions
Main Propulsion (CPP) and Bow Thruster
An efficient ME and Bow thruster operation is directly linked with maintaining correct parameters while at sea, supported by planned maintenance/overhauls in Port. Planned maintenance and overhaul routines are described in section 10. Following procedures shall be followed:
The pressures and temperatures of lubricating oil and cooling water systems shall be maintained as per manufacturer‘s specifications.
No alarm shall be neglected. It has to be immediately acknowledged and properly investigated in order to ascertain correct course of action.
At sea only one air receiver to be in service. The second receiver shall be fully pressed up and kept as standby.
Stern tube lubricating oil to be checked for water contamination once a week.

Preparing for Arrival Port (refer Checklists Form: E01 & Form: E03)
Before arrival in port, following procedures shall be observed:
Auxiliary Engine/Shaft Generator to be kept stand-by
Try out steering operation in manual (follow up and non follow up)
Start second steering gear unit in parallel and try out both steerings
Try out communication systems
Try out pitch control (CPP) on Ahead/Astern directions
Try out Bow Thruster controls in coordination with bridge
Try out ship‘s whistles
Stop fresh water generator (where applicable)
Change over low sea suction to high sea suction, if required

Preparing for Departure Port (refer Checklists Form: E01 & Form: E02)
Auxiliary Engine/Shaft Generator to be kept stand-by
Test controls and synchronise engine room clock
Try out ship‘s whistle
Press up air receivers and blow off any moisture from the system
Obtain propeller clearance from Bridge and turn the engine on turning gear
Start all the associated machinery required for ME/CPP and Bow thruster operation
Blow through the ME.
Start ME and run on zero pitch. Try out CPP in ahead and astern directions.
Try out steering gear
Put on power for forward and aft deck machinery
Inform Chief Engineer Officer whenever notices for ME on standby received.

Daily checks of Auxiliary Diesel Engines when on ‗Standby‘ mode
Starting air pressure normal; air receiver drained of water and starting air isolating valve is open.
Sump oil, rocker arm oil, turbocharger oil and governor oil and expansion tank levels are normal.
Try out the standby engine/turn the engine manually few times once a day. | Operating Instructions

Shipboard Operations (Machinery) | 
Pre-Starting Checks for manual start of Auxiliary Diesel Engines
Check sump oil, governor oil, fuel oil tank, turbocharger oil and expansion tank level and turn the engine if required.
Open starting air isolating valve and start the engine.

Post-Starting Checks of Auxiliary Diesel Engines
Check the pressures and temperatures of LO and cooling water systems.
Check the exhaust temperature of individual units and turbocharger (where applicable).
Check for leakage of water or oil from joints, unions etc.
If all parameters are normal, the engine can be put on load.

Running Checks of Auxiliary Diesel Engines
Tank levels of lube oil and cooling water system tanks normal
Auxiliary Engine sump level normal
Pressures and temperatures of lube oil and cooling water systems normal
Exhaust temperature of all cylinders normal
RPM, frequency and voltage normal
No leakage of water or oil on joints, unions etc. Leakages of lubricating oil and fuel oil shall be attended immediately.
As far as practicable, the generator shall be changed over every week so that running hours of all the generators are well balanced/staggered to prevent all generators falling due for overhaul around same time.
The exhaust pipe lagging shall be visually checked every day. If the lagging is oil soaked or damaged, the same shall be renewed.
The flywheel guard shall be properly secured. The engine turning rod shall be removed as soon as the work is completed (where applicable).

Purifiers
Operation of Diesel Oil/Lubricating Oil Purifier as applicable
To achieve effective and efficient purification of fuel oil, the following care shall be taken:
Purifier maker‘s instructions to be followed.
The flow rate to the purifiers shall be adjusted to optimum and shall be a little more than the actual consumption of the engine.
The purifier shall be desludged/cleaned at regular intervals.
Service and settling tanks shall daily be drained off water content.
Depending on availability of time and quality of fuel, purifiers may be run on tank to tank re-circulation.

Bilge Water Separator and Handling of Waste Oil
MARPOL regulations strictly prohibit discharge of oil and oily waste overboard without treatment. In order to prevent pollution, following measures shall be adopted:
Direct overboard valves from sludge and bilge pumps in Engine Room shall be locked in closed position. However, Emergency Bilge line shall not be locked, being a safety item.
The bilge water shall be discharged overboard only through 15 ppm separator and in strict compliance with MARPOL regulations. Sludge from purifiers and LO drain tanks etc. | Pre-Starting Checks for manual start of Auxiliary Diesel Engines

Check sump oil, governor oil, fuel oil tank, turbocharger oil and expansion tank level and turn the engine if required.
Open starting air isolating valve and start the engine.

Post-Starting Checks of Auxiliary Diesel Engines
Check the pressures and temperatures of LO and cooling water systems.
Check the exhaust temperature of individual units and turbocharger (where applicable).
Check for leakage of water or oil from joints, unions etc.
If all parameters are normal, the engine can be put on load.

Running Checks of Auxiliary Diesel Engines
Tank levels of lube oil and cooling water system tanks normal
Auxiliary Engine sump level normal
Pressures and temperatures of lube oil and cooling water systems normal
Exhaust temperature of all cylinders normal
RPM, frequency and voltage normal
No leakage of water or oil on joints, unions etc. Leakages of lubricating oil and fuel oil shall be attended immediately.
As far as practicable, the generator shall be changed over every week so that running hours of all the generators are well balanced/staggered to prevent all generators falling due for overhaul around same time.
The exhaust pipe lagging shall be visually checked every day. If the lagging is oil soaked or damaged, the same shall be renewed.
The flywheel guard shall be properly secured. The engine turning rod shall be removed as soon as the work is completed (where applicable).

Purifiers
Operation of Diesel Oil/Lubricating Oil Purifier as applicable
To achieve effective and efficient purification of fuel oil, the following care shall be taken:
Purifier maker‘s instructions to be followed.
The flow rate to the purifiers shall be adjusted to optimum and shall be a little more than the actual consumption of the engine.
The purifier shall be desludged/cleaned at regular intervals.
Service and settling tanks shall daily be drained off water content.
Depending on availability of time and quality of fuel, purifiers may be run on tank to tank re-circulation.

Bilge Water Separator and Handling of Waste Oil
MARPOL regulations strictly prohibit discharge of oil and oily waste overboard without treatment. In order to prevent pollution, following measures shall be adopted:
Direct overboard valves from sludge and bilge pumps in Engine Room shall be locked in closed position. However, Emergency Bilge line shall not be locked, being a safety item.
The bilge water shall be discharged overboard only through 15 ppm separator and in strict compliance with MARPOL regulations. Sludge from purifiers and LO drain tanks etc.

Handling of Sewage (MARPOL Annex IV) Sewage Management
In compliance with MARPOL Annex IV, discharge of sewage from the ship to sea shall be as per the rule requirement. Offshore vessels are fitted with a sewage holding tank and sewage transfer pump.
Discharging of sewage which is not comminuted or disinfested, is prohibited within the territorial waters (12 NM from the nearest land).
The sewage holding tanks shall be cleaned/inspected during planned lay up/dry-docking.
Holding tank shall be emptied out before entry into territorial waters. | Handling of Sewage (MARPOL Annex IV) Sewage Management

In territorial waters, sewage shall be collected in sewage holding tank and the sewage overboard discharge valve is to be kept shut to avoid any inadvertent discharge.
Before undertaking sewage discharge, it shall be ensured that the ship is enroute and is more than 12 NM from the nearest land and navigational speed is in excess of 4 knots or consistent with the discharge rate approved by the Administration. Discharge shall be carried out at a moderate speed so that the effluent does not produce visible floating solids nor does cause discoloration of the surrounding water.
Record shall be maintained in Sewage Discharge Log as under:

In dry-dock/lay-up having long port stay, the contents of the sewage holding tank, if used, shall be transferred to the port reception facility and receipts shall be obtained for records.

A standard discharge connection, in compliance with MARPOL Annex IV Reg. 10.1 shall be fitted to the ship‘s discharge pipe line to facilitate discharge of sewage to reception facilities. In dry-dock/lay-up having long port stay, the contents of the sewage holding tank, if used, shall be transferred to the port reception facility and receipts shall be obtained for records.

7.2.3.9   Handling of Garbage (MARPOL Annex V)
In compliance with MARPOL Annex V, disposal of garbage from the ship shall be as per the rule requirement. Garbage includes all kind of food, domestic and operational waste generated during normal operation of the vessel and liable to be disposed off continuously and periodically. Regulation totally prohibits disposal of plastics anywhere into the sea, and severely restricts discharges of other garbage from ships in coastal waters and ―Special Areas‖.
Vessel shall prominently display placards written in English, notifying the crew of the garbage disposal requirements.

Garbage Management Plan shall be available on board with written procedures for collecting, storing and disposing of garbage. Chief Officer shall the designated person incharge of implementing the Plan. Garbage Record Book shall be available on board to record all disposal, date, time, position of the ship and estimated quantity and shall be signed. The book shall be retained for a period of two years after the date of the last entry.

When Garbage is landed ashore in port, entries shall be made in the Garbage Record Book and receipts shall be obtained for records. The instructions on the cover page of the Garbage Record Book shall be complied with. | In dry-dock/lay-up having long port stay, the contents of the sewage holding tank, if used, shall be transferred to the port reception facility and receipts shall be obtained for records.

A standard discharge connection, in compliance with MARPOL Annex IV Reg. 10.1 shall be fitted to the ship‘s discharge pipe line to facilitate discharge of sewage to reception facilities. When Garbage is landed ashore in port, entries shall be made in the Garbage Record Book and receipts shall be obtained for records. The instructions on the cover page of the Garbage Record Book shall be complied with. | In dry-dock/lay-up having long port stay, the contents of the sewage holding tank, if used, shall be transferred to the port reception facility and receipts shall be obtained for records.

A standard discharge connection, in compliance with MARPOL Annex IV Reg. 10.1 shall be fitted to the ship‘s discharge pipe line to facilitate discharge of sewage to reception facilities. In dry-dock/lay-up having long port stay, the contents of the sewage holding tank, if used, shall be transferred to the port reception facility and receipts shall be obtained for records.

7.2.3.9   Handling of Garbage (MARPOL Annex V)
In compliance with MARPOL Annex V, disposal of garbage from the ship shall be as per the rule requirement. Garbage includes all kind of food, domestic and operational waste generated during normal operation of the vessel and liable to be disposed off continuously and periodically. Regulation totally prohibits disposal of plastics anywhere into the sea, and severely restricts discharges of other garbage from ships in coastal waters and ―Special Areas‖.
Vessel shall prominently display placards written in English, notifying the crew of the garbage disposal requirements.

Garbage Management Plan shall be available on board with written procedures for collecting, storing and disposing of garbage. Chief Officer shall the designated person incharge of implementing the Plan. Garbage Record Book shall be available on board to record all disposal, date, time, position of the ship and estimated quantity and shall be signed. The book shall be retained for a period of two years after the date of the last entry.

When Garbage is landed ashore in port, entries shall be made in the Garbage Record Book and receipts shall be obtained for records. The instructions on the cover page of the Garbage Record Book shall be complied with. | In dry-dock/lay-up having long port stay, the contents of the sewage holding tank, if used, shall be transferred to the port reception facility and receipts shall be obtained for records.

7.2.3.10   Prevention of Air Pollution (MARPOL Annex VI)
MARPOL Annex VI contains regulation for prevention of air pollution from ships and is focussed on properties of fuel oil and marine engines. There is significant and progressive change limiting SOx and NOx and emission of particulate matters. Vessel shall carry International Air Pollution Prevention (IAPP) compliance certificate along with supplement.
Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS) Emission Control – Reg. 12.
Deliberate venting of ODS such as the Freons and Halons often used in air conditioning, refrigeration and firefighting systems. The vessel shall comply with applicable provisions of the Annex restricting emission of ozone depleting substances. Regulation does not apply to permanently sealed equipment, where there are no refrigerant charging connections or potentially removable components containing ODS (such as domestic refrigerators). The vessel shall maintain a list of equipment containing ODS and an ODS record book in the following format.

Note: –	Part B shall be made for each single service made to the ODS system identified in Part A
Completed log sheet shall be kept permanently in ship‘s ODS record book.
A separate log sheet shall be used for each individual ODS system or equipment.
Entries in the ODS record book are to be recorded in terms of mass (kg) of the substance and are to be completed without delay on each occasion, with respect of the following:
Recharge, full or partial of equipment containing ODS
Repair or maintenance of equipment containing ODS
Discharge of ODS to the atmosphere (deliberate or non-deliberate)
Discharge of ODS to shore based reception facilities
Supply of ODS to the ship
The ODS record book may form part of an existing log book or electronic recording system as approved by the Administration.

Refrigeration Equipment Operating Procedure Regular Checks
Check parameters such as pressure, temperature, oil level in condenser and receiver, etc.
Check for leaks at least once every week by a detector and record results in log book.
Ensure all alarms and trips are operational.
Collect system gas in the condenser, if the plant is required to be kept off for more than 48 hours.
Consumption of refrigerant should be closely monitored and recorded.

Maintenance
Collect complete gas from the system into the condenser/receiver prior carrying out any maintenance on the system or on the compressor unit.
Observe maker‘s instructions.
Do not release any refrigerant to the atmosphere.

Action in case of Accidental Leakages
If any leakage is detected, system contents shall be collected suitably into a receiver/ receptacle and defects to be rectified.
When major repairs to refrigeration and A/C system are undertaken using shore assistance, the workshop shall be instructed to collect the system contents and recharge the system after repairs with minimum possible escape of refrigerant gas.
Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) Emission – Reg. 13
The emission of Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) to atmosphere to limit pollution is controlled mainly through engine design, tuning and maintenance. In compliance with the regulation, the operation of a diesel engine is permitted when an exhaust gas clearing system, approved by the Administration in accordance with NOx Technical Code, is applied to the engine to reduce on board NOx emissions. | Note: –	Part B shall be made for each single service made to the ODS system identified in Part A

Vessel shall comply with the rules in the MARPOL towards demonstrating compliance. The regulation does not apply to emergency diesel engines, lifeboat engines and any other device intended to be used solely in case of emergency.
Sulphur Oxides (SOx) and Particulate Matters – Reg. 14
SOx emission is a function of sulphur content of the fuel. Reducing sulphur content will result in lower particulate matter emissions. Progressively tighter limits are set for sulphur content in fuel worldwide (current global cap of 3.50 % sulphur content from 1st January 2012) and increasingly stringent limits are prevailing in emission control areas (Baltic Sea and North Sea – current cap is 1% sulphur content). Additionally, some areas such as North American Waters and EU have also stipulated stringent norms for sulphur content in fuel oil.

The Company recognizes the importance of the emission control and the regulations/ amendments with respect to emission of SOx and NOx. The offshore vessels are generally trading in the Indian coast (non SECA areas). Moreover, these vessels use only high-speed diesel oil which has sulphur content well below the permissible level. As such, the Regulations with respect to sulphur content in the fuel oil do not strictly apply to these vessels.

Shipboard Incineration – Reg. 16
Incineration outside an incinerator is strictly prohibited, except incineration of sewage sludge and sludge oil, which may be incinerated in boilers and other auxiliary power plants.
Incineration in Main or Auxiliary Power plant or boilers shall not take place inside ports, harbor and estuaries.

Onboard incineration of following is prohibited:
Cargo residues and related contaminated packing material.
Polychlorinated Biphenyles (PCBs).
Garbage containing more than traces of heavy metals.
Refined petroleum products containing halogen components.
Incineration of plastics is prohibited as per Garbage Management Plan. Notice to this effect shall be displayed near incinerator. If in doubt, items may be landed to shore reception facilities without incinerating onboard. Shipboard incineration of polyvinyl chlorides (PVCs) is permitted, if the vessel is fitted with an incinerator designed for this purpose and having a specific IMO type approval certificate.

Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that proper training is imparted on board to all Engineer Officers and ratings towards operating and maintaining the incinerator. Record of such training shall be maintained on board. | Vessel shall comply with the rules in the MARPOL towards demonstrating compliance. The regulation does not apply to emergency diesel engines, lifeboat engines and any other device intended to be used solely in case of emergency.

Bunkering
In determining the requirements of fuel and lubricants for the intended voyage, the Chief Engineer Officer shall observe the following guidelines. Before departure from port, the vessel shall have:
High speed diesel (HSD) oil for the main and auxiliary engines to undertake the intended voyage (including manoeuvring, wherever applicable) until the next port where replenishment is planned;
Reserve HSD for three days sea steaming, when the duration of voyage is less than fifteen days and reserve HSD for five days sea steaming, when the duration of voyage is more than fifteen days (The voyage reserve shall be exclusive of unpumpable quantities, if any.);
Main Engine crankcase oil to undertake the intended voyage until the next port where replenishment is planned;
Reserve Main Engine crankcase oil, one spare charge, apart from daily consumption;
Auxiliary Engine crankcase oil, required for three months' consumption;
On short coastal voyages, it may be possible to execute a voyage with a lesser reserve of fuel and lubricants. In such circumstances the Master shall, in consultation with Chief Engineer Officer, use his discretion to determine the safe quantity of spare/reserve fuel and lubricants, required for the intended voyage.

Procedure for Bunker Requisition
Bunker requisition shall be prepared in accordance with the requirements mentioned above. In addition, following points shall be noted:
Chief Engineer Officer, in consultation with the Master, shall calculate right quantity of bunker requirement after considering safety stock, unpumpable and specific requirements.
Bunker request can be sent by telex or fax and shall indicate:
Remaining On Board (ROB) of all grades of oil
Required quantities and grades at pre-designated port and ETA at that port
The request for bunker shall be sent to the base port prior arrival where the Operators will make arrangements for replenishment, as per the requirement.
Whenever Company owned vessels are not under charter and require bunkers, the request shall be made to the Bunker Cell. The Bunker Cell, in consultation with the Superintendent, shall arrange the bunkers accordingly and intimate the vessel.
Ship‘s staff engaged in bunker operations shall refer to the operating instructions and safety and pollution prevention requirements in the respective sections of SOPEP manual.
Any discrepancy in quantity/quality of bunkers shall be brought to the notice of the Agents, Bunker Cell and attending Superintendent by telex or fax and also the party involved, in writing.
A test sample shall be kept till bunkers are consumed or for at least 12 months from the date of delivery.
Bunkering Procedures (Refer Sample Checklist Form: E05)
(Checklist Form: E05 to be complied with before, during and after bunkering operations)
All efforts shall be made for safe bunkering of the vessel.
Chief Engineer Officer shall be the over all in-charge of the bunkering operation. | Bunkering

Chief Engineer Officer shall form a team of personnel involved in the bunkering operation.
System – diagram shall be posted at the bunker station.
Chief Engineer Officer shall prepare the bunkering plan and the bunkering plan shall be displayed at the bunkering station on the deck and at the engine control room.

The bunkering plan shall include the following:
Name of vessel
Type of product
Specification of product (density, viscosity, flash point etc.)
Number of person on duty during the oil transfer
Duties of each person/officer indicating their position/location and duties
Procedures and duty assignment (names) for tending mooring (Ford. & Aft.)
Procedure for operating the emergency shutdown, which includes name of person in the area of emergency and means of communication.
Procedure for topping up tanks
Procedures for closure of valves on completion of oil transfer.
Procedure for emergency contacts/communication (coast guard and local agent etc.) in case of accidental discharge of oil into the water.
Procedure for closing and opening the vessel openings
Drawing of on-line samples, if fitted
Procedure for emptying the discharge containment system and bunker flexible hoses. (Refer Form: E05A (Sample Bunker Plan)

Bunker Quality (MARPOL Annex VI - Reg. 18)
Bunkers ordered should confirm to the engine maker‘s specification and taking into consideration the sulphur content restrictions for SECA.
Prior bunkering, check that the bunkers are of the same specifications as ordered;
All fuel oils are to be obtained from duly registered suppliers (registered by the appropriate authority in the country in which they operate).
Bunker supplier is required to record details of fuel oil by means of a Bunker Delivery Note (BDN).
BDN must contain at least the following information:
Name and IMO number of receiving ship
Port
Date of commencement of delivery
Name, address and telephone number of marine fuel oil supplier
Product name(s)
Quantity (metric tonnes)
Density at 15oC (kg/cm3)
Sulphur content
A declaration signed and certified by the suppliers representative that the fuel oil confirms to Annex VI requirements
Individual bunker sample shall be obtained and retained on board. In case the bunker quantity comprises of contents of multiple barges/trucks, a separate BDN would need to be issued and obtained for contents of each barge/truck. | Chief Engineer Officer shall form a team of personnel involved in the bunkering operation.
System – diagram shall be posted at the bunker station.
Chief Engineer Officer shall prepare the bunkering plan and the bunkering plan shall be displayed at the bunkering station on the deck and at the engine control room.

The bunkering plan shall include the following:
Name of vessel
Type of product
Specification of product (density, viscosity, flash point etc.)
Number of person on duty during the oil transfer
Duties of each person/officer indicating their position/location and duties
Procedures and duty assignment (names) for tending mooring (Ford. & Aft.)
Procedure for operating the emergency shutdown, which includes name of person in the area of emergency and means of communication.
Procedure for topping up tanks
Procedures for closure of valves on completion of oil transfer.
Procedure for emergency contacts/communication (coast guard and local agent etc.) in case of accidental discharge of oil into the water.
Procedure for closing and opening the vessel openings
Drawing of on-line samples, if fitted
Procedure for emptying the discharge containment system and bunker flexible hoses. (Refer Form: E05A (Sample Bunker Plan)

Bunker Quality (MARPOL Annex VI - Reg. 18)
Bunkers ordered should confirm to the engine maker‘s specification and taking into consideration the sulphur content restrictions for SECA.
Prior bunkering, check that the bunkers are of the same specifications as ordered;
All fuel oils are to be obtained from duly registered suppliers (registered by the appropriate authority in the country in which they operate).
Bunker supplier is required to record details of fuel oil by means of a Bunker Delivery Note (BDN).
BDN must contain at least the following information:
Name and IMO number of receiving ship
Port
Date of commencement of delivery
Name, address and telephone number of marine fuel oil supplier
Product name(s)
Quantity (metric tonnes)
Density at 15oC (kg/cm3)
Sulphur content

Fuel supplier is required to provide a representative fuel sample on completion of bunkering. This sample, drawn at the ships receiving manifold, shall be sealed and signed by the supplier‘s representative and the Master or ship‘s Officer in charge of bunkering operations. This sample shall be kept under the ship‘s control until the corresponding fuel oil has been consumed, but in any case for at least 12 months from the date of delivery.

Bunker grade
