7.2.4.2   Fuel and Lub Oil Sample Testing
The Company has arrangements for bunker fuel sample testing with an approved fuel testing laboratory, having worldwide facilities for fuel oil testing, with their headquarters at USA and laboratories located in Singapore and Fujairah. Testing of fuels is carried out as per the internationally accepted procedures. The Company presently sends the samples of bunkers to Singapore and Fujairah on a random basis, based on the supplier‘s history or vessels requirement for testing. The bunker sample at other ports can also be tested, if required and the samples at these ports are collected by the agents, who dispatch same to the testing lab.
In Indian coast, fuel oil is sent for testing only if the need arises and the arrangement of testing shall be made by the operating department. | 7.2.4.2   Fuel and Lub Oil Sample Testing

On Indian coast, lub oil samples from main/auxiliary engines, reduction gear, bow thruster, windlass, steering gear, stern tube etc. are sent to laboratories through the operating department for analysis every six months or earlier if required. The analysis reports are maintained on board and oil charge is replenished, if advised.

Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP)
SEEMP applies to all vessels over 400 GT cover by MARPOL Annex VI. This management plan contains a list of majors to make the ship‘s in question more energy efficient. A SEEMP will have to be present on board all vessels at the first IAPP Certificate renewal or intermediate surveys after 1st January 2013 when an international Energy efficiency Certificate will be issued.

Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI)
The EEDI requirement will apply to new ships above 400 GT. The index is defined as grams CO2/capacity nautical miles. | On Indian coast, lub oil samples from main/auxiliary engines, reduction gear, bow thruster, windlass, steering gear, stern tube etc. are sent to laboratories through the operating department for analysis every six months or earlier if required. 7.2.5    Oil Record Book
An accurate records of operations listed in MARPOL 73/78 Annex I, shall be maintained in the Oil Record Book — Part I. All entries in the Oil Record Book shall be accurate and consistent with entries in any other shipboard log books. Oil Record Book — Part I shall be maintained up-to-date by the Chief Engineer Officer and Engineer Officer(s) designated by the Chief Engineer Officer.

Routine maintenance and repairs, if any, of Oily Water Monitoring and Control System and Oil Filtering Equipment, are to be duly noted in the Oil Record Book.
The instructions on the cover page of the Oil Record Book shall be complied with. | 7.2.5    Oil Record Book

Emergency Procedures in Engine Room
Enumerated below are the measures to be taken in case of various emergency situations in the Engine Room:

Black Out
Press General alarm switch for assistance
Emergency lighting will come on automatically on failure of running generator.
Start the standby Auxiliary Engine and take on load.
If running engine has tripped on overload, make sure to switch off all machinery, to avoid high starting current. There will be preferential trip for all the non-essentials.
All the auxiliaries in auto mode shall start automatically on restoration of power. The other Auxiliaries, which are not on auto mode and have been running prior to black out, to be checked and started.
Vent all the coolers and condensers once the main SW pump has started.
Once the normal power is restored, the emergency lighting will go off.
On restoration of normal power start the following equipment:
Domestic Refrigeration System
Accommodation AC.
Purifiers
All Engine Room blowers
Exhaust fans
Non Essentials as required

Grounding
Start auxiliary generator, change over load from shaft generator.
Main Engine and Bow Thruster shall be immediately stopped so as to prevent any damage to engine, CPP and the Bow thruster.
Change over to high sea suction.
All DB tank sounding pipe weighted cocks shall be kept shut and checked.
Check and record at regular intervals soundings of all Engine Room double bottom tanks. This would indicate the condition of ship's hull in way of Engine Room.
Continuously check all the machinery spaces and equipment.
Check conditions of stern tube seals and closely monitor header tanks for stern tube and shaft seal.
Main Engine not to be immobilized unless the vessel has refloated and is secured.
Main Engine (CPP) if used to refloat must be carefully monitored against overload.
Check ME crank web deflections after the vessel has refloated to assess any distortion or misalignment.

Fire in Engine Room
Sound Fire Alarm
Establish contact with Chief Engineer Officer and officer in charge of navigational/deck watch and communicate situation
Stop all ventilation fans in ER and shut off flaps
Attempt to control the fire by whatever means available, until arrival of emergency team. | Emergency Procedures in Engine Room

However, if situation becomes hazardous, all personnel in Engine Room shall retreat to respective Muster Location and report to the Command Team.
Emergency Team shall mount an organised attempt to extinguish fire.
The following measures shall be considered, in consultation with the Command of the vessel, to fight fire in Engine Room:
Stop bunkering and cargo operations.
Close quick closing valves to oil tanks and stop oil supply to engines.
Start emergency fire pump.
In case total Halon flooding in Engine Room is inevitable, all personnel shall be evacuated and accounted for.

Crankcase Explosion
Crankcase explosion can be caused due to ‗hot spots‘ in the engine crankcase, giving rise to flammable white mist. The ‗hot spots‘ in the crankcase may be done to overheated bearings etc.

Indications of Hot Spot
Increase in crankcase temperature
Smell
Irregular running of engine
Engine noise
White oil mist at the vent

Action
Vacate vicinity of crank case relief valves.
Stop engine earliest possible.
Keep turning the engine to prevent seizure, if practicable with standby LO pump running.

Do not open Crankcase Doors unless cooled down, to avoid risk of explosion. | However, if situation becomes hazardous, all personnel in Engine Room shall retreat to respective Muster Location and report to the Command Team.

7.2.7    Checklists for Key Machinery Operations
In this section, general procedures for key machinery operations have been provided. Sample of checklists for key machinery operations are provided hereunder for the guidance of the Chief Engineer Officer. Chief Engineer Officer shall ascertain the requirement of these generic checklists suiting ship-specific requirements for key machinery operations. These checklists shall be readily available to officers in charge of the engineering watch and other relevant engineer officers. Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that various checks as detailed in these checklists are carried out and verified while conducting respective operations. After satisfactory compliance of the checklist and starting/stopping of the equipment, proper entry shall be made in the Engine Room Log Book, confirming that all the steps of the particular equipment‘s checklist have been complied with.

Shipboard Operations (Deck Systems) | 
Deck Systems
Ship officers, while carrying out Deck duties listed in this section, are reminded of their obligation to comply with practices of prudent seamanship and industry guidelines on the subject, if any.

Ship‘s Draft
Information regarding ship‘s draft shall be available on board at all times.

It is the responsibility of officer in-charge of deck watch, also referred to as duty officer, to record vessel‘s draft visually or by all available means.

Drafts shall be recorded daily morning and evening when the vessel is along side berth or at an anchorage. The draft is to be recorded in the deck log book. It shall also be recorded positively prior departure from port and immediately after arrival at berth.
Towards recording ship‘s draft following procedures to be adopted by all vessels:
Duty officer shall read the vessel‘s arrival and departure drafts whilst reading the draft, the condition of sea and swell shall also be taken into account. In case the vessel is listed to any one side, it will be necessary to read the draft of the vessel on either side so as to obtain the mean draft forward, aft and amidships.
Entering of Arrival and Departure drafts in the official log book is a statutory requirement and shall be complied with.
Master shall be informed of the Draft readings either by the Chief Officer in the morning, on arrival and prior vessel‘s departure from port.
Whilst reading the draft overside, necessary precautions shall be taken into account to ensure safety of the officer checking the draft.

Soundings
All tanks soundings shall be taken once in a day. The overall responsibility for checking soundings of E/R use tanks and Bunker and Lubricating oil tanks lies with Chief Engineer Officer. The overall responsibility for checking soundings of fresh water/ballast and drill water tanks, cofferdams, void spaces, chain lockers etc. lies with Chief Officer.
In computing quantities in tanks, vessel‘s list and trim shall be taken into account and appropriate corrections to soundings made as per the trim/list correction tables on board.

In case any appreciable or unexplained differences in the soundings from the previous entries are noticed, the Master/Chief Engineer Officer shall be informed.

Separate sounding rod/line to be used for fresh water, ballast water and oil tanks.

Fresh Water/Drill Water
The Chief Officer is overall incharge of receiving fresh water/drill water.
Separate hose shall be used for receiving of fresh water. Such hoses shall be conspicuously marked for easy identification. | Deck Systems

Shipboard Operations (Deck Systems) | 
In case fresh water is received from the barges, it may be possible to inspect the condition of fresh water inside the barge by opening manhole doors, before the same is received on the vessel.
In case there is doubt about quality of water being received and if no viable alternative is possible, water is to be kept segregated and disinfecting procedures listed in the International Medical Guide for Ships may be followed prior to using same.

Ship‘s MOT Ladder
As these vessels have low freeboard, a short-length aluminium MOT ladder is normally used. The Chief Officer shall be responsible for supervising rigging, hoisting and lowering of the MOT ladder.
The following precautions shall be observed:
The MOT ladder shall be frequently monitored and adjusted as required at the berth by a seaman on deck watch.
The MOT ladder shall be clean and undamaged and complete in all respects. It shall be adequately illuminated at night.
Safety rails or ropes shall be taut at all times.
There shall be a lifebuoy with a heaving line and self-igniting light positioned near the top of the MOT ladder.
The MOT ladder shall be manned at all times.
The persons boarding the MOT ladder shall be limited as far as possible.
Special attention shall be paid when shore cargo handling equipment such as mobile cranes are moving along the quay close to the MOT ladder and may damage it.
As far as practicable, the means of access shall be sited clear of the cargo working area, in such a location that no suspended load passes over it.
MOT ladder, its attachments and equipment used for boarding must be properly maintained and the same to be inspected before use.
MOT ladders shall be fenced on both sides throughout its length by means of upper and lower rails, taut ropes or by some equally safe means.
The stanchions supporting the fencing shall be adequately secured against accidental displacement from their sockets.
MOT ladders shall be fitted with transverse treads at suitable stepping intervals, and have wheels or rollers at the foot to allow easy movement.
The safety net shall extend on board the ship from the top of the accommodation ladder on board the ship to the extremity of the bottom platform on the quay.

7.2.8.5   Pilot Ladder
Rigging of Pilot Ladder/Pilot Combination Ladder and its use shall be in compliance with SOLAS Chapter V and shall be undertaken under the supervision of officer in charge of deck watch. It is his duty to ensure that the pilot ladder is rigged and used properly and that pilot boarding area is sufficiently illuminated, clean and free of obstructions. Any specific instructions by concerned pilotage authorities on the subject may also be complied with. Also refer Bridge Procedure Guide for boarding arrangements. | In case fresh water is received from the barges, it may be possible to inspect the condition of fresh water inside the barge by opening manhole doors, before the same is received on the vessel.

Shipboard Operations (Deck Systems) | 
Propeller Clearance
The following precautions shall be taken:
For turning the propeller, clearance in port shall be given in writing only with the concurrence of the duty officer, who shall ensure that the propeller is clear of any obstructions.
During the time the vessel is in port especially when alongside a berth, when barges, mooring boats and workshop personnel could be expected to be in the vicinity of the propeller, Chief Officer/officer in-charge of deck watch shall ensure that a crewmember is posted aft for continuous watch till such time that the period the propeller is required to be kept clear.
The Chief Engineer Officer shall discuss with the Master and arrive at the minimum essential time for which clearance will be necessary.

Maintenance of Time Zones
The 0000-2400 system of time recording shall be used.
Chief Officer or any other navigating officer assigned by the Master for such duties shall be in charge of advancing or retarding of clocks as per time zone in consultation with Master.
Navigating officer shall issue instructions through the Master, in the shipboard instruction register as and when clocks have to be adjusted. Where practicable clocks shall be advanced/retarded at night to avoid normal work schedule getting disturbed.
Advancing/retarding of the clocks shall be recorded in the Deck Log Book and Engine Room Logbook.

Bridge Note Book/Movement Book/Automatic Logger System
Instructions provided on the inner front cover of the bridge note book/movement book shall be noted for compliance.
Officer in-charge of bridge watch/engineer officer in-charge of Engine Room watch shall ensure that the following entries are made in the movement book as per instructions provided on the cover page.
Additionally, timings of following events shall be recorded in the Bridge Note Book/ Movement Book:
calling forward and aft stations;
casting off first line/time all fast/closing of lock;
name of pilot and boarding/disembarking of pilot;
damages if any caused to port property or own vessel while berthing/casting of vessel;
letting go anchor, anchor brought-up time; and
oil spills observed in the vicinity, if any
From the record kept in the Bridge note book/movement book, the officer in-charge of Bridge watch shall transfer all important entries, using his own discretion in the log book before going off the watch.
Entries in respective movement books shall be initialled by the officer in-charge of the navigation watch and engineering watch.

The Movement Book is admissible legal evidence in the event of any mishap or dispute. | Propeller Clearance

letting go anchor, anchor brought-up time; and
oil spills observed in the vicinity, if any
From the record kept in the Bridge note book/movement book, the officer in-charge of Bridge watch shall transfer all important entries, using his own discretion in the log book before going off the watch.
Entries in respective movement books shall be initialled by the officer in-charge of the navigation watch and engineering watch.

The Movement Book is admissible legal evidence in the event of any mishap or dispute. | Propeller Clearance
The following precautions shall be taken:
For turning the propeller, clearance in port shall be given in writing only with the concurrence of the duty officer, who shall ensure that the propeller is clear of any obstructions.
During the time the vessel is in port especially when alongside a berth, when barges, mooring boats and workshop personnel could be expected to be in the vicinity of the propeller, Chief Officer/officer in-charge of deck watch shall ensure that a crewmember is posted aft for continuous watch till such time that the period the propeller is required to be kept clear.
The Chief Engineer Officer shall discuss with the Master and arrive at the minimum essential time for which clearance will be necessary.

Maintenance of Time Zones
The 0000-2400 system of time recording shall be used.
Chief Officer or any other navigating officer assigned by the Master for such duties shall be in charge of advancing or retarding of clocks as per time zone in consultation with Master.
Navigating officer shall issue instructions through the Master, in the shipboard instruction register as and when clocks have to be adjusted. Where practicable clocks shall be advanced/retarded at night to avoid normal work schedule getting disturbed.
Advancing/retarding of the clocks shall be recorded in the Deck Log Book and Engine Room Logbook.

Bridge Note Book/Movement Book/Automatic Logger System
Instructions provided on the inner front cover of the bridge note book/movement book shall be noted for compliance.
Officer in-charge of bridge watch/engineer officer in-charge of Engine Room watch shall ensure that the following entries are made in the movement book as per instructions provided on the cover page.
Additionally, timings of following events shall be recorded in the Bridge Note Book/ Movement Book:
calling forward and aft stations;
casting off first line/time all fast/closing of lock;
name of pilot and boarding/disembarking of pilot;
damages if any caused to port property or own vessel while berthing/casting of vessel;
letting go anchor, anchor brought-up time; and
oil spills observed in the vicinity, if any
From the record kept in the Bridge note book/movement book, the officer in-charge of Bridge watch shall transfer all important entries, using his own discretion in the log book before going off the watch.
Entries in respective movement books shall be initialled by the officer in-charge of the navigation watch and engineering watch.

The Movement Book is admissible legal evidence in the event of any mishap or dispute.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Deck Systems) | 
7.2.8.9   Shore Leave & Sailing Board
Company recommends that shore leave to normally cease 6 hours before scheduled sailing time of the vessel. In case of port stay of the vessel shorter than 12 hours, Master shall decide on granting of shore leave. Generally, shore leave shall cease 3 hours prior sailing. Master shall ensure that personnel who shall be carrying out watch keeping duties immediately on sailing are adequately rested to carry out their duties.
Sailing board shall be conspicuously displayed at the gangway indicating following details:
sailing time and date
name of the port vessel sails for
shore leave ceasing time
any other information Master may consider necessary.
The Master shall inform all departmental heads as soon as practicable regarding sailing time of the vessel and stoppage of shore leave.
All departmental heads shall advise ship‘s personnel from their respective departments regarding stoppage of shore leave time and ship‘s sailing time.
All departmental heads shall report to the Master regarding presence of all personnel on board, as required under the shore leave procedure.
Master shall take appropriate disciplinary action against the officer/rating failing to report in time or failing to report on board prior sailing.

7.2.8.10  Procedure for Issue of Formal Instructions on Board
When the Master is required to issue formal instructions in writing on matters of safety, pollution prevention and shipboard safety management, he shall use the shipboard instruction register. These instructions shall be circulated to Chief Engineer Officer, Chief Officer, 2nd Engineer Officer and other shipboard personnel that the Master deems practicable. All persons, to whom the instructions are circulated, shall acknowledge receipt of the instructions by signing the shipboard instruction register and also shall convey these instructions to other shipboard personnel working under them as necessary.
On vessels equipped with a public address system, the Shipboard Instruction Register may be supplemented by the public address system to issue formal instructions on board. | 7.2.8.9   Shore Leave & Sailing Board

Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
Special Operations on Offshore Vessels
This section enumerates typical offshore field related operations and only applies to vessels equipped for such operations.

Anchor Handling Operation
Since anchor handling operations are potentially dangerous and the hazards are inseparable from operation, risk assessment shall be made prior to anchor undertaking such operations. All crew members shall use personal protective equipments such as life jackets/life vests, helmet, safety footwear and boiler suit during the operation. Hand gloves, although falls in this category, it shall be noted that loose hand gloves can be dangerous while handling the ropes on a drum. Only personnel involved in the anchor handling operation shall be present at stations during the operation and trainees shall be supervised by experienced seafarers.

Location Plan
The rig will normally prepare a location plan indicating optimum anchor pattern and rig orientation.
Factors to be taken into consideration:
Prevailing weather
Tidal regime
Rig profile related to weather patterns
Anchor pattern (angles subtended between moorings) related to rig weather profile and dynamic loadings expected
Mooring scope
Initial anchor tensions

Equipment Checks
Before entering location of rig (and anchor handling ships), following shall be checked:
Power supply to winches/windlasses is available.
Hydraulic oil levels (if applicable)
Brake pad thicknesses.
Set brakes.
Function test controls.
Pennants, shackles, grapnels, chasers.
Navigation and survey equipment.
Weather conditions.
Current, predicted tidal rate and direction changes for the period of mooring operation.
On board and inter-ship communication.
Anchor handling tong/pelican hook and associated gear.
Lasso wires.

7.2.9.2	Towing Operations
As per MS Notice No.13 of 2008 issued by the Administration and IMO MSC Circ./884, the procedure for inspection and certification of towing permissions shall be complied with. | Special Operations on Offshore Vessels

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
Following requirements shall be adhered to:
Towing Voyage Permission is granted to the vessel for undertaking voyages originating from Port or place on Indian coast or oil development area along the coast or overseas with or without cargo of manned or unmanned towed objects during all seasons. However, it is advisable to refrain from commencing such voyages during foul weather season on the east or west coast of India (as per the seasonal period stated above).
The vessel shall comply with the Statutory Reporting under SOLAS-VTIMS/Company reporting and SAR Conventions to the concerned authorities and owner/operator during the intended voyage for her own safety, Safety of Navigation, protection of marine environment and conduct of Search and Rescue Operation.
A copy of towing permission, issued by recognized inspecting body, shall be placed on the vessel in the custody of Master. An original shall be retained by the owner/operator.
The vessel shall also be ready at all times to deal with any untoward incidents at sea in accordance with the ISM procedures, by adopting safe working including safe watch keeping/engineering and observance of good seamanship practices during the entire period of this operation.
IRS has been delegated by the Administration to issue towing permission including towing plan approval for voyages:
between Indian ports/places on the coast;
commencing from Indian port/coast and terminating in Offshore Development Areas (ODA) within EEZ or terminating at any overseas location.
However, for voyages commencing from ODA within EEZ to port or places on Indian coasts or overseas, IRS and other surveying companies have been delegated to issue towing permission, including towing plan approval.
During the inspection of towing ship, the visiting Surveyor shall verify the records, documents and certificates e.g. Statutory certificates including ships registry, certificate of survey, restricted loadline certificate (if applicable), restricted class certificate (if applicable) and Certificate of Competency of Master's and officers/crew.
Towing vessel shall also be inspected with respect to hull, machinery, closing appliances, navigational equipment, charts and publications, life saving appliances, light and sound signals, firefighting appliances, communication equipments, medical appliances and safe manning etc.
The towing permission, issued at the beginning or during fair weather seasons while trading on or around coast of India, shall remain valid for the entire fair weather season. However, during foul weather season, towing permission shall be granted for one voyage only, subject to satisfactory inspection.

Towing winches, towing pins
Main towing wires
Towing pennants
Tugger winch and wire
Spare towing wires
Spring ropes, shackles, thimbles and cordage
Securing equipment e.g. wires, chains, pelican hooks, shackles etc. | Following requirements shall be adhered to:

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
Stability
Stability calculations for the complete tow voyage shall be adequate and meeting the minimum criteria.
Care shall be taken to ensure that the tow rope does not form a large angle with respect to the centre line of the ship at any time during the towing operation, to avoid the danger of vessels capsizing.
Communication
Establish proper radio communications between towing vessels and tow.
Towing Speed
This will be fixed taking into account fuel consumption, motion induced stress on towed unit and power available.
Towing Arrangements and Equipment
Two main towing lines of adequate strength and length should be available during location moves and ocean towages.
It is recommended that at least two wire towing pennants of breaking strength equal to approximately 90% breaking strength of the main towline be carried on board.
Lookout
When towing self propelled or thruster manoeuvred assisted units, continuous lookout shall be maintained with regard to the possibility of over run by the towed unit.
Safety
As far as practicable, connection/disconnection of tow lines should be attempted during the hours of day light.
Master shall ensure that the vessel maintains position during the period of connection/ disconnection of tow lines.
Prior commencement of the operation, it shall be ensured that all necessary equipments are at site and the entire operation on deck is done under supervision of a responsible officer.
Personnel working on deck shall wear safety helmets/vests prior undertaking the connection/disconnection of tow lines.
The paying out process to commence only after the crew have been withdrawn into the accommodation.

7.2.9.3   Dynamic Positioning Operation
Some of the offshore vessels are fitted with DP-1 system (c POS + c JOY) as per the requirement of Operators. The DP system is surveyed by the Class and Class notation ‗GS – KK‘ is assigned to such vessels.
The DP system is capable of maintaining position within 5 meters in sea state 3, which means DP is not expected to be used when wind force is more than 15 knots. DP operation details, when used and not used due to weather conditions or any other reason, are to be recorded in a separate log.

Guidelines issued by the Operator in ‗Marine Procedures for OSVs‘ shall be followed for using the DP system. | Stability

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
Maintenance procedures laid down in maker‘s manual (M/s. Kongsberg Maritime A.S., Norway) shall be followed. Operating division shall be informed to arrange for maker‘s service engineer assistance in case of malfunction of the DP system.

General Guidelines for D.P. Operation
The distance of the DP vessel from the installation should not be less than the distance given in the capability plot of the vessel. Due consideration is also to be given to the prevailing weather conditions, duration of intended stay and any other circumstances, which may develop in due course to ascertain/change the closest distance of the vessel from the installation.
Most appropriate vessel heading should be selected to reduce the load on the thrusters and increase the redundancy of the system. Escape route should be identified prior to the commencement of the operation to be used in case of any exigency. The same is to be established and discussed between all departments (Deck, Engine, Diving).

While preparing a passage plan, an escape route shall be identified. The escape route selected should provide a clear path for the vessel to follow, when making a routine or emergency departure from the installation. Other vessels must stay clear of the escape route. The escape route should, if possible, extend 500 meters from the installation.

The DP operator should have an unrestricted view of the working area. Simulation of single thruster failure and capability of vessel to hold position to be worked out and recorded. Diving Superintendent and Chief Engineer Officer shall be advised accordingly.

Double bottom tanks carrying fuel oil, which provide stability to the vessel, shall be kept full in heavy weather to prevent possible structural damage to the vessel.

Tie up with DP vessel for Cargo/Bulk Transfer
At times, offshore vessels are required to tie up DP vessel for carrying out cargo/bulk transfer operation. Before undertaking such operation, Master shall refer checklist Form: OSV001 for guidance.

External Firefighting Operations by OSVs
Upon receiving instructions from charterers/OIM, inform divisional Superintendent and proceed at full speed giving the best ETA to the controlling platform.
Suspend all operations on board and proceed for assistance.
Inform all concerned departments on board about the incident. A meeting shall be held among the Departmental Heads and ONGC I/C to plan the intended operation.
Inform ECR regarding the emergency operation being planned to be undertaken and advise them to have the fire monitors and related machinery tried out/kept ready/required for fire fighting operations.
Establish radio contact with the controlling platform and advise best ETA.
OSVs must be stationed on the windward side of the installation on fire to counteract the ahead thrust generated by the monitors more effectively and to achieve the maximum | Maintenance procedures laid down in maker‘s manual (M/s. Escape route should be identified prior to the commencement of the operation to be used in case of any exigency. The same is to be established and discussed between all departments (Deck, Engine, Diving).

While preparing a passage plan, an escape route shall be identified. The escape route selected should provide a clear path for the vessel to follow, when making a routine or emergency departure from the installation. Other vessels must stay clear of the escape route. The escape route should, if possible, extend 500 meters from the installation.

The DP operator should have an unrestricted view of the working area. Simulation of single thruster failure and capability of vessel to hold position to be worked out and recorded. Diving Superintendent and Chief Engineer Officer shall be advised accordingly.

Double bottom tanks carrying fuel oil, which provide stability to the vessel, shall be kept full in heavy weather to prevent possible structural damage to the vessel.

Tie up with DP vessel for Cargo/Bulk Transfer
At times, offshore vessels are required to tie up DP vessel for carrying out cargo/bulk transfer operation. Before undertaking such operation, Master shall refer checklist Form: OSV001 for guidance.

External Firefighting Operations by OSVs
Upon receiving instructions from charterers/OIM, inform divisional Superintendent and proceed at full speed giving the best ETA to the controlling platform.
Suspend all operations on board and proceed for assistance.
Inform all concerned departments on board about the incident. A meeting shall be held among the Departmental Heads and ONGC I/C to plan the intended operation.
Inform ECR regarding the emergency operation being planned to be undertaken and advise them to have the fire monitors and related machinery tried out/kept ready/required for fire fighting operations.
Establish radio contact with the controlling platform and advise best ETA.
OSVs must be stationed on the windward side of the installation on fire to counteract the ahead thrust generated by the monitors more effectively and to achieve the maximum

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
drenching of the seat of fire. Also, better station keeping capability is achieved when heading into the wind and monitors trained right astern.
OSVs must be stationed on the windward side as close as is safe and practicable to achieve the maximum drenching. Any attempt to fight the fire while on the move with monitors directed abeam or close to the beam must be avoided as this generates turning moments which will be hard to counteract and may result in close quarter situation.
Before arriving within 500 mtrs. off the installation, stop the ship dead in a safe area before giving controls to the ECR to engage the FI-FI pump.
After FI-FI monitors have been started and control restored to wheelhouse, try out all bridge controls including slewing of the monitors from remote locations and locally.
Ensure that effective communications internal as well as external exist at all times.
As Main Engine and thruster power will be restricted when monitors are in use, caution should be exercised when using them to prevent overload.
Enroute the incident site, following shall be kept in readiness:
Have the fire monitor drain cocks closed and positioned for starting FI-FI operations?
Keep crane with personal transfer basket in readiness to pick up survivors.
Instruct and keep the hospital ready for use.
Keep stand-by generators and FI-FI pumps in readiness.
Radio Officer shall constantly monitor the situation.
Report to On Scene Commander (OSC), if any, or else take charge of FI-FI operation and instruct other vessels in the vicinity accordingly. Fire monitors should be started/stopped as per requirement of the controlling platform OSC.
On receiving instructions from controlling station, switch on fire monitors, start spraying water uniformly and move the vessel gently astern so that the spray covers the entire area on fire. Spraying of water may have to be done for cooling the adjacent areas.
Inform controlling station regarding the commencement of fire fighting/rescue operation.
Fire monitors shall be stopped once the fire is completely extinguished.
A close watch shall be maintained to detect/monitor, re-ignition at the original seat of fire.
Vessel shall remain in location till clearance from the controlling platform is received.
Form: OSV002 shall be referred for guidance.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
In case of any leak, depressurize the system before rectifying the leaks.
In case of Fuel Oil —
Check SOPEP equipment and firefighting appliance and keep same ready near manifold.
Place ‗save all‘ under the discharge manifold. In case of a leak:
Stop fuel oil pump immediately.
Inform ECR to drain the system by opening the by-pass valves.
Take all precautions as per Bunker Checklist Form: E05 and record same.
Keep starting rate/pressure low and gradually increase.
After completion of discharge of Cement or Barite, following checks to be made:
ECR to confirm that all related machinery has been stopped
Confirm rig/installation has shut its deck/manifold valves.
Shut ship‘s discharge valve.
Following to be done for venting the tank:
Alter the ship‘s heading sufficiently, so that relative wind on deck does not carry the residual cement/barite on to the ship.
Open appropriate valve on bridge console.
Instruct the seaman on deck to open the vent valve gradually (As the pressure drops in the tank, the vibration on the vent hose will gradually decrease. The vent valve can then be progressively opened)
After the tank pressure drops to zero, lift the vent hose on deck and stow properly. Form: OSV003 shall be referred for guidance.

7.2.9.7	Passenger Transfer to/from Installation
Prior to undertaking the operation of passenger transfer, checklist Form: NAV021(OS) shall be referred for safe approach to the installation.
Form: OSV004 shall be used for guidance during transfer of passengers to and from installations/vessel.
Proper communication shall be established with all concerned with the operation.
Transfer basket and rigging material shall be of approved quality.
Passengers, including patients/escorts, shall wear personal protective equipment, such as life jacket, helmet etc. and shall be given basic safety briefing before undertaking transfer operation.
Weather and sea condition shall be conducive.

7.2.9.8	Bunkering at Sea while Enroute
Masters of OSVs should take into consideration the forces that come into play when two vessels are moving in the same direction at very close quarters.
When tied up along side, Bow-to-bow, the two bows are likely to repulse each other and hence strong and sufficient number of bow ropes must be used.

7.2.9.8	Bunkering at Sea while Enroute
Masters of OSVs should take into consideration the forces that come into play when two vessels are moving in the same direction at very close quarters.
When tied up along side, Bow-to-bow, the two bows are likely to repulse each other and hence strong and sufficient number of bow ropes must be used.
Masters must check whether the prevailing state of sea and swell will permit a safe transfer operation while tied up. A better appraisal can be achieved by sailing on a

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
parallel course at the same speed for sometime at a distance of about one ship‘s length from each other and observing the interaction between the two vessels.
Adequate number of fenders (min. 2) of correct size and spaced correctly must be used.
As there will be little or no change in course once tied up, ensure that sufficient sea room exists ahead for the entire duration of stay alongside.
The bunker hose used should be of sufficient length to allow for reasonable amount of play. However, care should be taken to see that no part of the hose goes between the ships. Seamen should be posted on deck when bunkering is in progress to tend to the hose from time to time.
It is advisable to have the crew on both ships at stand bye to disconnect and cast off at short notice.
Once tied up ensure the speeds are matched correctly. Judicious use of bow thruster may be considered to ease the strain on the ropes.
Close watch on the mooring ropes must be kept at all times. In addition to the above, all precautions mentioned in Bunker Checklist Form: E05 must be observed.
Form: OSV005 shall be referred for guidance.

7.2.9.9   Pull Back Operations behind Tanker‘s Stern
ETA must be conveyed to tanker and present pull back vessel well in advance so that they are ready on arrival.
When within 2-3 cables off the tanker, convey your readiness to pick up the tanker‘s stern rope (pull back rope).
After the tanker has given final clearance and the present pull-back vessel has cast off the pull-back rope and cleared away sufficiently, commence approach very slowly keeping the Norwegian buoy right ahead. Care should be taken not to override the buoy or disturb the existing layout of the buoy and its pick up rope in water. Hence, speed must be at minimum so that the vessel can be stopped dead with minimum use of stern power when the buoy has reached very close to the bow ready to be picked up.
Bow thruster must be switched off when about 50 meters. from the buoy to prevent accidental fouling. The approach for the final 50 meters. must be done with the help of Main Engines and rudder only.
As the buoy and pick up rope will be unsighted from the forward conning station when it has reached close to the bow, it is essential that one officer is stationed at the forecastle deck with walkie-talkie to guide the Master for the final few meters.
Crew must be ready on forecastle deck with grapnel and Windlass power on.
When the buoy has reached close enough to the bow, the grapnel should be smartly thrown towards the pick rope so that it hooks onto the rope correctly. Several attempts may be required to achieve this. Master must ensure that the vessel is kept as steady as possible during this operation. Use of bow thruster is strictly forbidden at this stage.
Once the grapnel has hooked onto the pick up rope, lead the grapnel rope through the forward bow-eye, through the bollard and onto the drum of the Windlass and heave in slowly. Care must be taken to keep the pick up rope and the pull back rope slack by keeping the bow of the ship close to them. The duty officer should guide the Master properly during this time. | parallel course at the same speed for sometime at a distance of about one ship‘s length from each other and observing the interaction between the two vessels.
Adequate number of fenders (min. 2) of correct size and spaced correctly must be used.
As there will be little or no change in course once tied up, ensure that sufficient sea room exists ahead for the entire duration of stay alongside.
The bunker hose used should be of sufficient length to allow for reasonable amount of play. However, care should be taken to see that no part of the hose goes between the ships. Seamen should be posted on deck when bunkering is in progress to tend to the hose from time to time.

Close watch on the mooring ropes must be kept at all times. In addition to the above, all precautions mentioned in Bunker Checklist Form: E05 must be observed.
Form: OSV005 shall be referred for guidance.

Care must be taken to keep the pick up rope and the pull back rope slack by keeping the bow of the ship close to them. The duty officer should guide the Master properly during this time.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Special Operations) | 
After confirmation has been received from the forecastle deck that the eye of the tanker‘s pull back rope has been placed around the bollard, slowly pull astern till the rope has taken just enough tension and the vessel has straightened astern of the tanker.
Inform the tanker time of making fast the pull back rope and take instructions from them.
If the tanker is satisfied with their position with respect to the SBM, they may instruct the pull back vessel to stop Main Engines and keep them at 10 minutes notice. Before giving controls to ECR for stopping the engines, it shall be ensured that the vessel is safely placed with respect to the tanker. Vigil against recoil of the pull back rope should be kept.
Short notice at the tanker stern means at 10 minutes notice. Hence, inform ECR/CEO to keep the Main Engines always at 10 minutes notice.
Wheelhouse should always be manned by one navigational watchkeeping officer who will keep a sharp look out for drift towards the stern of the tanker especially during calm weather and during neap tides.
When moving with the pull back rope to the port or starboard quarters of the tanker (as per their instructions), care should be taken to see that the rope is not too slack to foul the propeller while taking up stations to pull back.
When asked to pull, increase speed gradually so that no undue shock load is put on the rope. The speed should be gradually increased to the extent desired by the tanker.
During very calm sea conditions, when pulling is likely to be prolonged and from various angles, it may be desirable to make fast the pull back rope on the port or starboard quarter of the ship. This position would afford better manoeuvrability as the pulling would now be done in ahead direction which in turn would mean effective use of rudders and an extra option of using the bow thruster, if required. However, when deciding to make fast the pull back rope on the stern of the vessel, the following precautions should be taken:
When backing up to pick up the Norwegian buoy, do so cautiously so as not to foul the propeller.
The Norwegian buoy and pick up rope must be kept directly astern (behind stern roller) when approaching and till such time it has been pulled on to the deck with the capstan and the eye of the pull back rope put on the stern bollard.
No attempt shall be made to pick up the buoy from ship side close to the quarter as there is every chance of rope getting sucked into the propeller as the Master will be unsighted from aft conning station when the buoy has come up close to the quarter.
During the entire stay in this position, vigil must be exercised to see that sufficient tension is maintained on rope so that it does not come close to stern to foul the propeller.
To facilitate the above, it is recommended that one shaft be kept running always and a minimum pitch of 2-3 degrees maintained in ahead direction which will ensure reasonable tension on the rope always. Another advantage of doing this is that the vessel is always ready to carry out pulling operations as given by the tanker without any loss of time especially at night when reaction time is more.
Form: OSV006 shall be referred for guidance.

All necessary precautions must be taken to ensure that the pull back rope does not brake when pulling the pull back rope does not foul the ships propellers and the ship does not drift towards the tanker when all is stopped. | After confirmation has been received from the forecastle deck that the eye of the tanker‘s pull back rope has been placed around the bollard, slowly pull astern till the rope has taken just enough tension and the vessel has straightened astern of the tanker.

Inform the tanker time of making fast the pull back rope and take instructions from them.
If the tanker is satisfied with their position with respect to the SBM, they may instruct the pull back vessel to stop Main Engines and keep them at 10 minutes notice. Before giving controls to ECR for stopping the engines, it shall be ensured that the vessel is safely placed with respect to the tanker. Vigil against recoil of the pull back rope should be kept.
Short notice at the tanker stern means at 10 minutes notice. Hence, inform ECR/CEO to keep the Main Engines always at 10 minutes notice.
Wheelhouse should always be manned by one navigational watchkeeping officer who will keep a sharp look out for drift towards the stern of the tanker especially during calm weather and during neap tides.
When moving with the pull back rope to the port or starboard quarters of the tanker (as per their instructions), care should be taken to see that the rope is not too slack to foul the propeller while taking up stations to pull back.
When asked to pull, increase speed gradually so that no undue shock load is put on the rope. The speed should be gradually increased to the extent desired by the tanker.
During very calm sea conditions, when pulling is likely to be prolonged and from various angles, it may be desirable to make fast the pull back rope on the port or starboard quarter of the ship. This position would afford better manoeuvrability as the pulling would now be done in ahead direction which in turn would mean effective use of rudders and an extra option of using the bow thruster, if required. However, when deciding to make fast the pull back rope on the stern of the vessel, the following precautions should be taken:
When backing up to pick up the Norwegian buoy, do so cautiously so as not to foul the propeller.
The Norwegian buoy and pick up rope must be kept directly astern (behind stern roller) when approaching and till such time it has been pulled on to the deck with the capstan and the eye of the pull back rope put on the stern bollard.
No attempt shall be made to pick up the buoy from ship side close to the quarter as there is every chance of rope getting sucked into the propeller as the Master will be unsighted from aft conning station when the buoy has come up close to the quarter.
During the entire stay in this position, vigil must be exercised to see that sufficient tension is maintained on rope so that it does not come close to stern to foul the propeller.
To facilitate the above, it is recommended that one shaft be kept running always and a minimum pitch of 2-3 degrees maintained in ahead direction which will ensure reasonable tension on the rope always. Another advantage of doing this is that the vessel is always ready to carry out pulling operations as given by the tanker without any loss of time especially at night when reaction time is more.
Form: OSV006 shall be referred for guidance.

All necessary precautions must be taken to ensure that the pull back rope does not brake when pulling the pull back rope does not foul the ships propellers and the ship does not drift towards the tanker when all is stopped.

7.2.9.10  Equipments for UKOOA Compliance
As per Operator‘s requirements, some of the offshore vessels are provided with additional equipments for UKOOA compliance. Though these equipments are not covered under statutory requirements, they are to be maintained on board for inspections by Operators only:
18 Nos. EEBD sets
1 No. Fast Rescue Craft (FRC) – 9 Persons Capacity with 2 Nos. outboard motors
2 Nos. Dutch Hooks
12 Nos. Lifebuoys
30 Nos. Arm Bands
Additional Medicines as per UKOOA guidelines
1 No. Fresh Water Generator (Reverse Osmosis)
1 No. Rescue Basket (for 2 persons)
Maker‘s instruction manual shall be followed for maintenance of the above items and same shall be included in the PMS.

7.2.9.11 Vessel specific additional requirement of stability, as applicable to anchor handling tug cum supply vessels (AHTS)
Master to strictly adhere to the approved loading conditions included in the IRS approved trim & stability booklet.
In case of any deviation in loading condition, master to ensure compliance with the KGMAX envelope of draught versus trim as approved by IRS, besides the applicable mandatory stability criteria as per is code, 2008. Please refer section 7 of intact stability booklet.
Vessel to use only tank no.57 for the purpose of roll stabilization and roll stabilization is permitted only in the ballast conditions as approved by IRS.
The maximum allowed tension on the wire ropes at the time of anchor handling operations is 91tons. Master to ensure the following arrangements are functioning properly before performing the anchor handling operation.
Control System to monitor the wires
The over tension alarm when wire tension exceeds the set value.
The brake release arrangement to release the tension, when the tension exceeds the alarm set value (same not to exceed 91 Ton).
While loading/unloading any cargo en-route/at sea and while using up of consumables (FO, FW…), the IRS approved sequence must be followed in order to maintain the required forward trim and for limiting the list within 2 degrees. Please refer section 2.5.1 and 2.5.4 of stability booklet
Ballast operations not be carried out at sea unless so permitted by the approved loading conditions. Please refer section 2.5.2 of stability booklet.
Fuel oil tank no. 34 is to be used only as cargo tank. From this tank, FO not to be consumed for ship‘s purpose. To prevent accidental use of FO for ship‘s purpose from tank 34, a portable spool piece has been provided which is to be removed and kept near its vicinity, blank flange to be put from where the portable spool piece is removed. For details refer schematic drawing v‐394‐4320‐fo cargo system‐rev‐d in section 10.
The disposition and stowage of deck cargo (location, LCG and VCG) to follow the IRS approved stowage plan to ensure that the VCG and trim are within permissible values | 7.2.9.10  Equipments for UKOOA Compliance

7.2.10   Reporting
The ship‘s performance and condition of hull and shipboard equipment shall be assessed by the Technical Superintendent through visits to the vessels assigned to him at least once in six months and through reports/returns received from the ship as detailed in the tables provided in this sub-section.
The Technical Superintendent shall, based on the above information, initiate corrective actions as may be necessary viz. instructions to Master and Chief Engineer Officer, update maintenance planning and instruct repairs while availability of anticipated spares, stores and service suppliers shall be checked.
Reports/Returns from ship
The vessel shall submit regular reports/returns to the Technical Department of respective Division in the standard formats provided on board. The following pages provide a detailed matrix of reports/returns required to be sent by the vessel and the frequency of such reports/ returns.
Follow-up action arising from Superintendent‘s/Group I/C‘s instructions, if any, shall be duly recorded, complied with and communicated to the Technical Department. | 7.2.10   Reporting

7.2.11	Procedures to be followed for the familiarisation of Superintendents and Crew for Newly Acquired Vessels
When vessels under construction are being inducted into the fleet, the safety familiarisation for the top four senior officers onboard will be carried out by the respective site manager prior to delivery of the vessel. The safety familiarisation of Radio Officer/Electro Technical Officer/Electrical Officer shall be carried out by the site manager through the respective technical staff from the yard as applicable.

When second hand vessels are being inducted into the fleet, the safety familiarisation for the top four senior officers as well as Radio Officer/Electro Technical Officer/Electrical Officer onboard will be carried out by the technical officer in-charge of taking over process through respective technical staff from the seller/yard as applicable.

Checklist Form: SS006A to be referred prior new/second hand acquisition. | 7.2.11	Procedures to be followed for the familiarisation of Superintendents and Crew for Newly Acquired Vessels

Shipboard Operations (Cargo Procedures) | 
Cargo Procedures on Other Cargo Ships (OSVs/PSVs)

Safety
All cargo operations shall be supervised by the officer in charge. It is the duty of all personnel connected with the cargo or bunkering operations to have due regard for their own and other person‘s safety. No operation shall be undertaken without careful consideration being given to all risks involved and steps to mitigate any undue risk. If dangerous cargo/chemicals in small quantity are required to be carried, precautions as per IMDG Code and Material Safety Data Sheets are to be observed. Class approved Procedure & Arrangement Manual available on board, shall also be followed.

Preparation of decks used for cargo handling operations
Efforts shall be made to keep the designated area clean and oil free. Any oil soaked saw dust or other absorbent material shall be cleaned up and disposed of to prevent fire risk and accidental fall. All lashing gear and cargo handling equipment shall be stored in the appropriate place and not left scattered on deck.
Oil drums, stores etc. shall be stowed away from the cargo handling area. Areas on deck which are not to be used for cargo stowage shall be clearly marked.

Personnel in area of cargo handling operations
All personnel and particularly new personnel and passengers shall be made aware of the dangers existing on the offshore vessels, especially when working alongside a rig or production platform crane.

Use of cargo handling equipment
Cargo handling equipment/gear shall not be used by ship‘s staff, unless the Chief Engineer Officer/Ship‘s Responsible Officer is satisfied that the equipment is in a safe operational condition. The responsible person shall ensure the equipments are maintained in safe state throughout the operation.

Cargo Work
Decisions on cargo operations with regard to equipment, communications and safety procedures etc. shall be made with the agreement of the Master, OIM and the crane operator.
Effective communication shall be maintained between the bridge and deck crew. All lifts shall be checked, prior being discharged to an offshore installation.

The officer incharge of deck operations shall have a full view of the cargo operations and personnel and be able to sight the crane wire and hook during operation. He shall ensure that all deck crew stand clear of all lifts to and from the deck of the vessel.

Cargo carrying units shall be visually checked for loose items such as tools, debris etc. prior commencing discharge/loading. If such items are noticed while a cargo carrying unit is being lifted, the installation should be advised immediately.

Generally miscellaneous cargo (drill strings, various piping, machinery, chemicals etc.) is loaded on deck depending on the requirements of various offshore installations. The cargo | Cargo Procedures on Other Cargo Ships (OSVs/PSVs)

Generally miscellaneous cargo (drill strings, various piping, machinery, chemicals etc.) is loaded on deck depending on the requirements of various offshore installations. The cargo

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Cargo Procedures) | 
may be pipes or boxes/barrels/pallets etc. Care shall be taken to ensure that barrels/pipes are properly lashed. Pallets shall not be loaded on top of pipes. Smoking is strictly prohibited while loading/discharging of cargo is in progress on deck.
While using plastic coated slings, following precautions shall be exercised:
Ensure visual check of each sling to confirm good condition
Check that each bundle has been tightly slung
Avoid lifting too many bundles at one time
Ensure deck crew is well clear prior to commencing the lift and watch each lift until it is either safely landed on, or clear of the deck
At times, offshore vessels may load chemicals in packaged form for onward delivery to the mother vessels or to the offshore installations. These drums or pallets shall be properly stored and secured in a safe location on deck. Whenever chemicals are loaded on the vessel, all precautions required as per the Material Safety Data Sheets shall be exercised. The MSDS for the chemicals being carried shall be readily available to the Officer on watch. Crew and other persons involved in handling, storage, securing shall be briefed on the basis of the MSDS sheets. Copies of the MSDS sheets should be filed on board.

Risk Assessment
When required to carry out non routine cargo handling operations, the Master shall conduct a risk assessment on work to be done e.g. working in marginal weather with heavy lifts, and discuss the operation with the crew.
The Logistic coordinator shall provide the vessel with a copy of the vessel load list and dangerous goods list for each installation/port to be visited in sufficient time to permit proper stowage of cargo for the route envisaged.

Cargo which is not safe for handling, not adequately packed, not properly marked or not properly documented shall not be accepted for loading
The Master is responsible for the safe and correct loading of the vessel. He shall liaise with Logistic Co-ordinator/OIM to ensure that the vessel is loaded correctly. The Logistic Co- ordinator/OIM is responsible for providing information on cargo to be loaded including relevant declarations for dangerous goods and proper packing and labelling of dangerous goods.

The Master must receive prior notification from the OIM, if dangerous goods are to be included in back loaded cargo, so that appropriate stowage and/or segregation may be arranged.

All cargo to be back-loaded shall be inspected by competent person on the installation, who signs the dangerous goods declaration and packing certificate where required. | may be pipes or boxes/barrels/pallets etc. Care shall be taken to ensure that barrels/pipes are properly lashed. Pallets shall not be loaded on top of pipes. Smoking is strictly prohibited while loading/discharging of cargo is in progress on deck.
While using plastic coated slings, following precautions shall be exercised:
Ensure visual check of each sling to confirm good condition
Check that each bundle has been tightly slung
Avoid lifting too many bundles at one time
Ensure deck crew is well clear prior to commencing the lift and watch each lift until it is either safely landed on, or clear of the deck
At times, offshore vessels may load chemicals in packaged form for onward delivery to the mother vessels or to the offshore installations. These drums or pallets shall be properly stored and secured in a safe location on deck. Whenever chemicals are loaded on the vessel, all precautions required as per the Material Safety Data Sheets shall be exercised. The MSDS for the chemicals being carried shall be readily available to the Officer on watch. Crew and other persons involved in handling, storage, securing shall be briefed on the basis of the MSDS sheets. Copies of the MSDS sheets should be filed on board.

Risk Assessment
When required to carry out non routine cargo handling operations, the Master shall conduct a risk assessment on work to be done e.g. working in marginal weather with heavy lifts, and discuss the operation with the crew.
The Logistic coordinator shall provide the vessel with a copy of the vessel load list and dangerous goods list for each installation/port to be visited in sufficient time to permit proper stowage of cargo for the route envisaged.

Cargo which is not safe for handling, not adequately packed, not properly marked or not properly documented shall not be accepted for loading
The Master is responsible for the safe and correct loading of the vessel. He shall liaise with Logistic Co-ordinator/OIM to ensure that the vessel is loaded correctly. The Logistic Co- ordinator/OIM is responsible for providing information on cargo to be loaded including relevant declarations for dangerous goods and proper packing and labelling of dangerous goods.

The Master must receive prior notification from the OIM, if dangerous goods are to be included in back loaded cargo, so that appropriate stowage and/or segregation may be arranged.

All cargo to be back-loaded shall be inspected by competent person on the installation, who signs the dangerous goods declaration and packing certificate where required. | may be pipes or boxes/barrels/pallets etc. Care shall be taken to ensure that barrels/pipes are properly lashed. Pallets shall not be loaded on top of pipes. Smoking is strictly prohibited while loading/discharging of cargo is in progress on deck.

Shipboard Operations (Cargo Procedures) | 
Carriage of Refrigerated Containers
When offshore supply boats are required to carry refrigerated containers, the following procedures shall apply:

It shall be confirmed that the containers are in good working order. Defective containers shall not be accepted and shall be brought to the attention of the shippers for repair prior acceptance.
The ship‘s electrician shall be in attendance to supervise the electrical connection/ disconnection to ship‘s power and check during the voyage. Refrigerated containers shall be discharged to respective offshore installations at the first opportunity to avoid damage to the containers while other cargoes are being discharged/loaded at various installations.

7.8.7    Cargo Securing
The Master shall ensure that cargo and all deck equipment are adequately secured for all anticipated weather conditions during the voyage as per approved Cargo Securing Manual available on board. Irrespective of weather, sea conditions and short run, cargo shall be properly secured. Lashings shall be in place before sailing and until cargo is discharged.
The securing of cargo on unit, shall be checked before being accepted for shipment and any deficiencies remedied prior to their acceptance. The Master has the authority to carry out random inspections of containers prior loading. If inspection of any container reveals inadequate stowing, lashing or securing arrangements, inadequate marking or labelling of dangerous goods, or if the safety status of the container is in doubt, he can refuse the container for loading.
The OIM should confirm the securing of cargo in open top cargo carrying units and half height cargo carrying units. It shall be ensured that open topped waste cargo carrying units are fitted with net or permanent cover.

Cargo lashings shall be checked by the Chief Officer prior to sailing and during passage. Lashing equipment is to be inspected from time to time and on a quarterly basis, by a responsible officer, designated by the Master. Lashing material inspection and maintenance shall be recorded quarterly. Sub standard or defective lashing equipment shall not be used, even as a temporary measure.

Lashings shall be rigged so as to deny initial movement. When determining the type and extent of lashing required, the Master shall consider a number of factors. These shall include but not limited to motion characteristics of ship, anticipated weather, nature of cargo, probable order of discharge, stability, IMDG Code, installation restrictions such as orientation, crane outreach and capacity, heavy, large or awkward shaped lifts, Possible back load requirements and access to cargo.

As a general rule, heavier and larger lifts shall be stowed towards the crash rails whilst smaller lifts shall be stowed towards the centre. This will ensure the large lifts can be secured against the rails whilst affording protection to smaller lifts. | Carriage of Refrigerated Containers

Shipboard Operations (Cargo Procedures) | 
Ship‘s officers shall advise the OIM on where and how cargo shall be stowed, including any requirement for special sea fastenings. Personnel not directly involved with cargo handling operations must keep clear of working area at all times.

Rejection of Cargo
Master shall bring to the attention of OIM, any deficiencies in lifting gear or damaged cargo carrying unit when accepting cargo on board. The Master shall notify the OIM of defective lifts and return these to the installation.
On receipt of any improperly secured lifts, Master shall inform the OIM immediately and request that the lift be returned to the installation for rectification, provided that doing so does not constitute a safety hazard in itself.

Should returning the lift be impractical or dangerous, the Master shall request equipment from platform to enable the ship‘s crew to rectify the defects on board the vessel. In any event, the incident must be recorded in the vessel‘s log book and a report prepared for forwarding to OIM and to the Operator at base port.

Cargo Handling Damages (Ship or Cargo)
Stevedore Damage
It is essential that during cargo operations, a careful watch is kept for any damage caused to the vessel and her equipment by stevedoring operations. A damage report is to be completed in every case giving fully comprehensive details of the damage. Notice of any damage should be brought to the attention of the Operator.
During loading operations, the officer on watch shall inspect all units as they come on board and record and report to the Operator of any damage found.

Cargo Damage on Passage
In case of actual or suspected damage to cargo during the passage, remedial action shall be taken immediately and the Master shall inform the Operator and make note of protest on arrival at the next port/offshore installation and record in official log book. Closed containers shall not normally be opened at sea except in case of emergency such as fire, spillage etc.

7.8.9 Ballasting/Deballasting Operations in conjunction with Cargo Handling Operations
All engineer officers shall be familiar with the correct operation of the ballast pump and system and ballasting/deballasting shall be done under the supervision of a responsible engine officer.
Efforts shall be made during cargo operations to maintain the trim and the heel of the vessel within reasonable limits to ensure safe operations.
Ballast tanks shall be kept either pressed up or empty at all times; ideally only stability tanks can be kept in slack condition. When topping off tanks, the rate of pumping shall be reduced by opening the overside valve or another tank to reduce the risk of over pressurising a tank. | Ship‘s officers shall advise the OIM on where and how cargo shall be stowed, including any requirement for special sea fastenings.  | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Shipboard Operations (Cargo Procedures) | 
Loadline and Stability Requirements
The Master shall ensure that the vessel has sufficient stability during all stages of the voyage. The loadline conditions are to be strictly adhered to and any port draught restrictions taken into account when loading.

Cargo Transfer Operations
Before cargo transfer commences, the following requirements are to be satisfied:
Details of cargo to be loaded/unloaded have been communicated to the OIM.
An effective system of communication between the person supervising cargo handling on the supply vessel, the crane driver, the installation‘s deck crew and the bridge exists.
All crew members involved or stationed in the region of cargo handling activities should wear safety helmets, safety shoes, and other protective clothing where applicable.
Suitable life-saving appliances are available on cargo deck.
Mud tanks shall not be pressurised until the deck connections are made and confirmed by responsible officer.
Bulk transfer connections shall be confirmed before pumping of cargo commences with particular attention being given to the possibility of cross connections.
No attempt shall be made to disconnect hoses if the line is pressurised. Chief Engineer Officer/duty engineer must confirm that the line pressure is zero before the hoses are disconnected.
In case of leaks in the pipelines/hoses/connection points, pumping operation shall be discontinued and leak rectified before resuming operations.
While working with offshore installations, a continuous watch on weather parameters shall be kept.
OSVs working with installations during change of tide shall monitor the change in direction of the tide and alter heading and position as necessary. If required, cargo operations shall be stopped until a fresh safe heading is taken-up. Vessels tied to a Rig with mooring ropes and anchor down may have to stop cargo operations altogether before onset of the next tide.
OSVs tied-up to Rigs during cargo operations in tidal waters shall decide well in advance when to stop cargo operations so that there is sufficient time to stop cargo operations, disconnect hose, cast-off mooring ropes and pick-up anchor before the next tide change.
Sufficient sea-room shall be maintained between vessel and installation (sufficient for the crane to reach) and the safe working-heading planned in such a manner that the vessel shall be able to pull-out to safety in the event of an emergency.
When working with drill ships/DP vessels/other Floaters, ensure Yokohoma fenders (minimum 2 Nos.) and proper size and are in place. Those fenders shall be correctly spaced so that the forward fender does not slip under the flare of the ship‘s bow. Constant watch on the state of the fenders shall be kept as it has a tendency to deflate/ puncture in moderate sea conditions resulting in ship to ship contact.
When tied up, adequate number of mooring ropes shall be used and continuously monitored.
When tied up, Main Engines and Bow Thruster (if required) shall be in operation and ready for immediate use. Judicious use of Main Engines/Bow Thruster can be made to ease the strain on the ropes.
Effective external/internal communications shall be maintained at all times. | Loadline and Stability Requirements

For bulk discharge, ensure hose is of sufficient length for the prevailing weather conditions. Ensure hose does not foul any deck structures, cargo or shipside fenders.
Before commencement of bulk discharge ensure connection on deck has been confirmed and discharge valve on deck and the respective valve on the installation is open.
Ensure proper slings for different types of cargo is being provided by the installation.
Ensure safety hook is attached to the running-block of the crane. Open hooks should be strongly discouraged as it can cause serious injury to crew working on deck.
Sufficient rope, dunnage and chain binders shall be used when loading pipe cargo.
When full load of pipe cargo is carried ensure vessel has sufficient reserve buoyancy allowing for retention of sea water inside the pipe.
Masters shall continuously monitor the station-keeping capability of their vessel when working with an installation and abort operations and pull out to safety well before station-keeping limits are reached.
Before and after discharging cement or barite, the pipes shall be blown through to clear obstructions/residues.
When working on the Lee side of an installation, care shall be taken to remain clear of the machinery cooling water discharge from the installation.
When working on the Lee side in moderate sea conditions, vessel is likely to ship sea- water on deck over the stern-roller which may cause cargo to shift resulting in damage to deck fittings and injury to seamen. In such cases Masters shall alter the working heading to minimize shipment of water. If this is not possible, cargo operations on the Lee side shall be temporarily stopped or working on the weather side shall be considered.
All persons engaged in cargo operations shall wear personal protective equipment and crew shall place themselves in such a manner that there is always an escape route available so as to avoid being trapped by moving load. Tag lines shall be used to control loads as they are lowered or raised. To avoid injury, loads from installations shall be allowed to land on deck and pulled into position later with the tugger winch.

The safe haven on both sides of the deck between bulwark and crash rail shall be used to avoid injury from moving cargo. | For bulk discharge, ensure hose is of sufficient length for the prevailing weather conditions. Ensure hose does not foul any deck structures, cargo or shipside fenders.

When working on the Lee side of an installation, care shall be taken to remain clear of the machinery cooling water discharge from the installation.
When working on the Lee side in moderate sea conditions, vessel is likely to ship sea- water on deck over the stern-roller which may cause cargo to shift resulting in damage to deck fittings and injury to seamen. In such cases Masters shall alter the working heading to minimize shipment of water. If this is not possible, cargo operations on the Lee side shall be temporarily stopped or working on the weather side shall be considered.
All persons engaged in cargo operations shall wear personal protective equipment and crew shall place themselves in such a manner that there is always an escape route available so as to avoid being trapped by moving load. Tag lines shall be used to control loads as they are lowered or raised. To avoid injury, loads from installations shall be allowed to land on deck and pulled into position later with the tugger winch.

The safe haven on both sides of the deck between bulwark and crash rail shall be used to avoid injury from moving cargo. | For bulk discharge, ensure hose is of sufficient length for the prevailing weather conditions. Ensure hose does not foul any deck structures, cargo or shipside fenders.
Before commencement of bulk discharge ensure connection on deck has been confirmed and discharge valve on deck and the respective valve on the installation is open.
Ensure proper slings for different types of cargo is being provided by the installation.
Ensure safety hook is attached to the running-block of the crane. Open hooks should be strongly discouraged as it can cause serious injury to crew working on deck.
Sufficient rope, dunnage and chain binders shall be used when loading pipe cargo.
When full load of pipe cargo is carried ensure vessel has sufficient reserve buoyancy allowing for retention of sea water inside the pipe.

Safety & Security
Safety Training
Safety Training shall have two components, namely
Shipboard training;
Shore-based training.

Shipboard Training
Shipboard safety training shall consist of:
Safety Familiarisation in accordance with STCW Code A-VI/1;
Induction Familiarisation in accordance with ISM Code 6.3;
Fire Drill and Abandon Ship Drill and Training in accordance with SOLAS Ch. III;
Other Emergency Drills in accordance with ISM Code 8.0.

Familiarisation Training
All personnel who are assigned to any shipboard duty will have to undergo on board Safety Familiarisation concerning elementary safety matters before being assigned their duties. This requirement will apply to officers, petty officers, ratings and TNOCs.
Shipboard personnel, who are newly assigned to a ship, shall take full advantage of every opportunity provided to become familiar with shipboard equipment, operating procedures and other arrangements needed for the proper performance of their duties. Immediately upon arriving on board for the first time, they have the responsibility to become acquainted with the ship‘s working environment, particularly with respect to new or unfamiliar equipment, procedures or arrangements.

Safety officers shall plan and impart familiarisation. The familiarisation shall take place as soon as practicable after the personnel arrive on board the ship. The familiarisation shall be sufficient to ensure that personnel are able to:
communicate with other persons on board on elementary safety matters and understand safety information symbols, signs and alarm signals;
know what to do if:
a person falls overboard,
fire or smoke is detected, or
the general emergency alarm signal is sounded;
identify muster and embarkation stations and emergency escape routes;
locate and don life-jackets;
raise the alarm and have basic knowledge of the use of portable fire extinguishers;
take immediate action upon encountering an accident or other medical emergency before seeking medical assistance on board;
close and open the fire, weather tight and watertight doors fitted on that particular ship other than those for hull openings.

The Safety Familiarisation Checklist provided at the end of this section [Form: SS006(OS)] shall be used to impart safety familiarisation to all relevant personnel. This checklist shall be duly filled for each person who has been imparted safety familiarisation. A copy of this | Safety & Security
