 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
checklist shall be provided to the person. Another copy of the checklist shall be filed in File No.306.
In addition to the familiarisation and awareness of all ship‘s personnel detailed above, onboard familiarisation, training and instructions which shall include, but not necessarily limited to, avoid incidents of back injuries caused by manual lifting, body parts getting caught in a rotating, reciprocating and other moving machinery and injuries to hands and fingers due to use of sharp tools, improper tools and worn out tools and injuries due to improper launching and handling of lifeboats and lifeboat winches and operation and use of the ship‘s safety equipment, shall be imparted to all ship‘s personnel as soon as possible after they join the vessel. Safety officers shall plan and impart such training. Where appropriate, the assistance of other shipboard personnel may be taken to impart such training on board. A schedule of such training shall be created on board by the safety officers, in consultation with the Master. Such training shall cover:
Operation and use of ship‘s survival crafts
Location, use and function of:
Ship‘s pyrotechnics, lifebuoys and man-overboard markers
SARTs, EPIRB and Portable two-way VHF radiotelephone.
Ship‘s medical locker and first aid kits.
Thermal protective aids
Fireman‘s outfit
Emergency Escape breathing Device (EEBD)
Fixed and portable foam system
Fixed gas fire-extinguishing systems
Fire hoses and nozzles
Portable extinguishers
Fire detection and alarm systems
Anti pollution equipment
Location of emergency escapes
Problems of hypothermia, first-aid treatment
Special instructions necessary for the use of the ship‘s life-saving appliances in severe weather and severe sea conditions.
The safety officers shall obtain guidance regarding the above equipment and safety systems from the SOLAS Training Manual & Fire Safety (Ref. SOLAS Ch. III Reg. 35), where applicable and same shall be kept updated.

Shipboard Emergency Drills

Drills and Training
Drills provide an opportunity to verify that the life-saving and firefighting systems are working and that all associated equipment is in place and in good working order, ready for use.
Drills should be conducted with an emphasis on learning and be viewed as a learning experience, not just a task to meet a regulatory requirement to conduct drills. Whether they are emergency drills required by SOLAS or additional special drills conducted to enhance the competence of the ship‘s personnel, they should be carried out at safe speed (consistent with safety). Through conduct of these drills, shipboard personnel shall familiarise themselves with their duties and the equipment and senior officers may explain to them difficult elements during the drills.

Each member of the crew shall participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill every month. These drills shall take place within 24 hours of the ship leaving port if more than 25% of the shipboard personnel have not participated in abandon ship and fire drills on board that particular ship in the previous month. Abandon ship drill and fire drill shall comply with SOLAS Chapter III.

In addition to abandon ship and fire drills, emergency drills shall be organised every fortnight to practice contingency response (refer Section 8, Emergency Preparedness, of the Shipboard SMS Manual).

Training the ship‘s personnel is an important component of drills. Onboard training will familiarise ship‘s personnel with the ship systems and the associated procedures for use, operation and drills [Form: SS006(OS)]. During drills, the objective is to develop appropriate ship‘s personnel competencies, enabling effective and safe utilisation of the equipment required.

Drills shall be planned in such a way that due consideration is given to regular practice in various emergencies that may occur depending on the type of ship and its cargo. Drills, shall as far as practicable, be conducted as if there were an actual emergency. Equipment used in drills shall immediately be brought back to its full operational condition and any faults or defects in the equipment discovered during drills shall be remedied as soon as possible.

Shipboard Security
Ship‘s personnel shall be guided by the Ship Security Plan & System available on board.

Personal Safety
Personal Working Clothes
Working clothes shall be close fitting with no loose flaps or strings. Normally long-sleeved boiler suits shall be used during any work in which there is risk to upper torso, arms or legs. However, in circumstances where long-sleeves hinder work, short sleeves are preferable to sleeves rolled up. Loose, torn or ragged garments are a hazard. However, in circumstances where long-sleeves hinder work, short sleeves are preferable to sleeves rolled up. Loose, torn or ragged garments are a hazard. Loose kerchiefs, sweat rags or

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
similar pieces of cloth slung around the neck shall not be worn as they can get caught inside moving equipment and machinery.

Personal Protection Equipment
In order to reduce risk of injury while working on deck, in holds, in tanks and in machinery spaces all personnel shall wear personal protection equipment. Such personal protection equipment shall consist of:
appropriate personal working clothes;
safety helmets;
suitable safety footwear (not having steel studs, with oil-resistant anti-skid soles and preferably with steel toe inserts);
working gloves;
safety goggles/spectacles;
ear plugs/ear muffs;
safety belt/harness
respiratory masks.
life jacket/life vest
Safety helmets shall also be worn in any place where there is risk of head injury by falling from heights; being struck by falling or flying objects; striking to objects or structures.
Safety footwear is to be worn during all work in which potential danger to feet exists. Such activities will normally include all work outside the accommodation area, including work in engine room/machinery spaces, on deck, enclosed spaces and stores areas. Open and unprotected footwear such as slippers, clogs, sandals and similar footwear shall not be used while working.

Working gloves (loose fitting type) shall be used as they are designed to allow the hand to slip out and thus avoid it getting caught in machinery or in ropes and wires. If gloves are assessed to be inappropriate for tasks requiring dexterity and feel, or it is considered by that gloves may increase the risk of snagging of the hands, they may be removed. However, greater caution needs to be exercised during the task.
It is advisable to remove rings before working on deck or in machinery spaces.

Eye protection shall be used against mechanical, chemical and radiation hazards. Suitable eye protection shall be worn when grinding, drilling, working on a lathe, chipping, scaling, hammering, using a cold chisel, handling power tools, handling chemicals, welding, cutting, or doing any other work of a similar nature. Spectacles shall be worn with a suspending chord.

Ear protection shall be used when working in spaces having a high noise level. Ear protection such as ear plugs or ear muffs shall be worn to protect hearing. In extremely high noise level conditions both ear muffs and plugs shall be worn.

Safety belts/harnesses with lifelines shall be worn by all personnel working at a height of two metres or more, or where there is a potential to fall greater than two metres. | similar pieces of cloth slung around the neck shall not be worn as they can get caught inside moving equipment and machinery.

Personal Protection Equipment
In order to reduce risk of injury while working on deck, in holds, in tanks and in machinery spaces all personnel shall wear personal protection equipment. Such personal protection equipment shall consist of:
appropriate personal working clothes;
safety helmets;
suitable safety footwear (not having steel studs, with oil-resistant anti-skid soles and preferably with steel toe inserts);
working gloves;
safety goggles/spectacles;
ear plugs/ear muffs;
safety belt/harness
respiratory masks.
life jacket/life vest
Safety helmets shall also be worn in any place where there is risk of head injury by falling from heights; being struck by falling or flying objects; striking to objects or structures.

Safety in Workplace

Procedure for Assessment and Management of Risk
As defined in section 1.1, combination of the likelihood and consequence(s) of a specified hazardous event occurring.
Risk Understanding



What can go	How likely is it?		What are the wrong?		impacts?


The Company recognises and practises the use of risk assessment to identify hazards and minimise risks for shipboard operations involving safety of ships, personnel on board and protection of environment. It is considered that:
Risk assessment imposes a discipline on the shipboard personnel to consider safety aspect in detail during an operation, to think about what might go wrong and what is available to prevent or mitigate same and to consider the relevance of previous accident experience.
Risk assessment, when done properly, will yield an understanding and useful insights into ways that safety might be improved.
This process may provide reassurance that an important and reasonably practical step has been taken to anticipate what might go wrong and what could be done to prevent it.
The Company shall endeavour to address and reduce the risks to a level As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) having regard to its own Safety, Occupational Health & Environment Protection Policy.
Hazard: Source or situation with a potential to harm in terms of injury or ill health, damage to property/workplace/environment or a combination of these.
Risk: Combination of the likelihood and consequence(s) of a specified hazardous event occurring e.g. grounding, collision, fire, explosion, foundering, casualty etc.
Risk = Probability X Consequence
Risk Assessment: Process of identifying hazards and evaluating risks to health and safety arising from these hazards taking account of the existing risk controls (or, in the case of a new activity, the proposed risk controls).
Risk Controls: Workplace precautions, for example, physical safeguards, containment of airborne contaminants and noise, safety systems of work, competency, and personal protective equipment.
Tolerable Risk: Risk at a level that can be accepted provided risk controls are implemented to reduce risk as low as is reasonably practicable.
Acceptable Risk: Risk that is regarded as insignificant either as it stands, or as a result of risk controls.
Risk Assessment Process includes:
Hazard or Risk Identification i.e. to recognise the existence of some kind of hazard and try to define its characteristics. | Safety in Workplace

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
Risk Estimation i.e. scientific determination of risk characteristics usually providing a quantitative measurement.
Risk Evaluation i.e. a reasonable estimate of the risk‘s scope and acceptance.
Risk Management Process includes:
Making a decision about accepting or revising such risks.
Restricting and confining the chances of risks within acceptable limit at a reasonable cost.
Risk assessment need not be complicated. There are no fixed rules about how risk assessment should be undertaken. The assessment will depend upon type of ship, nature of operation and the type and extent of hazard and risk. The assessment is not expected to cover risks which are not reasonably foreseeable. A suitable risk assessment shall be made for safety of shipboard personnel in the normal course of their duties, arising directly from the work activity and which has a potential to harm the persons undertaking the work.
Elements of Risk Assessment
Work Activity


Identify hazards to ship, personnel and environment


Estimate Risk


Determine the tolerability of the risks


Prepare Risk Control Action Plan to improve risk controls as necessary


Review adequacy of Action Plan – confirm whether the risks are now tolerable


Ensure risk assessment and controls are effective and up-to-date

Since risks are associated almost with every activity, risks which are considered trivial and where no further precaution is required, need not be assessed. Risk assessment shall be carried out in the situations such as:
Key Shipboard Operations (R) – these are identified and checklists are included in the Shipboard SMS Manuals. During such operations, risk assessment shall be carried out,

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
considering the existing control measures. The residual risks, if any, shall be suitably addressed by introducing appropriate additional control measures.
Maintenance of Critical Equipment and Systems (C) – these are identified in the Shipboard SMS Manuals.
Non-routine (NR) Activity/Operation is planned to be undertaken.
Management of Change (MOC) – such as proposed change in activities, organisation or material/equipment.
Changes noticed during operation – the risk assessment shall be redone.
Hazard Identification
Risk assessment should be seen as a continual process. The risk in a workplace should be assessed for identification of hazards before work begins on any task using the Risk Assessment Register. For operations where valid risk assessment does not exist, the assessment shall be carried out using the Form: RA001. An assessment shall be reviewed and updated as necessary, to confirm that it reflects any significant changes of equipment or procedure.
Risk Assessment Activity
The risk assessment shall be carried out by a team of individuals directly involved in the operation and having a good understanding of risk assessment method used.
The team shall consist of the personnel from management and operation levels.
The risk assessment shall be approved by Safety Officer, in consultation with Master, for all shipboard operations.
If additional safety controls are required for a particular hazard for which risk assessment already exists and the controls can be applied by the vessel using the available resources on board, the Master is authorised to apply additional controls, as necessary and intimate operating division.
Having carried out the risk assessment, if a residual risk is identified in an unacceptable region, same shall be forwarded to the Superintendent who, in consultation with the Group I/C, will introduce further control measures to bring the risk to ALARP level and approve the risk assessment. The approval done by shore office shall be conveyed to the Master. Approvals shall be maintained in appropriate locations (File No.315).
Risk Assessment Related Training
Management level shipboard officers joining vessels after 01.07.2010 are required to have undergone training in risk assessment. Pending fulfilment of training requirements, such officers shall be given briefing on risk assessment aspects prior their posting by the operating division.
Educational Series CD containing training material on hazard identification and risk assessment shall be provided to the vessels. Master shall ensure that all shipboard personnel are adequately briefed on risk assessment aspects and understand the contents of the CD upon joining. Evidence of such briefing imparted to all shipboard personnel shall be maintained on board.

The risk is determined by estimating the potential of severity of harm and the likelihood that the harm will occur. | considering the existing control measures. The residual risks, if any, shall be suitably addressed by introducing appropriate additional control measures.

Trivial | 1 | No further action required

Review of Risk Assessments
Validity of risk assessments and the processes shall be reviewed by the controlling office from time to time and such reviews shall be communicated to the vessels.
MOT Ladder & Accesses
Safe access to the ship in port shall, where possible, be ensured by an MOT ladder that can be adjusted to cope with any movement of the ship. The safe access shall land at a clear part of the quay, when the vessel is alongside. The MOT ladder or equivalent ship-shore access shall be under effective surveillance by ship‘s personnel on gangway duty to ensure safe access and egress.
Any means of access and the deck leading to the accommodation shall be adequately illuminated during the hours of darkness, and at other times as necessary. A lifebuoy shall be provided in an easily accessible position at the shipboard end of the MOT ladder, together with a buoyant lifeline of a length suitable for the vessel but not less than 30 metres. Wherever practicable, a safety net shall be rigged under the gangway or accommodation ladder so as to prevent persons from falling on to the quay or between the quay and the ship. Any defects to the MOT ladder or other means of safe access, which may cause a hazard, shall be made good before further use.
Ropes, Wires & Moorings
Following precautions shall be taken when handling ropes and wires:
Always wear gloves when handling wires or ropes.
Always stand well clear of a wire or rope under load.
Never stand in the bight of a wire or rope.
Do not have more people than necessary in the vicinity of a rope or wire under load.
Do not use a wire direct from a stowage reel that has been designed only for stowing.
Do not stand too close to the winch drum when handling wires and ropes. | In order that risk assessment produces a clear view of the issues and answer to the question

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
Wire or rope on a drum end shall not be handled unless a second person is available to remove or feed the slack rope.
Line handlers must stand well clear of the potential patch of ‗snap back‘ path.
Following precautions shall be taken during mooring/unmooring operations:
Comply with all available industry guidelines and safe working practices on mooring operations.
Do not surge synthetic fibre ropes on the drum end. Always walk a winch back to ease the weight off the rope.
Do not stand too close to a winch drum or bit when holding and tensioning a line. Stand back and grasp the line about one metre from the drum or bit.
Do not leave loose objects in the line handling area; if a line breaks it may throw such objects around as it snaps back.
Do not apply too many turns on the winch drum when heaving in a line. Generally four turns shall be taken with synthetic lines.
Remain in control of the line being handled. Ensure that the ‗tail end‘ of the line is secured on board to prevent complete loss. If the line does take charge, do not attempt to stop it with the feet or hands as this can result in serious injury.
The tension in a line shall not be assessed by kicking or standing on it; this is dangerous.
Winch operator shall understand the controls and see the officer or person in charge for instructions. Do not leave winches and windlasses running unattended. Do not stand on the machinery itself to get a better view.
Avoid placing wire and synthetic ropes on the same bollard or mooring hook.
The low coefficient of friction of synthetic ropes necessitates extreme care when easing out from around bitts, cleats or other holding devices.
Knots weaken a rope, even after they are removed. Never knot mooring ropes.
Mooring winches shall be taken off automatic self-tensioning mode.
On completion of mooring the winch shall be left with the brake on and out of gear.
Brake holding power is always greater than the heaving power. Once the brake starts to slip (render) it is impossible to heave in, unless forces causing the slippage are reduced.
Ensure that the ―heave-in‖ and ―slack-out‖ directions are clearly marked on the winch handles and controls, as well as on visible portion of drums.
Attend to oil leaks from hydraulic winches, it can lead to personnel slipping on deck and injuring them.
All mooring operations shall be done under supervision of responsible officer.
Precaution shall be taken when handling tug-ropes/wires (making fast or letting go tugs).
While carrying out task familiarisation, briefing on mooring operations shall be emphasised.
7.10.4   Portable Power Tools
Electrical power tools shall never be used in areas where a flammable atmosphere is likely to exist, such as: bunker tanks, crankcase, working in close proximity of process/production platform etc.
Power tools fitted with guards, shall be used with guards at all times.
Particular attention shall be given to the route the electrical supply lead will take and precautions taken to ensure that doors, etc. will not chafe or damage the lead. | Wire or rope on a drum end shall not be handled unless a second person is available to remove or feed the slack rope.
Line handlers must stand well clear of the potential patch of ‗snap back‘ path.
Following precautions shall be taken during mooring/unmooring operations:
Comply with all available industry guidelines and safe working practices on mooring operations.
Do not surge synthetic fibre ropes on the drum end. Always walk a winch back to ease the weight off the rope.
Do not stand too close to a winch drum or bit when holding and tensioning a line. Stand back and grasp the line about one metre from the drum or bit.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
The tool shall be thoroughly inspected before use and if any defects are found, it shall be reported to the responsible officer.
Always disconnect the tool from the electrical supply when not in use or when accessories are being fitted. This precaution will prevent accidental operation of the tool, which could result in a serious injury.
Wandering cables to electrical tools shall not have joints or junctions; they shall be through-run cables from the power socket to the tool.
Electrical cables shall be adequately insulated.
Air hoses to pneumatic equipment shall be such that they have electrical continuity, if the equipment is used in non-gas-free atmosphere.
Hand Tools
Extensions to spanner shanks shall not be practised to gain extra purchase, as this may lead to breaking the spanner and could result in injury to the operator. Loose hammer heads are another common cause of accidents from hand tools; they sometimes fly off, injuring personnel or damaging equipment. Never use a file without a handle. Make sure that the heads of cold chisels are properly dressed and do not allow them to ‗spread‘, hammers will slip off them and injure your hand. Ensure that all jagged edges are taken off any hand tools, as they can cause injury.
Lifting Appliances
All lifting gear shall have valid test certificates.
Quadrennial examination and testing of all lifting appliances and loose gear on board shall be carried out by a competent person every five years.
No lifting appliance shall be used unless the annual thorough examination by a competent person has been carried out.
Before cranes and other lifting appliances are used, an inspection and check of all wires, safety arrangements, brakes clutches etc., shall be carried out by the Chief Officer/Second Engineer Officer.
All lifting equipment shall be maintained in accordance with its maintenance schedule.
Each item of lifting gear on board shall be clearly and legibly marked with its safe working load.
No lifting appliance shall be used after repair or modification without first being tested by a competent person.
A record of examinations and tests mentioned above shall be maintained in the Register of ship‘s Lifting Appliances and Cargo Handling Gear. This register is the standard international form, as recommended by the International Labour Office, in accordance with ILO Convention No. 152.

7.10.7   Machinery Spaces
Bilges shall never be pumped overboard. Great care shall be taken when using the oily- bilge separator to avoid the passing of oil to the overboard line. Any bilge pumping operation shall be in compliance with MARPOL 73/78, and local regulations. All Engineer Officers on board shall be fully familiar with the applicable pollution regulations.

Safety & Security | 
BILGES MUST NOT BE PUMPED OUT EXCEPT WITH PERMISSION OF CHIEF ENGINEER OFFICER

All ladders, grating and floor plates are to be fastened, maintained free of debris, obstructions, oil, grease or other material, which would make them slippery. When gratings, floor plates, hand rails, ladders, etc. are removed for access to repairs or other purposes, the openings are to be roped off.
Escape routes from machinery spaces shall be well marked. All doors shall operate easily and door accesses shall be kept clear of obstructions. Ladders in escape routes shall be maintained in good condition. Escape routes shall be well lit.
Column type gauge glasses fitted with self-closing valves or weighted cocks are not to be secured in the open position under any circumstances, as the glasses are easily broken. Weighted cocks on sounding pipes of the fuel oil system shall not be kept wedged open.
Oil drips shall be prevented and if the leak cannot be prevented, then oil shall be collected in a suitable ‗save all‘ containing sand. Any accumulation of oil shall be immediately mopped up and no loose flammable material allowed remaining where a source of ignition (hot surfaces, naked flames, electric sparks etc.) may occur.
Any electric machine is to be isolated from its power supply before work is started on either the mechanical or electrical part. This is to be done by opening the appropriate switch or breaker and subsequent removal of fuses. The following notice shall be displayed in locations where power supply has been isolated:
REPAIRS IN PROGRESS POWER SUPPLY ISOLATED DO NOT RESTORE POWER

A fuse puller is to be used when fuses are removed or replaced in fuse boxes.
Particular care is to be exercised when hand turning is used instead of power, for example as on some deck machinery e.g. boat winches.
Defective electrical circuits, including portable lights, shall be promptly repaired.
No repairs shall be undertaken on electrical installations outside the accommodation or Engine Room, when the vessel is stationed in the vicinity of process platform.
Wooden staging is to be used for any electrical maintenance work on the generator flat and near switchboards.
Earthing of electrical equipment shall be restored after repairs.
Precautions described in section 7.11.1 shall be taken during hotwork.
7.10.8   Work Aloft
Insufficiently experienced seamen shall not work aloft unless accompanied by an experienced seaman or adequately supervised. All work aloft shall be under the supervision of the Chief Officer or deck serang. Rigging and gear used shall be carefully checked and any equipment showing signs of deterioration shall be replaced immediately. Personnel working aloft shall be required to wear a tended Lifeline and safety belt/harness. | BILGES MUST NOT BE PUMPED OUT EXCEPT WITH PERMISSION OF CHIEF ENGINEER OFFICER

7.10.9	Work near Ship's Whistle
Before work is commenced in the immediate vicinity of the ship‘s whistle, the following shall be done:
Officer in-charge of the watch shall be informed.
Power to whistle shall be shut off.
Suitable warning notices shall be posted both on the Bridge and in the Engine Room.
Work near Antenna
Before work is done on masts or other places in close proximity to radio aerials, the Radio Officer and officer in-charge of the navigational watch shall be informed so that he refrains from transmitting or gives adequate warning to persons before transmitting, and suitable warning notice shall be displayed in the Radio Room.
Before work is commenced in the vicinity of the radar scanner, the officer in-charge shall be informed so that radar can be isolated and a warning notice posted at the radar to prevent its use. Before work commences the man performing the work shall ensure that the foregoing precautions have been taken and that the following warning notice has been displayed:

WARNING !!
MEN AT WORK NEAR RADAR SCANNER
DO NOT SWITCH ON RADAR

Work on Funnel
Before rigging stages or chairs, or other duties are undertaken on top of the funnel, the Chief Engineer Officer and officer in-charge of the engineering watch shall be informed so that arrangements can be made to prevent until work is completed. The following warning notice shall be displayed in the Engine Control Room.

WARNING !!
MEN AT WORK ON FUNNEL
Work Overside
Personnel working overside shall be required to wear a tended lifeline, safety belt and safety harness. Safe staging and access is to be provided. No work requiring personnel to go overside shall be done while the vessel is underway.
Painting
Paints may contain toxic or irritant substances, and the solvents may give rise to flammable and potentially explosive vapours, which may also be toxic. Paints containing organic compounds can be particularly dangerous. Wherever possible, the hazards of the paint shall be ascertained and precautions taken to avoid hazardous exposure. Avoid hazardous exposure to paints in interiors and enclosed spaces by ventilating the space. Painting shall not be carried out in the vicinity of hot work areas. Paints shall not be stored in any space other than designated paint stores and paint lockers. | 7.10.9	Work near Ship's Whistle

Safety & Security | 
Painting in Enclosed Spaces/Tanks
Precautions to be taken while undertaking any painting work in enclosed spaces/tanks
Continuous ventilation of the area to be ensured
Regular monitoring and checking the atmosphere inside the space/tank
All electrical equipment to be flame proof
Swimming
Ship‘s personnel may be sometimes tempted to indulge in swimming in the sea, near the ship. This activity has many attendant risks and has led to the loss of life, in the past. Swimming from the ship, either alongside or at anchor is prohibited.
Welding and Flame Cutting
All welding and flame cutting operations shall be subject to the procedures described in Section 7.11.1.
Operators shall be proficient in the process of welding/flame cutting.
There shall be effective ventilation of the space within which welding/flame cutting operations are in progress.
Welding/flame cutting equipment shall be inspected by a competent person before use to ensure that it is in a serviceable condition.
The operator shall wear:
welding helmet with a suitably coloured transparent eye piece. Eye goggles or a hand held shield may be a suitable alternative in appropriate circumstances;
leather working gloves;
leather apron (where appropriate);
long sleeve natural fibre boiler suit.
The operator shall wear dry clothing.
The operator's clothing shall be free of grease, oil and other flammable substances.
During electric arc welding the operator shall also wear electrically non-conducting footwear.
7.10.16   Unattended Spaces
In general, vessels will have certain spaces which remain unattended and unnoticed e.g. unoccupied cabins, unused store rooms, lockers, mast houses, etc. Procedures are to be adopted to check these spaces in a routine manner once in a month to ensure that —
No loose electrical connection or abnormalities exists. Fans, lights etc., which are not in use, are to be kept switched off to prevent possible short circuiting, heating up which could cause fire.
No combustible or unwanted materials to be stored in such spaces.
No leaking of oil, water or accumulation of unwanted liquids.
No infestation of cockroaches, insects and vermin.
Free of stowaways (in stowaway prone areas).
No other potentially hazardous situation exists.
7.10.17   Safety in Dry Dock
During the dry-docking and lay up repairs, Master shall continue to remain responsible for the safety of the vessel and all the officers and crew members. Chief Engineer Officer shall continue to be responsible for the safety of E.R., machinery spaces and other spaces under his specific charge. | Painting in Enclosed Spaces/Tanks

Welding/flame cutting equipment shall be inspected by a competent person before use to ensure that it is in a serviceable condition.
The operator shall wear:
welding helmet with a suitably coloured transparent eye piece. Eye goggles or a hand held shield may be a suitable alternative in appropriate circumstances;
leather working gloves;
leather apron (where appropriate);
long sleeve natural fibre boiler suit.
The operator shall wear dry clothing.
The operator's clothing shall be free of grease, oil and other flammable substances.
During electric arc welding the operator shall also wear electrically non-conducting footwear.
7.10.16   Unattended Spaces
In general, vessels will have certain spaces which remain unattended and unnoticed e.g. unoccupied cabins, unused store rooms, lockers, mast houses, etc. Procedures are to be adopted to check these spaces in a routine manner once in a month to ensure that —
No loose electrical connection or abnormalities exists. Fans, lights etc., which are not in use, are to be kept switched off to prevent possible short circuiting, heating up which could cause fire.
No combustible or unwanted materials to be stored in such spaces.
No leaking of oil, water or accumulation of unwanted liquids.
No infestation of cockroaches, insects and vermin.
Free of stowaways (in stowaway prone areas).
No other potentially hazardous situation exists.
7.10.17   Safety in Dry Dock
During the dry-docking and lay up repairs, Master shall continue to remain responsible for the safety of the vessel and all the officers and crew members. Chief Engineer Officer shall continue to be responsible for the safety of E.R., machinery spaces and other spaces under his specific charge. | Painting in Enclosed Spaces/Tanks
Precautions to be taken while undertaking any painting work in enclosed spaces/tanks
Continuous ventilation of the area to be ensured
Regular monitoring and checking the atmosphere inside the space/tank
All electrical equipment to be flame proof
Swimming
Ship‘s personnel may be sometimes tempted to indulge in swimming in the sea, near the ship. This activity has many attendant risks and has led to the loss of life, in the past. Swimming from the ship, either alongside or at anchor is prohibited.
Welding and Flame Cutting
All welding and flame cutting operations shall be subject to the procedures described in Section 7.11.1.

Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure that the safe working practices are adopted by the yard and no hot work is undertaken unless the boundaries of the hot work location are identified.
The escape routes shall be clearly marked and explained to the yard‘s ship repair Manager. The ship/yard communication shall be established and understood for any emergency. VHF channel and telephone number of shore emergency stations like fire brigade, ambulance etc. shall be noted by all concerned and displayed on the notice board at the gangway, Engine Room and the control room.
It shall be the responsibility of the Master, along with the Chief Engineer Officer, attending Superintendent and shipyard, to ensure all preventive and safety measures are adopted to avoid potential hazards and minimise risks to the vessel, personnel and the environment while the vessel is laid up for dry-docking and repairs. In order to effectively manage risks and hazards during dry-docking and repairs, following procedures are recommended:
Daily safety meetings with the shipboard management team, superintendent and responsible persons from the shipyard. Day to day work planning, precautions to be taken for hot work, enclosed space entries, ballasting-deballasting activities and other potential hazardous operations could be discussed and suitable precautionary preventive action taken.
Emergency response procedures shall be drawn up in advance in case of fire, accidental leakage of gas or oil, personnel injury and natural calamities.
Fire patrol round the clock.
Establishing effective modes of communications and emergency signals.
Emergency contact numbers of fire stations, hospitals, first aid posts, Police and other authorities/agencies and names of responsible persons from whom assistance may be required in a potential emergency.
Instructions and precautions regarding operation of valves and pumps etc. which could cause accidental release of gas or other medium detrimental to safety.
Availability of fire-fighting mediums, such as water in fire mains, fire extinguishers and other extinguishing medium.
Ensuring safe and adequate access, ventilation, lighting and staging.
Regular Monitoring and checking the atmosphere of enclosed and confined spaces where man entry may be required. Use of Work permits is to be followed.
Drawing up of precautions for carrying out hot work. Use of Work Permit shall be strictly followed.
Fencing of all openings and display of caution signs to avoid falls and tripping.
Verification of shipyard safety department procedures so that both the ship and the yard can maintain safe working conditions on the vessel.
Routine cleanliness of the vessel during dry-dockings and repairs to be carried out. Garbage, Sludge and Debris to be promptly removed from the vessel, as this may be the cause of accidents and pollution. Final cleaning and removal of all staging, repair material and debris to be carried out prior vessel‘s departure from the Yard.
Ballasting/deballasting activities have to be discussed and planned and prior approval sought from shipyard. Trials and tests of machineries are to be carried out after obtaining the consent of engineer in charge of the yard, obtaining a work permit and after ensuring that the machine/equipment is boxed back fully and is operational. 7.10.18	Safety Precautions during Underwater Inspection/Repairs
During underwater inspections/repairs, ship‘s crew should follow all safety precautions and monitor effective communication between ship‘s staff and workshop till completion of work.
Permission from Port Authorities shall be obtained.
During the diving operations, Flag ‗A‘ shall be hoisted.
Proper communication, including contingency signals, between diving team supervisor and the vessel shall be established and maintained throughout the operation.
Safety Management Team onboard to hold a meeting in the presence of diving team supervisor for task planning and risk assessment/work permit (Form: SS008), isolation of tagging requirements to correct proposed procedure and proper record to be maintained.
Prior commencement of diving/underwater operations, Chief Engineer Officer must ensure Main Engines/all Propulsion Equipment are shut down/isolated.
Steering gear/rudder to be locked with a warning notice ―NOT TO SWITCH ON‖ at the control panels.
Pumps for major sea suction/inboard and outboard discharge to be put off.
All types of electric/electronic transmission underwater shall be isolated.
Underwater/diving operation shall commence only after all necessary precautions are taken and clearance obtained from Master/Safety Officer.
During the period underwater operations are in progress, a continuous watch shall be maintained to ensure that the area is kept well clear of barges, mooring boats and other workshop personnel working in the vicinity.
7.10.19   Potential Emergency Situations such as Tsunami/Earthquake etc.
For emergency situations which are unpredictable natural calamities like Earthquake/ Tsunami, following are the guidelines:
Tsunamis are caused because of various factors. Major causes are —
Underwater earthquakes;
Severe volcanic activities;
Earthquakes are caused due to the tectonic plates either moving against each other or moving towards each other.
Actions to be taken on receipt of Tsunami/Major Earth Quake warning
Whenever Tsunami warning is issued and there is sufficient time to move from port to open sea, Master of the vessel shall take following into consideration when planning his vessel‘s action.
Ensure the watch-keeping officers keep effective watch in port even when the vessel is safely moored or anchored. Special measures, such as readiness of main propulsion system, bow/stern thrusters units, emergency towing arrangements, anchoring system and securing arrangements for the ramps/unitised cargo may be initiated by the Master, in the event of unforeseen circumstances such as Tsunami waves hitting ports and harbours.
Ensure LSA equipments life boats/life rafts etc are secured and ready for emergency use.
If Tsunami Warning has been issued and there is sufficient time to move vessel to deep waters, then contact Port Control to ask their plan for shifting vessels from the port. | Trials and tests of machineries are to be carried out after obtaining the consent of engineer in charge of the yard, obtaining a work permit and after ensuring that the machine/equipment is boxed back fully and is operational. The tests have to be carried out under the supervision of competent and responsible persons.

Inform port control the expected time of readiness and any other assistance required viz. pilot, tugs, mooring boat and mooring gang etc.
The Master of the vessel shall follow the prescribed Port regulations and Port Traffic Signals during the manoeuvres from berth to open sea, where permitted to cast off vessel without assistance of the Pilot.
Prevention of Infestation
Cleanliness or good housekeeping is one important means of controlling pests and rodents onboard. Vessel has to use pesticide or undergo the process of fumigation for control of such infestation.
The Company has contractual arrangements with shore-based agencies to carry out disinfestation/fumigation onboard ships when in port, as per requirement. Usually, disinfestation, by spraying insecticides in the accommodation areas, galleys, messroom etc., is arranged by the operating division on Master‘s request. Fumigation, if required, shall be arranged by the operating division after a major lay-up or dry-docking of the vessel. The precautions required to be taken by the ship‘s personnel are given by the authorised contractor in the form of a brochure every time either during disinfestation/fumigation and same shall be complied with.
Use of Mobile Phone/Tablet/Laptop
The use of mobile phone poses risk in hazardous areas onboard ship. As per International Safety Guide for Oil Tankers and Terminals, mobile telephone use in hazardous area is prohibited unless it is intrinsically safe and certified for use in such areas. Therefore, all shipboard personnel should realize this risk and take appropriate precautions. Instructions regarding use of mobile phones onboard are as follows:
Mobile phone is not to be used in hazardous areas unless intrinsically safe.
During navigational watch, engine room watch or cargo watch mobile phone/Tablet is not to be used.
Use of Laptop in work place such as navigating bridge, CCR, ECR or in deck and engine room offices by officers and crews are to be restricted.
Laptop/Mobile Phone should not be kept in charging mode unattended as it has risk of short circuiting/over heating and is a potential fire hazard.
Use of Mobile Phone and Laptop by visitors onboard is to be restricted/controlled by the Master of the vessel.
Visitors should be asked to switch off their mobile phone/Tablet before boarding the vessel. They should be briefed about the risk and the requirements at boarding point.
Whenever permitted for use in exceptional circumstances involving safety and security of the vessel it should be used with due diligence.
Local/terminal/port requirements for mobile telephone carriage and use should be complied with.

flammability (including the risk of explosion);

flammability (including the risk of explosion);
corrosivity towards man and materials;
Toxicity.
Chemicals carried or used on board will have labels to indicate their hazard classification under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code (IMDG Code). These labels provide

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
a convenient indication of the hazards of each chemical. Vessel shall have MSDS sheets for the chemicals carried.
The disposal of used chemical and it‘s containers to be done as per procedures specified in MSDS.
Whenever shipboard personnel handle flammable, corrosive or toxic chemicals, it shall be done under the supervision of a competent officer.
Following precautions shall be taken for flammable chemicals:
Avoid source of ignition near such chemicals;
Storage areas shall be adequately ventilated.
Following precautions shall be taken when handling corrosive chemicals:
Vessels and containers used to store these chemicals shall be resistant to them;
All parts of the body, especially eyes, shall be covered;
If corrosive chemical falls on the skin, wash with plenty of fresh water;
Do not use material, such as cotton waste, to mop up spilled corrosive chemicals; wash down with fresh water.
Following precautions shall be taken when handling toxic chemicals:
Remove all clothing contaminated by toxic chemicals;
Do not store contaminated personal wear in accommodation areas;
When handling such chemicals, keep hands away from mouth and face;
Wash thoroughly after handling toxic chemicals.
7.10.23	Handling Asbestos Materials on board
Refer MSC Circ.1045 for the guidelines for maintenance and monitoring of on-board Materials containing Asbestos.
The purpose is to set up a maintenance and monitoring programme with the principal objective of minimising exposure to asbestos fibres of anyone on board (viz. passengers, crew, riding crews, maintenance personnel in port etc) while the ship is in service.
Planned repairs or removal of such materials should be carried out by the specialist personnel and not normally by crew.
Following are the guidelines for the maintenance and monitoring of on board materials containing asbestos.
Inventory and Condition Assessment of Asbestos-containing materials
During acquisition, an initial ship inspection to be performed by a qualified professional to investigate the possible presence of asbestos-containing materials on board the ship and, if any are identified, to locate them and assess their condition.
The Ship-builders are required to provide issuance of an asbestos-free declaration (see
Annexure – 2) by the manufacturer as supporting documentation.
Also they shall provide their own overall asbestos-free declaration (see Annexure – 1), before delivery of ship, together with the relevant supporting documentation such as the asbestos-free declarations issued by the manufacturers, sampling-check reports, test reports and the qualification certificates of the expert parties and/or the laboratories (if applicable). | a convenient indication of the hazards of each chemical. Following precautions shall be taken for flammable chemicals:
Avoid source of ignition near such chemicals;
Storage areas shall be adequately ventilated.
Following precautions shall be taken when handling corrosive chemicals:
Vessels and containers used to store these chemicals shall be resistant to them;
All parts of the body, especially eyes, shall be covered;
If corrosive chemical falls on the skin, wash with plenty of fresh water;

Following precautions shall be taken when handling toxic chemicals:

Also they shall provide their own overall asbestos-free declaration (see Annexure – 1), before delivery of ship, together with the relevant supporting documentation such as the asbestos-free declarations issued by the manufacturers, sampling-check reports, test reports and the qualification certificates of the expert parties and/or the laboratories (if applicable). | a convenient indication of the hazards of each chemical. Vessel shall have MSDS sheets for the chemicals carried.
The disposal of used chemical and it‘s containers to be done as per procedures specified in MSDS.
Whenever shipboard personnel handle flammable, corrosive or toxic chemicals, it shall be done under the supervision of a competent officer.
Following precautions shall be taken for flammable chemicals:
Avoid source of ignition near such chemicals;
Storage areas shall be adequately ventilated.
Following precautions shall be taken when handling corrosive chemicals:
Vessels and containers used to store these chemicals shall be resistant to them;
All parts of the body, especially eyes, shall be covered;
If corrosive chemical falls on the skin, wash with plenty of fresh water;
Do not use material, such as cotton waste, to mop up spilled corrosive chemicals; wash down with fresh water.
Following precautions shall be taken when handling toxic chemicals:
Remove all clothing contaminated by toxic chemicals;
Do not store contaminated personal wear in accommodation areas;
When handling such chemicals, keep hands away from mouth and face;
Wash thoroughly after handling toxic chemicals.
7.10.23	Handling Asbestos Materials on board
Refer MSC Circ.1045 for the guidelines for maintenance and monitoring of on-board Materials containing Asbestos.
The purpose is to set up a maintenance and monitoring programme with the principal objective of minimising exposure to asbestos fibres of anyone on board (viz. passengers, crew, riding crews, maintenance personnel in port etc) while the ship is in service.
Planned repairs or removal of such materials should be carried out by the specialist personnel and not normally by crew.
Following are the guidelines for the maintenance and monitoring of on board materials containing asbestos.
Inventory and Condition Assessment of Asbestos-containing materials
During acquisition, an initial ship inspection to be performed by a qualified professional to investigate the possible presence of asbestos-containing materials on board the ship and, if any are identified, to locate them and assess their condition.
The Ship-builders are required to provide issuance of an asbestos-free declaration (see
Annexure – 2) by the manufacturer as supporting documentation.
Also they shall provide their own overall asbestos-free declaration (see Annexure – 1), before delivery of ship, together with the relevant supporting documentation such as the asbestos-free declarations issued by the manufacturers, sampling-check reports, test reports and the qualification certificates of the expert parties and/or the laboratories (if applicable).

The following written procedures for purchasing and controlling the supply of asbestos free material, equipment and components should be established:
supplier evaluation and selection methods,
asbestos free verification practices for supplied products, and
issuance of an asbestos-free declaration (see Annexure – 2) by the manufacturer as supporting documentation.
After vessel‘s acquisition, Company will ensure that materials containing asbestos are prohibited to be used on board the ships during ships‘ operation. In order to regulate the repairs, supplies, modifications and maintenance activities, following needs to be followed:
For the supply of stores/spares to vessels, the requirement of asbestos free materials/items needs to be mentioned in the tender/requisition.

Work Permits & Enclosed Space Entry

Permit to Work
A permit to work shall be used for any task that might be deemed hazardous, on board the vessel. The permit is not essential for all tasks. Ship‘s personnel shall not make the permit to work system over complicated. Permits shall be normally used for entry into enclosed spaces, hot work, electrical work and cold work in hazardous areas. Chief Engineer Officer shall be the responsible officer for issue of the permit to work in machinery space areas. Chief Officer shall be the responsible officer for issue of the permit to work in areas other than machinery spaces. Before issuing a permit, the responsible officer shall satisfy himself that the conditions at the site, or of the equipment to be worked on, are safe for the work to be undertaken and a risk assessment should be carried out prior issuance of work permit (Ref. 7.10.1) Where port and local regulation require any particular permit-to-work to be issued by the appointed shore authority, vessel shall comply with such regulations.
The issue of permit-to-work is subject to the approval of the Master. The responsibility of ensuring that safe conditions exist for the work in question rests upon the responsible officer issuing the permit-to-work. The responsible officer shall personally ensure that the correct procedures are understood and followed by all concerned. It shall be remembered that the act of filling in a permit does not in itself make the job safe. It is the thoroughness in complying with the conditions called for in the permit that makes the permit effective.

The following forms for permit-to-work are provided at the end of this section:
Hot work permit (Form: SS001)
Cold work permit (Form: SS002)
Electrical isolation permit (Form: SS003)
Entry into enclosed spaces — Safety Checklist (Form: SS004)
Underwater Work Permit (Form: SS008)
Working Aloft/Overside (Form: SS010)

Hot Work Permits
Before the issue of such a permit is authorised the following conditions shall be met:
The area and any equipment to be worked on shall be free of flammable material and in a non-flammable atmosphere as well as being isolated from sources of hydrocarbons by means of disconnecting, blanking or inserting blinds. No reliance shall be placed on closed valves.
The degree of risk and potential sites of accidental release of hydrocarbons in the area shall be fully assessed and corrective action, if any, taken.
No hot work shall be done on pressure vessels and high-pressure piping.
The work area shall be clear of any combustible material such as oil soaked rags, wood, sediments etc.
Welding and all other equipment being used shall be in good condition and where required be appropriately earthed.
Fire fighting equipment shall be ready for immediate use.
The atmosphere shall be checked and found free of flammable gases/vapours. | Work Permits & Enclosed Space Entry

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
The frequency of atmosphere monitoring shall be established and use of portable continuous gas detector alarms considered. Atmospheres shall be re-tested after breaks in work periods and every hour, regardless of whether continuous gas detector alarms are in use.
There shall be effective means of containing and extinguishing welding sparks and molten slag.
Personnel involved shall be briefed or trained regarding the safety practices to be adopted during hot work.
A fire watch shall be kept during all hotwork and for an appropriate time after hotwork is completed, with fire hoses laid out and portable fire extinguishers at the scene of welding operations.

Before permitting hot work on board, additional hazards such as entry into enclosed spaces may have to be considered. Hot work on board ship shall be prohibited until all applicable regulations and safety requirements have been met and a permit to work has been issued.

Isolation of Electrical Equipment
A permit to work shall be issued indicating that the electrical supply of the equipment has been isolated, whenever work is to be carried out on electrical equipment, or on equipment powered by electricity.
Electric isolation can be effected by locking off switchgear or complete removal of fuses.
Consideration shall be given to a system of control which prevents the accidental reconnection of supply — for example by labelling of switches and by displaying warning notices.

Entry into Enclosed Spaces
Enclosed space means a space which has any of the following characteristics:
limited openings for entry and exit;
inadequate ventilation; and
is not designed for continuous worker occupancy,
and includes, but is not limited to, cargo spaces, double bottoms, fuel tanks, ballast tanks, cargo pump-rooms, cargo compressor rooms, cofferdams, chain lockers, void spaces, duct keels, inter-barrier spaces, boilers, engine crankcases, engine scavenge air receivers, sewage tanks, and adjacent connected spaces etc. as applicable.
A consolidated ship specific list prepared by the Safety Officers and approved by the Master showing the name, location and the purpose of all the enclosed spaces onboard every vessel as applicable, shall be maintained and displayed.
Adjacent connected space means a normally unventilated space which is not used for cargo but which may share the same atmospheric characteristics with the enclosed space such as, but not limited to, a cargo space access way.
Competent person means a person with sufficient theoretical knowledge and practical experience to make an informed assessment of the likelihood of a dangerous atmosphere being present or subsequently arising in the space.
Responsible person means a person authorized to permit entry into an enclosed space and having sufficient knowledge of the procedures to be established and complied with on board, in order to ensure that the space is safe for entry. | The frequency of atmosphere monitoring shall be established and use of portable continuous gas detector alarms considered.  | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
Attendant means a person who is suitably trained within the safety management system, maintains a watch over those entering the enclosed space, maintains communications with those inside the space and initiates the emergency procedures in the event of an incident occurring.
Respective Safety Officer onboard shall be competent and responsible person trained in enclosed space hazard recognition, evaluation, measurement, control and elimination, meeting statutory requirement and applicable rules and regulations.
Crew members should be trained, as appropriate, in enclosed space safety, including familiarization with onboard procedures for recognizing, evaluating and controlling hazards associated with entry into enclosed spaces.
Crew members with enclosed space entry or rescue responsibilities shall participate in an enclosed space entry and rescue drill to be held onboard the ship at least once every two months as specified in the Emergency Drills Program (Form: EM005D(OS).
Each Enclosed Space Entry & Rescue Drill shall include:
checking and use of personal protective equipment required for entry;
checking and use of communication equipment and procedures;
checking and use of instruments for measuring the atmosphere in enclosed spaces;
checking and use of rescue equipment and procedures; and
instructions in first aid and resuscitation techniques.

Following instructions pertain to entry into any enclosed or confined space in which it is foreseeable that the atmosphere may at some stage contain toxic or flammable gases or vapours, or be deficient in oxygen, to the extent that it may endanger the life or health of any person entering that space. Such an unsafe atmosphere may be present or arise subsequently in any enclosed or confined space including double bottoms, cargo tanks, pumprooms, fuel tanks, ballast tanks, peak tanks, cofferdams, void spaces, duct keels, inter-barrier spaces, sewage tanks, cable trunks, pipe trunks, pressure vessels, battery lockers, chain lockers, inert gas plant scrubber and blower spaces, engine crankcase, boilers and the storage rooms for CO2 and other media used for fire extinguishing or inerting.
Should there be any unexpected reduction in or loss of the means of ventilation of those spaces that are usually continuously or adequately ventilated, then such spaces shall also be dealt with as dangerous spaces.
When it is suspected that there could be a deficiency of oxygen in any space, or that toxic gases, vapours or fumes could be present, then such a space shall be considered to be a dangerous space.

General Precautions for entry into an enclosed space
An enclosed space shall be entered only when explicit permission has been granted by the Master or responsible officer with the knowledge of Master and only after all appropriate safety checks have been carried out.
Before entry is allowed into enclosed spaces, the space shall be thoroughly ventilated to ensure an adequate oxygen level and absence of toxic gases.
An entry permit signed by the Master or responsible officer shall be issued before entry. The entry permit should contain a clear indication as to its maximum period of validity, which, in any event, should not exceed 12 hours. The entry shall be preferably permitted during day light in normal working hours, except in case of exigency.

checking and use of communication equipment and procedures;
checking and use of instruments for measuring the atmosphere in enclosed spaces;
checking and use of rescue equipment and procedures; and
instructions in first aid and resuscitation techniques.

Following instructions pertain to entry into any enclosed or confined space in which it is foreseeable that the atmosphere may at some stage contain toxic or flammable gases or vapours, or be deficient in oxygen, to the extent that it may endanger the life or health of any person entering that space. Such an unsafe atmosphere may be present or arise subsequently in any enclosed or confined space including double bottoms, cargo tanks, pumprooms, fuel tanks, ballast tanks, peak tanks, cofferdams, void spaces, duct keels, inter-barrier spaces, sewage tanks, cable trunks, pipe trunks, pressure vessels, battery lockers, chain lockers, inert gas plant scrubber and blower spaces, engine crankcase, boilers and the storage rooms for CO2 and other media used for fire extinguishing or inerting.
Should there be any unexpected reduction in or loss of the means of ventilation of those spaces that are usually continuously or adequately ventilated, then such spaces shall also be dealt with as dangerous spaces.
When it is suspected that there could be a deficiency of oxygen in any space, or that toxic gases, vapours or fumes could be present, then such a space shall be considered to be a dangerous space.

General Precautions for entry into an enclosed space
An enclosed space shall be entered only when explicit permission has been granted by the Master or responsible officer with the knowledge of Master and only after all appropriate safety checks have been carried out.
Before entry is allowed into enclosed spaces, the space shall be thoroughly ventilated to ensure an adequate oxygen level and absence of toxic gases.
An entry permit signed by the Master or responsible officer shall be issued before entry. The entry permit should contain a clear indication as to its maximum period of validity, which, in any event, should not exceed 12 hours. The entry shall be preferably permitted during day light in normal working hours, except in case of exigency.
The Master or a responsible officer shall ensure: | Attendant means a person who is suitably trained within the safety management system, maintains a watch over those entering the enclosed space, maintains communications with those inside the space and initiates the emergency procedures in the event of an incident occurring.
Respective Safety Officer onboard shall be competent and responsible person trained in enclosed space hazard recognition, evaluation, measurement, control and elimination, meeting statutory requirement and applicable rules and regulations.
Crew members should be trained, as appropriate, in enclosed space safety, including familiarization with onboard procedures for recognizing, evaluating and controlling hazards associated with entry into enclosed spaces.
Crew members with enclosed space entry or rescue responsibilities shall participate in an enclosed space entry and rescue drill to be held onboard the ship at least once every two months as specified in the Emergency Drills Program (Form: EM005D(OS).
Each Enclosed Space Entry & Rescue Drill shall include:
checking and use of personal protective equipment required for entry;
checking and use of communication equipment and procedures;
checking and use of instruments for measuring the atmosphere in enclosed spaces;
checking and use of rescue equipment and procedures; and
instructions in first aid and resuscitation techniques.

Following instructions pertain to entry into any enclosed or confined space in which it is foreseeable that the atmosphere may at some stage contain toxic or flammable gases or vapours, or be deficient in oxygen, to the extent that it may endanger the life or health of any person entering that space. General Precautions for entry into an enclosed space

The entry shall be preferably permitted during day light in normal working hours, except in case of exigency.
The Master or a responsible officer shall ensure:

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
That the space has been thoroughly ventilated by natural or mechanical means.
Effective ventilation will be maintained continuously while personnel are inside.
The atmosphere of the space at different levels is tested for oxygen deficiency and harmful vapours before making man entry. The enclosed space atmosphere should be monitored at regular intervals while personnel are inside.
That breathing apparatus, safety belt or safety harness and lifeline is worn by all persons entering the space where there is any doubt as to the adequacy of ventilation or testing before entry.
Lifelines, safety harness, approved breathing apparatus, stretcher and resuscitation equipment are ready for use by a rescue team at the entrance to the enclosed space.
A separate means of access, if available, is used as an alternative means of escape in an emergency.
The lines of communication for dealing with emergencies is clearly established and understood by all concerned.
A responsible member of the crew is in constant attendance outside the enclosed space, in the immediate vicinity of the entrance and in direct contact with a responsible officer, on a walkie-talkie radio.
The attending crew member is advised that under no circumstances shall he enter the tank in the event of an emergency, before help arrives.
The officers on watch both on deck and in the Engine Room shall be informed before any enclosed space is entered.
Should it become necessary to enter any enclosed space to effect rescue of personnel from within, a responsible officer shall continuously supervise the operation.
Filter respirators are not designed to protect the wearer from effects of toxic vapours or deficiency of oxygen. They shall not be used for entry into enclosed spaces.
Due regard shall be paid to the difficulty of movement when self-contained breathing apparatus is worn in confined tanks, such as double bottoms/peak tanks and the problem in the recovery of an incapacitated person in these circumstances.
A tank or compartment which has been ballasted or has contained water and has been left empty for any length of time may be deficient in oxygen, because the rusting of steel gradually extracts oxygen from the air in the compartment. Any such compartment, which has been closed for any length of time, shall be treated as suspect and thoroughly ventilated before man entry is attempted. A similar hazard exists in newly painted compartments, which have been insufficiently ventilated. In addition, evaporating paint solvents may be toxic also.
Toxic and explosive gases can be generated in compartments such as bilge wells by the decomposition of organic material in water.

Use of Tools, Lights and Electrical Equipment in Enclosed Spaces
Tools should not be carried into enclosed spaces, but should be lowered in a plastic bucket or canvas bag to avoid the possibility of them being dropped. Before any hammering or chipping is undertaken, or any power tool is used, the Responsible Officer should be satisfied that there is no likelihood of hydrocarbon vapour being present in the vicinity.
Unless the compartment is designated safe for Hot Work, non-approved lights or non- intrinsically safe electrical equipment must not be taken into an enclosed space. Only | That the space has been thoroughly ventilated by natural or mechanical means.

approved safety lighting or intrinsically safe electrical equipment should be used in enclosed spaces that are liable to experience hydrocarbon vapour re-contamination.

Removal of Sludge, Scale and Sediment
When removing sludge, scale or sediment from an enclosed space, periodic gas tests should be undertaken and continuous ventilation should be maintained throughout the period the space is occupied.
There may be increase in gas concentrations in the immediate vicinity of the work and care should be taken to ensure that the atmosphere remains safe for personnel. It is strongly recommended that personal gas monitors are used by some or all of the persons engaged in the work.

Work Boats (Rafting)
Any work involving the use of work boats in cargo tanks presents additional hazards and following precautions must be taken:
Work boats used for tank repair work and tank inspections should be fit for the task for which they are to be employed. Before and during their use within an enclosed space, all conditions for entry, including the use of an entry permit should be observed (Ref. I6.4).
All deck apertures, such as tank washing plates, should be opened and effective ventilation maintained continuously while persons are in the tank.
The work boat should only be used when the water surface is calm.
The work boat should only be used in tanks containing clean ballast water.
The water level should be stationary throughout the operation.
All personnel working in the compartment should wear a buoyancy aid.
A Responsible Person should act as lookout at the top of the tank and if the boat is working at a point remote from the tank hatch, an additional lookout should be positioned a little way down the access ladder at a point where a clear view of the boat is provided.

Non Gas Free and Suspect Compartments
It is stressed that entry into tanks, which are known to be non-gas free, or oxygen deficient can only be permitted, with a view to save life and/or to avoid pollution, when there is no other alternative. In this highly hazardous situation, the personnel involved shall be well trained in the use of breathing apparatus and aware of the dangers of removing their breathing apparatus while in the hostile atmosphere.
When it is necessary to enter a tank or compartment where it is suspected that the atmosphere is to be undertaken in a manner that will avoid creating an ignition hazard. contains toxic gas or is deficient in oxygen, or that these conditions are likely to occur during the period of occupation, an officer shall be responsible for continuous supervision of the operation and shall ensure that:
Entry into the above space is made only after issuance of permit for Entry into Enclosed Space (Form: SS004) by the Master, stating that there is no practicable alternative to the proposed method of entry and that such entry is essential to save life and/or to avoid pollution.
A permit has been issued by the Master stating that there is no practicable alternative to the proposed method of entry and that such entry is essential to the safe operation of the ship. | approved safety lighting or intrinsically safe electrical equipment should be used in enclosed spaces that are liable to experience hydrocarbon vapour re-contamination.

Ventilation is provided where possible.
Concerned personnel use breathing apparatus and lifeline.
The number of persons entering the compartment is kept to a minimum consistent with the work to be performed.
Means of communication are provided and a system of signals is agreed and understood by the personnel involved.
Spare sets of breathing apparatus and resuscitators are available outside the compartment, and a standby party is in attendance in case of emergency.
Work to deal with above emergencies is to be undertaken in a manner that will avoid creating an ignition hazard.

Working in Domestic Fridge/Cold Chambers
While working inside cold chambers or any other enclosed spaces where refrigerant gas line (freon gas) or evaporator equipments are present, adequate precautions shall be taken to ensure that the space is ventilated prior to entering such spaces and during the course of work, if any, inside such spaces. Refrigerant gas such as Freon, although not toxic in nature, can asphyxiate when inhaled in copious amount.

Notices
A ship-specific list of designated enclosed spaces shall be displayed at prominent places for information of the personnel. The following notice shall be prominently displayed on Notice Boards and at entrances to enclosed spaces to inform personnel of the precautions to be taken when entering tanks or other enclosed spaces:
ENCLOSED SPACES CAN KILL
	Do not enter without permission
	Ensure safety checks are done before entry
	Leave the space if ventilation fails
	Confirm communication method with person outside before entry
	Ensure you are familiar with any apparatus to be used


Protective Equipment and Clothing
It is important that all those entering an enclosed space wear suitable clothing and they make use of protective equipment, which may be provided on board for their safety. Safety practices and precautions listed in Section 7.11.2 shall be complied with.

Evacuation from Enclosed Spaces
If any of the conditions stated on the entry or work permit become unsafe, after personnel have entered the tank, space or compartment, responsible person standing-by at the entrance to the space, shall ensure that all personnel vacate the space immediately. After the situation has been re-assessed and safe conditions restored, a fresh permit (Form: SS004), with appropriate revisions shall be issued. Instructions/guidelines given in Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seamen (Chapter 17 – Entering Enclosed or Confined spaces) shall also be referred to before making entry into enclosed spaces. | Ventilation is provided where possible.

Fire Prevention

Cause of Fire
Shipboard personnel shall exercise due care and comply with applicable regulations. All efforts shall be made to ensure that all fire fighting equipment is maintained in good order and ready for use. The integrity of the constructional features provided on board to prevent fires, shall not be disturbed in any manner.
The causes of fire on board include:
Oil spray from loose or broken pipe fittings splashing on high temperature surfaces,
Accumulation of soot in uptakes and exhaust gas economisers,
Flammable liquids leaking through faulty or damaged pipe work;
Ignition of oil soaked insulation,
Overheating of hot surfaces in close proximity of oil lines,
Overheating of machinery,
Defects in lagging,
Carrying out hot work without proper precautions,
Spontaneous combustion of oil-soaked natural fibre,
Poor housekeeping.
Overheating of flammable liquids and fats,
Overheating of deep-fat fryers,
Greasy flues,
Hot surfaces,
Defective electrical connections,
Build up of hydrogen in the battery room.
Ignition of cargoes liable to self-heating and spontaneous combustion,
Damage to packages containing hazardous cargoes,
Accumulation of flammable material in sweepings etc.

Fire Precautions
The following precautions shall be taken to prevent shipboard fires:
Any oil leakage shall be rectified as soon as possible and any leakage or spillage cleaned up immediately.
Shield high temperature spots that are sources of ignition from fire risks by splashing of oil.
All insulating material, which has been removed for inspection of equipment, shall always be replaced.
Do not allow oil accumulation in drip trays.
Oily waste and rags shall be placed in metal containers that shall be provided for the purpose. The contents of these containers shall be safely disposed of.
Test remote shut-off devices at frequent intervals.
Avoid oil tank overflows by ensuring proper gauging facilities.
Do not store flammable material in machinery spaces, particularly around boiler casings or engine exhausts and uptakes or in the funnel.
Take appropriate precautions when conducting hot work. | Fire Prevention

Do not store flammable material in machinery spaces, particularly around boiler casings or engine exhausts and uptakes or in the funnel.
Take appropriate precautions when conducting hot work.

Safety & Security | 
Maintain Engine Room clean.
Galleys shall be adequately ventilated. Over cooking areas exhaust ventilation shall be available. The uptakes and filters shall be cleaned once in three months or earlier if necessary to remove oily deposits.
Care shall be taken to ensure that pans or fat are not left unattended in the oven or on hot plates/burners.
Keep the galley clean.
Battery rooms shall be kept clear of any equipment, including other electrical equipment, likely to provide a source of ignition. This room shall not be used as a store room. Battery room shall be effectively ventilated to avoid accumulation of hydrogen.
Persons entering the battery room shall ensure that they do not introduce any source of ignition, for example by smoking, lighting matches or taking in an open flame or an un- approved portable lamp for inspection.
Portable electric tools and appliances shall not be used where flammable vapour is suspected to be present.

Smoking Restrictions
Smoking shall not be permitted on workplaces on board except in places specifically permitted by the Master. Areas where smoking is permitted shall be properly defined and indicated and suitable non-spill ashtrays shall be provided. Typically, smoking may be permitted in officers and crew messrooms.

Smoking regulations shall be conspicuously displayed on ship‘s notice board.
Smoking on bunks is prohibited.
Smoking on board is strictly prohibited in ports where local regulations and safe working practices prohibit it.
Careless disposal of smoking materials is prohibited at all times.
No person shall be allowed to smoke in any area where painting is being or has been carried out until the paint has thoroughly dried.
Personnel shall not carry cigarettes, lighters or matches outside such permitted areas, and the risk of creating a hazard by so doing shall be impressed on all personnel.
After smoking, personnel shall take care to ensure that all butts and ashes are properly extinguished, and placed in a non-spill ashtray.
Personnel shall not smoke whilst using aerosols.
Cigarette butts and matches shall not be thrown out through portholes at any time.
No Smoking signs shall be posted as warning notices in areas where smoking is prohibited.
