7.13	Hygiene & Health

Shipboard Occupational Health and Safety Programme (SOHSP)
A Shipboard Occupational Health and Safety Program (SOHSP) is a systematic plan to identify and control hazards and respond to emergencies.
All personnel from on board and ashore need to be directly involved in developing, implementing, evaluating and if required, modifying the SOHSP.
Specific ways the ship staff and shore staff can contribute to effective SOHSP include:
Participating in periodic ship inspection
Evaluating health and safety programme materials
Developing standard operating procedures that incorporate safe working practices
Conducting Job Safety Analysis (JSA)/Job Hazard Analysis (JHA)
Participating in accident/illness/near miss investigation
Developing solutions to occupational health and safety complaints
The core function of SOHSP is prevention. Health and safety hazards and unsafe operating procedures need to be identified and addressed so that they will not endanger ship staff or public and will not cause any damage to the vessel, cargo or third party property. Potential hazards must be systematically anticipated, identified, evaluated and controlled.

Regular inspection of the workplace and work processes and procedures help in identifying existing hazards and finding corrective action. Such actions are a proactive approach to ensure workplace health and safety. Job hazard analysis, risk assessment, risk management methodologies are some of the tools, which enable evaluation and control of hazards.
Types of hazards include:
Hazardous Atmosphere due to oxygen deficiency, flammable or toxic gases or vapours and biological agents
Chemical Hazards such as battery acid and solvents and proper handling of ship generated hazardous waste
Biological Hazards, such as bacteria, viruses, dusts, and molds. Biological hazards are often called "biohazards".
Physical Hazards, such as noise, vibration, heat, radiation, electricity, uncontrolled mechanical energy, shifting of cargo etc.
Ergonomic Factors, such as fatigue, workstation designs, poor team practices
Collision, Grounding or ramming and their resultant impacts
Drowning
Ship staff needs to be appropriately trained in their occupational health and safety responsibilities, such as risk assessment and risk management, incident investigation and root cause analysis; in order to enable them to carry out their responsibilities diligently. Training links occupational health and safety policies with specific job practices and raises awareness and skill levels of an individual to an acceptable standard.
Effectiveness of SOHSP on board ship needs to be demonstrated by maintaining proper records of injury and illness data. Maintaining such data would enable identification of trends and patterns that associate the injury or illness with a common cause, which can then be | 7.13	Hygiene & Health

addressed. A Record of Medical Treatment in cases of Illness or Personnel Injury shall be maintained on board, in the format given at the end of this section. A copy of this report shall be forwarded to the Sr. Vice President (Fleet Personnel) every quarter.
SOHSP requires prompt investigation of all shipboard personnel injuries, occupational illnesses and ‗near miss‘ incidents. These occurrences need to be analysed to identify the primary cause and contributing factors so as to avoid recurrence.

Another important aspect of SOHSP is providing information on various hazards, safety rules, standard operating procedures and emergency procedures to outsiders (third party), who visit the ship and are likely to be exposed to ship and cargo hazard. Similarly, information on potential hazards related to work conducted by contract or third party personnel on board is also required to be provided to the ship. Such exchange of information between the ship and third party may be accomplished by way of exchanging safety data sheets (SDS) or similar arrangement. This exchange of information shall identify ship hazards and hazards presented by the work intended by third party, as also actions towards health and safety of ship‘s crew and that of third party. A sample format, giving general instructions to all visitors, is included at the end of this section. These instructions to all visitors shall be displayed on board near the gangway. Ships may devise their own instructions to suit specific requirements.

Important Definitions related to SOHSP
Hazard: Source or situation with a potential to harm in terms of injury or ill health, damage to property, damage to workplace environment or a combination of these.
Hazard Identification: Process of recognising that a hazard exists and defining its characteristics.
Job Hazard Analysis (JHA): is a procedure, which helps integrate accepted safety and health principles and practices into a particular operation.
Occupational Health and Safety: Conditions and factors that affect well-being of employees, temporary workers, contractor personnel, visitors and any other person in the workplace.
Risk: Combination of the likelihood and consequence(s) of a specified hazardous event occurring
Risk Assessment: Overall process of estimating the magnitude of risk and deciding whether or not the risk is tolerable.
Risk Management: is a process of measuring or assessing risk and developing strategies to manage it.
Tolerable Risk: Risk that has been reduced to a level that can be endured by the organization having regard to its legal obligations and its Occupational Health and Safety Policy.
For further guidance on Shipboard Occupational Health and Safety Programme, refer following:
Engineering Circular No. 56 dated 11.08.2005 issued by DGS
OHSAS 18001:2007, Guidelines for the implementation of OHSAS 18001 | addressed. Hygiene
Good housekeeping is essential to ensure shipboard hygiene.
All places where food is stored, galleys, stores, mess rooms, dining spaces, common spaces and other accommodation areas shall be inspected every week, by the Master, for cleanliness, freedom from insects or rodent infestation.
De-ratting and disinfestation of galleys, stores, mess rooms, dining spaces, common spaces and other accommodation areas shall be carried out by ship‘s personnel every month. Shipboard personnel shall not touch dead rats with bare hands, instead, dead rats shall be removed with tongs or other equivalent means.
Shipboard personnel coming into contact with harmful substances shall thoroughly wash their face and hands with soap, or other suitable cleansing agents, before taking any food or drink or shall follow the special personal cleansing instructions which they have been given for the particular substance they are handling.
Members of the catering department shall be impressed upon that their personal hygiene is very important for achieving high standards of hygiene on board. They shall:
Wash hands and fingernails before handling food.
Report all injuries, open wounds and sores, illness, rashes and spots to the Chief Officer.
Not smoke in galleys, pantries, store rooms or other places where food is prepared.
Cooks to wear aprons and caps while cooking and serving. Stewards and pantry staff to wear clean clothes/uniform while in attendance.
Meals shall not be consumed in the cabins as it leads to lowering of hygiene standards and is detrimental to good housekeeping. Meals shall not be kept in cabins. Meals shall be served/eaten only in designated mess rooms.
As far as practicable, meals shall be taken during scheduled meal timings only. Master may amend/adjust meal timings to suit the operational requirements of the ship. All officers shall wear uniforms while having meals in the messroom except during exceptional and emergency situations when they may have meals in clean boiler suits or suitable appropriate dress. Officers must be in uniform or in appropriate and clean dress when in the officer‘s lounge.
It is the responsibility of all shipboard individuals to ensure high standards of personal cleanliness. Officers on navigational watches should be in neat and clean uniforms. Other personnel on watches should be in clean and proper boiler suits or in attire appropriate for the work and prevailing weather and climatic conditions.

Health
Safeguarding the health of shipboard personnel is an important function of safety.
The Master has the overall responsibility for administering prompt medical treatment to ill or injured personnel on board.
The vessel shall carry on board the International Medical Guide for Ships Medical First Aid Guide for Use in Accidents Involving Dangerous Goods, Ship Captain‘s Medical Guide.
The Chief Officer shall be designated as the vessel‘s Medical Officer.
The Chief Officer is directly responsible for administering prompt medical treatment to ill or injured personnel on board. | Hygiene

De-ratting and disinfestation of galleys, stores, mess rooms, dining spaces, common spaces and other accommodation areas shall be carried out by ship‘s personnel every month. Shipboard personnel shall not touch dead rats with bare hands, instead, dead rats shall be removed with tongs or other equivalent means.
Shipboard personnel coming into contact with harmful substances shall thoroughly wash their face and hands with soap, or other suitable cleansing agents, before taking any food or drink or shall follow the special personal cleansing instructions which they have been given for the particular substance they are handling.
Members of the catering department shall be impressed upon that their personal hygiene is very important for achieving high standards of hygiene on board. They shall:
Wash hands and fingernails before handling food.
Report all injuries, open wounds and sores, illness, rashes and spots to the Chief Officer.
Not smoke in galleys, pantries, store rooms or other places where food is prepared.
Cooks to wear aprons and caps while cooking and serving. Stewards and pantry staff to wear clean clothes/uniform while in attendance.
Meals shall not be consumed in the cabins as it leads to lowering of hygiene standards and is detrimental to good housekeeping. Meals shall not be kept in cabins. Meals shall be served/eaten only in designated mess rooms.
As far as practicable, meals shall be taken during scheduled meal timings only. Master may amend/adjust meal timings to suit the operational requirements of the ship. All officers shall wear uniforms while having meals in the messroom except during exceptional and emergency situations when they may have meals in clean boiler suits or suitable appropriate dress. Officers must be in uniform or in appropriate and clean dress when in the officer‘s lounge.
It is the responsibility of all shipboard individuals to ensure high standards of personal cleanliness. Officers on navigational watches should be in neat and clean uniforms. Other personnel on watches should be in clean and proper boiler suits or in attire appropriate for the work and prevailing weather and climatic conditions.

Health
Safeguarding the health of shipboard personnel is an important function of safety.
The Master has the overall responsibility for administering prompt medical treatment to ill or injured personnel on board.
The vessel shall carry on board the International Medical Guide for Ships Medical First Aid Guide for Use in Accidents Involving Dangerous Goods, Ship Captain‘s Medical Guide.
The Chief Officer shall be designated as the vessel‘s Medical Officer.
The Chief Officer is directly responsible for administering prompt medical treatment to ill or injured personnel on board. | Hygiene

 | SHIPBOARD
SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
The Chief Officer is directly responsible to the Master for maintaining stock of medicines and upkeep of medical equipment on board.
The vessel shall carry on board medicines as per the list provided in the International Medical Guide for Ships.
Except in emergency, medical services in port shall be arranged through the ship‘s agent, or Company medical facilities.
In case of emergency where immediate medical aid is required, the facilities most readily obtainable shall be used. If no facilities are readily available competent medical advice shall be requested by the most reliable and effective means of communication available.
If the services of a doctor are required immediately upon arrival in port, a request shall be made by the most reliable and effective means of communication available to the ship‘s agent.
Seafarers are required to report all illnesses and injuries to the Chief Officer promptly, so that adequate medical attention may be given.
Ill or injured personnel shall be checked at frequent intervals and provided medical treatment according to the International Medical Guide for Ships, Medical First Aid Guide for Use in Accidents Involving Dangerous Goods.
In cases of serious illness or injury, a responsible member of the crew shall be assigned to the patient to provide constant attention. Personnel having contagious diseases shall be segregated at once to prevent spread of the disease to others.
In serious cases of illness or injury where life may be endangered, consideration shall be given to the advisability of proceeding to the nearest port where medical aid may be obtained.
When an ill or injured person is landed ashore from the vessel, the following persons shall be notified promptly:
Chief Medical Officer
Sr. Vice President (Fleet Personnel Department)
Group In-charge (Technical Department)
And the ship‘s agent at the port of transfer giving particulars regarding the case.
If a member of the crew loses his life, either due to illness or injury, aboard the vessel or while ashore, the Master shall immediately notify by the quickest possible means, the following persons giving name and rank of the deceased and cause of death:
Chief Medical Officer
Sr. Vice President (Fleet Personnel Department)
Group In-charge (Technical Department)
Designated Person Ashore
Next-of-kin of the deceased
It is the responsibility of individual crew members to look after their own health. Attention shall be paid to consuming suitable diet, regular exercise, avoidance of excess alcohol and tobacco consumption, avoidance of recreational drugs and taking precautions against infectious diseases. Crew members should particularly guard against contacting sexually transmitted diseases. In particular Crew members should be advised to take precautions to avoid contacting the dreaded illness Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) which may eventually lead to death. Crew members should be instructed that risks could be minimised by adhering to safe sex practises i.e. using condoms. | The Chief Officer is directly responsible to the Master for maintaining stock of medicines and upkeep of medical equipment on board.

Ban on cooking in cabins etc.
All cooking on board shall be confined to the galley only. Cooking in the cabins/spaces other than galley is a very big fire hazard and can lead to major fire incidents. Such cooking also affects the health and hygiene standards on board.
No electric hot plate, toasters, ovens or any other improvised devices are to be used in the cabins. | Ban on cooking in cabins etc.

7.14	Safety Equipment

Safety Register
Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure proper maintenance of the safety equipment carried on board the vessel. Maintenance of lifesaving appliances and portable fire-fighting appliances (outside machinery spaces) shall be under the charge of the Chief Officer. Maintenance of portable fire-fighting appliances (within machinery spaces) and fixed fire- fighting appliances shall be under the charge of the Second Engineer Officer and other engineer officers, supervised by the Chief Engineer Officer. Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall maintain a record of inspections and maintenance carried out on safety equipment in the Master‘s Safety Register and Chief Engineer Officer‘s Safety Register. The Safety Register shall contain columns as indicated below:
Name of Equipment:
Details of Inspection, including	Action Taken	Date Defect	Signature Date	Routines carried out and Defects		for Defects		Rectified		and Date
noticed

Specifications, details of inspection and maintenance routines for each equipment shall precede entries regarding each equipment, in the Safety Register.
A list of Items to be included in Master‘s Safety Register and Chief Engineer Officer‘s Safety Register is provided below for guidance. A ship specific list of safety items to be routinely inspected on board shall be developed by the Master and Chief Engineer Officer and included in the respective registers.

7.15	Critical Equipment and Critical Systems
Critical equipment/system is that, the sudden failure of which may result in hazardous situation. In compliance with the Code, procedures are in place to ensure that these systems are adequately maintained and specific measures established to promote the reliability of these equipment/systems. These specific measures include, but are not limited to, following:
testing of stand-by arrangements
testing of alarm functions
lubricating oil analysis
cooling water treatment
filter cleaning
function testing
routine replacement of critical components
alternate running of stand-by machinery
systematic inspections/surveys by statutory bodies
engine performance monitoring
Although the configurations and the stand-by systems for each vessel are different, procedures adopted to identify critical equipment/system are common to all. It is recognised that all equipments are important for the proper operation of the vessel. If most of the equipments on board the ship are considered as critical, the usefulness of the actual critical equipments becomes limited.
The risk assessment and root cause analysis of various past accidents, near-miss/hazardous occurrence method have been adopted for identifying the critical equipment and the list has been made to meet ISM Code criteria and limited to safety and environmental protection.
The levels of criticality of equipments/systems are considered as under:
Level A – Critical without redundancy nor procedures of replenishment
Level B – Critical with redundancy and procedure for replenishment
Level C – Not Critical
The Company in general has identified the following as critical equipment/systems:
Emergency Air Compressor and Engine
Emergency Lighting System
Engine Room Bilge Alarms
Fire Alarms
Fire Pumps
Fire & Smoke Detection Systems
Fixed Firefighting System
Main Switch Board
Shipboard Incinerator
Oily Water separator and filtering equipment
Windlass
Master/Chief Engineer Officer of the vessel shall review the contents of the list and include equipments to the critical item list depending upon its unique feature and past history. The reason for inclusion shall be available on board.
The system of maintenance of critical equipment has been included in the PMS. Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall highlight each specific task with respect to Critical Equipment | 7.15	Critical Equipment and Critical Systems

Master/Chief Engineer Officer of the vessel shall review the contents of the list and include equipments to the critical item list depending upon its unique feature and past history. The reason for inclusion shall be available on board.
The system of maintenance of critical equipment has been included in the PMS. Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall highlight each specific task with respect to Critical Equipment

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Safety & Security | 
so that shipboard personnel responsible for maintenance can effectively prioritise the work and people actually doing the work understand that they are working on a critical equipment.
The list of critical equipment/systems shall be periodically reviewed and amended, if need arises, based on the outcome of SMS reviews, internal/external safety management system audits and reported accidents, near misses/hazardous occurrences.
If any item is malfunctioning, system shall be promptly checked and fault rectified. In case it is not possible to rectify the fault immediately, alternate temporary methods such as amending parameters may be adopted. A notice/sign indicating the non-conforming status of the equipment shall be displayed prominently. Departmental Heads shall issue necessary instructions to monitor the alternate system.
Risk assessment shall be undertaken whenever carrying out maintenance of critical equipment/system. Refer section 7.10.1 in this regard.
Testing of Stand-by Arrangements
Stand-by arrangements for various machineries/systems shall be tried out by putting them into use at regular intervals as per PMS. All stand-by machineries/systems shall be identified and their change-over intervals shall be specified. Record of change-over shall be maintained on board for verification.
Spares for Critical Equipment
Minimum quantity of spare parts required for identified critical equipment shall be determined and maintained on board. The stock position of the spare parts shall be forwarded to the operating division on monthly basis and records shall be maintained on board. Whenever spares are used, same shall be indented on emergency basis in order to maintain required stock of spares on board (Ref. section 10.6.2).
The offshore vessels operated by the Company are generally sister vessels, falling in 2/3 groups and operate mainly in the offshore field on the coast. These vessels are of compact size having space constraint for storage. Also, if the vessels are incapacitated due to failure of critical equipment, they can be easily brought to the base port with the help of other offshore vessels which are readily available in the vicinity. In consideration of same, the operating division may stock required spares for critical equipment at the base port for use in emergency, instead of keeping all the spares in each of the sister vessels. However, frequently consumed spares shall be maintained on board.
Responsibility
Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall be responsible to:
Identify additional ship-specific critical equipment/systems if required
formulate regular routines and testing schedules for such equipment/systems
implement maintenance schedules and maintain records
inform superintendent suitably
Emergency Equipment
Failure of emergency equipment such as rescue boat engines, emergency fire pump and engine, emergency lighting etc. usually leads to detention of the vessel during FSI/PSC inspections. Hence, it shall be ensured that these emergency equipments are maintained and kept in readiness at all times, especially in cold climatic conditions. | so that shipboard personnel responsible for maintenance can effectively prioritise the work and people actually doing the work understand that they are working on a critical equipment.

Safety on Offshore Vessels

Spark Arresters
Vessels which are required to close an installation must have spark arresters fitted to all exhaust stacks and the Master shall ensure that they operate efficiently. Any other source of ignition on the open deck shall be prevented.

Fire or Gas Alarms
On hearing fire or gas alarms on an installation, the Master shall comply with the Operator‘s guidelines and any requirements of the particular installation. This does not relieve the Master of the responsibility to ensure the safety of own vessel/personnel.

Boarding Unmanned Structures
Going alongside an unmanned structure shall be avoided unless specifically permitted by the person responsible for that structure and:
Transfer of personnel from an OSV and vice versa shall be done using a transfer basket, specially designed and certified.
Prior to boarding an unmanned structure, the Master shall ensure that reasonable means exist for recovering the personnel from the structure and weather is conducive.
Personnel boarding an unmanned structure shall comply with the Master‘s instructions with regard to boarding and leaving the structure.
Vessel shall remain in close proximity of the structure during the entire operation.
Personnel required to board an unmanned structure shall be accompanied by at least one other person.
Personnel boarding the unmanned structure shall done personal protective equipment and carry radio communication facility, hand torch and life jackets.
Personnel shall not remain on an unmanned structure during the hours of darkness.
The transfer operation shall be abandoned if in the opinion of the Master, the safety of personnel and ship is likely to be in jeopardy and the OIM shall be informed.

7.16.4	Personnel Transfer by Boat
Transfer of personnel from vessel to vessel/installation shall take place only with agreement of persons responsible for both the units.
When transfers are contemplated during the hours of darkness, the Master shall take into account the additional hazards. If there is any doubt, the operation shall be postponed until daylight hours. Life-jackets and survival suits shall be worn by both crew and passengers during transfer. Safety helmets shall be worn by crew and passengers when within 50 meters of any unit. The progress of the transfer craft shall be closely watched to ensure any emergency aid needed is given at once. Other vessels in the vicinity shall be advised of boat transfers. | Safety on Offshore Vessels

Emergency Preparedness

General
This section of the manual outlines procedure for Shipboard Emergency Response.

At sea, the responsibility for shipboard emergency response rests with the Master, assisted by Chief Engineer Officer and Chief Officer. Where a casualty occurs in territorial waters or port limits, the national authority and/or the port authority may be involved and the Master's freedom of action may be thereby constrained. This would be particularly so, if the hazards relevant to the casualty could put third parties and property at risk. In these latter circumstances, contingency plans may need to be adapted quickly to take account of the requirements of the shore authorities. However, the basic considerations in these circumstances are still of the same nature as those when the ship is at sea.

Master‘s priority actions should take into consideration:
Safety of life at sea;
Avoidance of marine environmental pollution;
Prevention of damage to ship;
Safe carriage of cargo at sea.
In every emergency situation, the Master must promptly evaluate the situation and assess the extent and nature of assistance needed if any, in order that he can prevent deterioration of the situation.

The procedures outlined in this section shall be used to initiate emergency response from all shipboard personnel. These procedures cover the following main group of shipboard emergencies:
Groups of Emergency	Type of Emergency

Abandon Ship

Fire		Fire on board
Fire in vicinity of ship (e.g. fire on nearby offshore platform/structure etc.)

Damage to Ship		Collision
Grounding/Stranding
Hull/Structural Failure
Flooding
Heavy Weather Damage*
ME/CPP/Bow Thruster Failure*
Steering Gear Failure*
Electrical Power Failure* | Emergency Preparedness

8.2	Emergency Drills
Emergency drills shall be carried out regularly to test the effectiveness and clarity of emergency plans, and to develop the confidence and competence of the personnel who may be involved in actual emergencies.
Actions to counter potential emergency situations shall be practised in drills. In addition to fire, abandon ship drills, and as required by the SOLAS Convention and national regulations, emergency drills covering all emergencies listed in Section 8.1 of this manual shall be conducted routinely in order to develop and maintain confidence and proficiency on board.

Emergency drills shall be conducted in accordance with Form: EM005D(OS), provided in this section 8 of the SMS Manual.

Emergency drills shall be realistic in nature and endeavour to replicate real life emergency situations, as far as practicable without endangering shipboard personnel or vessel.

Records of all emergency drills conducted on board shall be maintained in the deck logbook and in the official log book, where applicable. Log book entries regarding emergency drills shall also be duly filled in the Deck/Engine Room logbooks. Master shall maintain a record of comments, analysis and conclusions of each drill in a copy of the format provided in Form: EM006. Duly filled copies of this form shall be filed in File No. 306.

For the purpose of ensuring effective Ship-Shore communication, the vessel shall establish contact with the Group I/C once a year and maintain record of same, while carrying out one of the drills. Also refer section 8.4.1. | 8.2	Emergency Drills

Emergency Organisation

Organisation of Emergency Teams
For emergency response, the ships complement shall be divided into three teams namely:
Command Team
Emergency Team
Boat Preparation Team
Formats for:
Emergency Muster List — Form: EM005A(OS),
Emergency Muster Duties — Form: EM005B(OS),
Abandon Ship Muster Card — Form: EM005C(OS) and
Emergency Drills and Briefings – Schedule — Form: EM005D(OS) are provided at the end of this section.

The Chief Officer, or any other officer deputed by the Master, shall duly fill and maintain the above formats up-to-date. Form: EM005A(OS) shall be updated on change of personnel and verified.

A complete set of formats, namely Form: EM005A(OS), Form: EM005B(OS), Form: EM005C(OS) and Form: EM005D(OS) shall be displayed at the following locations:
Navigating Bridge
Engine Room
Officer‘s and Crew Accommodation Spaces

8.3.2	Alarm and Initial Response
The general emergency alarm consists of seven or more short blasts followed by one long blast on the ship's whistle or siren and additionally on an electrically operated bell.

	
The fire alarm shall consist of continuous sounding of an electrically operated bell.


The abandon ship signal shall consist of the general emergency alarm signal followed by the spoken word 'ABANDON SHIP' by the Master of the vessel or Chief Officer in the event of incapacity of Master.

In the event of a shipboard emergency that requires emergency response from all shipboard personnel, the general emergency alarm signal shall be sounded. | Emergency Organisation

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Emergency Preparedness | 
The fire alarm shall be used in emergency situations listed below: Group of Emergency	Type of Emergency
Fire		Fire on Ship
Fire in Vicinity of Ship (e.g. fire on near by offshore platform/structure etc.)

At sea, at anchor or in port, on hearing the general emergency alarm signal or fire alarm, all shipboard personnel shall muster at the designated Emergency Muster Locations. This ensures that available resources are known and missing persons identified. A maximum state of readiness is promptly established and a standardised response to the emergency is achieved, allowing for co-ordinated and controlled remedial action.

At sea, at anchor or in port, on hearing the abandon ship signal or fire alarm, all shipboard personnel shall muster at the designated Boat Stations.

In vessels provided with a public address system, the Command Centre shall, immediately after sounding the alarm, announce in clear and unambiguous language:
the nature of emergency; and
the instructions for emergency actions.

The initial response required from all personnel on hearing the emergency alarm shall be:
Collect life jacket;
Dress in long sleeved boiler suit or attire providing equivalent protection;
Shoes and safety helmet; and
Proceed to Muster Station.
Exceptions to the above-mentioned response will be:
Chief Engineer Officer shall contact Command Team to obtain maximum information about the emergency and then proceed to wheel house and assist Master, as per requirement. Chief Officer shall ‗secure‘ current operations, before proceeding to the Muster Stations.
Watch keeping on the Navigating Bridge to be done by the Master. Watch keepers in the Engine Room shall remain on watch until relieved.
Bridge duty seaman shall ensure that a portable radio set is handed over to each team leader.
Cook shall ensure that galley is ‗secured‘ before proceeding to Muster Station.
An individual shall respond in the following manner on discovery of an emergency:
On discovery of the emergency, raise the alarm.
Provide the Command Team with as much information as possible.
Attempt to control the emergency by whatever means available, until relieved by the Emergency Team.
Should the situation become hazardous to the individual, he must retreat to his respective Muster Location and report to the Command Team. | The fire alarm shall be used in emergency situations listed below: Group of Emergency	Type of Emergency

Muster Location
The muster locations of the various teams shall be selected after due consideration of the layout of a particular vessel. The team leader or his deputy shall take charge of the muster and report to the Command Team.

Duties of Teams
On hearing the alarm, the Command Team shall:
Muster at designated muster location;
Command and control;
Ensure efficient muster;
Detail Search Party as required;
Maintain safe navigational watch;
Maintain time event record;
Conduct internal communication;
Conduct external communication.
Master shall direct the Emergency Teams to provide information relating to the emergency. The Master shall assess the situation from the reports received from team leaders and develop an appropriate response strategy. Master shall direct the Emergency Team and Boat Preparation Team on specific action to be taken.

The Emergency Team shall:
Muster at designated muster location;
Prepare emergency equipment as ordered by Command Team (including fireman‘s outfit and other portable safety appliances as required);
Fight and control emergency;
Carry out other emergency response as ordered by command team;
Conduct internal communication.
The Boat Preparation Team shall:
Muster at designated muster location;
Equip survival crafts and other life saving appliances;
Prepare survival craft;
Prepare other life saving appliances;
Carry out other emergency response as ordered by Command Team;
Conduct internal communication.
Conduct other support activities. | Muster Location

When the ship is involved in any incident which:
threatens safety of life at sea,
involves discharge or threatens discharge of harmful substances resulting from damage to ship or its equipment,
endangers safety of ship and its cargo,
the Master shall report details of the incident without delay to the nearest coastal state by means of the fastest communication channel available to him. In the absence of any prescribed format by the coastal state, the initial report to be sent to the government of the coastal state shall be in the format given in Form: EM001.
Reports shall be transmitted either:
to the nearest Maritime Rescue Co-ordination Centre (MRCC) satellite communication system; or
to the nearest appropriate coast radio station on appropriate frequency; or

Emergency Preparedness | 
to the designated radio station of a ship reporting system, when the ship is within the boundaries of the system.

In any emergency, in addition to the statutory obligations laid down by international law, national and international regulation, the vessel shall establish contact, on top priority, with the Company by the most efficient means available at hand. For this purpose, a single point contact number (mobile phone number) has been developed and intimated to the vessels. However, Master may use any other communication channel available at hand to establish contact with the Company. The contact list for the Company and Offshore Department is available in this manual and is updated from time to time.

The vessel shall contact the respective Gp. I/C for the vessel. If the respective Gp. I/C is unavailable, the respective Sr. Vice President and/or attending superintendent shall be contacted. If the situation warrants, the Master shall not hesitate to contact Director (T&OS)/DPA and/or the Chairman and Managing Director directly.

Where applicable, the ONGC In-charge of the vessel also to be informed at the earliest opportunity.

The vessel shall promptly notify the Gp. I/C regarding an emergency on board, using the format provided in Form: EM001. Situation reports shall be sent regularly to the Gp. I/C, using the format provided in Form: EM002.

In the event of a probable or actual discharge of oil from the vessel, the approved Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) shall be activated by the vessel.

Internal Communication
Whenever an emergency occurs, it is important to have an efficient internal communications between the Command Team, Emergency Team and Boat Preparation Team.
It is an established fact that poor internal communication is the root cause of many marine incidents/casualties. It is also an area where least training is imparted. Hence, communication drills are an essential part during emergency drills on board. Merely conducting a drill and recording the same to fulfil the ISM requirement is not enough. Drills and training for any emergency response vary from ship to ship and crew to crew. However, requirement for a two-way understanding between the officer in charge and crew members who are actually responding to the emergency, is most important.

One or a combination of the following internal communication systems shall be used:
Telephone
Self-powered Phone
VHF/UHF Portable Transceiver Radio (Walkie-Talkie)
VHF
Public Address System
If all above systems fail or are unavailable for some reason, a messenger shall be designated for internal communication between various groups. | to the designated radio station of a ship reporting system, when the ship is within the boundaries of the system.

Emergency Procedures
The Master shall take whatever action is possible to remedy the emergency situation, initially making the best use of the ship's own resources until outside assistance can be obtained.
A plan of action should be developed taking account of the following factors:
The nature, circumstances and urgency of the situation.
The various ship systems (main propulsion, steering, electrical, cargo, etc.) that remain operative and how they can be applied to relieve the situation.
The ability of the ship's personnel to minimise or nullify the effects of the casualty and to restore the ship's capability.
The use of alternative means to overcome the operational deficiency.
The natural effects of wind, sea, current, etc. and ways to take advantage of them.
The use of outside assistance and the measures to be taken on board the ship to accommodate such assistance.
The risk of pollution.
If the ship is in imminent peril and if all else fails, the extreme measures to be taken to avoid loss of life, to minimise damage to property and to mitigate the effects of pollution.

Following pages provide guidance on items, which may be considered by the Command of the vessel, when formulating an incident-specific emergency response. Action taken in an emergency shall take into consideration safety of life and property and prevention of environmental pollution. Master may supplement the above-mentioned items with ship- specific and incident-specific procedures.

Search & Rescue Operations
Whenever search and rescue operation is conducted at sea, either to rescue own shipboard personnel fallen overboard accidentally or otherwise; or to rescue distressed personnel of any other vessel at sea, the checklist Form: EM015 shall be followed.
Marine Rescue Co-ordination Centre (MRCC/RCC) shall be informed about the necessary rescue operations being undertaken and their advice on the matter shall be sought. On completion of the search and rescue operations, when the personnel are rescued, the MRCC/RCC shall be informed regarding calling off of the operation.

In cases where the Master is convinced that the ‗area of interest‘ has been thoroughly searched and believes that the chances of locating the missing person(s) are remote (very low probability), he shall call off the operation, in consultation with MRCC/RCC. The operating division shall be kept informed in compliance with Form: EM015.

Forms for Emergency Preparedness
Below listed Forms shall be used during various types of emergencies. It shall be ensured that all the items enumerated in the forms (as applicable to specific ship type), are suitably dealt with while using such forms. | Emergency Procedures

Emergency Preparedness | 
Legal Aspects
Entries in Log Books and Other Documents
Entries in Log Books and other documents, whether official or not, must be accurate, factual and indisputable. All Log Books and documents are to be completed in ink and in neat and legible writing. Erasures, blanks or other incorrect entries rendered are not acceptable. The following method is to be adopted:
rule through the incorrect entry by a single straight line and initial in the margin.
make the correct entry and put initials again.
Restriction of information
No statement or declaration should be made to the media by ship's personnel until advice has been received from the Company. In the event that contact with the Company cannot be readily established, advice should be obtained from the local representative of the vessel's P&I Club. In the event of the Master being compelled to record a statement or report, he shall clause such statement or report as follows:
―Submitted without prejudice and not as an admission of liability‖
Other Party
Should the Company's vessel be involved in a collision with another vessel, the Master, the owner or the agent of the other vessel must be held responsible in writing for all damages and/or losses sustained by the parties having lawful interest in the Company's vessel.
An acknowledgement of receipt of such letter should be obtained. Receipt of a similar letter from another vessel, or from a shore installation involved in the incident should be acknowledged as follows:
"Signed for receipt only and not as an admission of liability"
When any damage is sustained by or inflicted on another vessel or a shore installation, the Master should ensure, through the agent, that the Master or agent of the other vessel or the representative of the shore installation, as the case may be, is invited to attend the damage survey of his vessel and to agree to the extent of such damage. Likewise, the Master, through the agent, should ensure that the surveyor acting on behalf of the Company should be present at the damage survey of the other vessel or shore installation.
Assistance from Other Vessels
When the vessel suffers a casualty or is otherwise in a position of peril, the Master must assess the need for external assistance. Efficient communication is the key to prompt availability of external assistance. The Company would be in a better position to organise external assistance for the vessel provided there is effective communication between the ship and the Company.
Salvage services do not need to be rendered under contract, provided they meet the following criteria. There are three basic criteria which must be met for services to be regarded as salvage:
Firstly, the subject of the salvage should be in danger, although not necessarily imminent danger.
Secondly, the services rendered by salvors must be beneficial to the salved property.
Thirdly, the services rendered must be successful. | Legal Aspects

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Emergency Preparedness | 
In most cases, where time and circumstances permit, the Company together with the Master will agree with the salvors to the terms on which the salvage services will be rendered with the authority of other parties with interests in the vessel who will benefit from the salvage services. Therefore, in the event salvage services are required, it is important that the Master informs the Company, as soon as, a casualty occurs to prevent salvage services becoming more urgent and consequently more expensive.
However, in cases of absolute urgency, the Master may engage salvage services under the Lloyd's Standard Form of Salvage Agreement (current edition – LOF-2011). A copy of this form is appended to this sub-section. It must be stressed that only the Command of the vessel has authority to reach an agreement in cases where the vessel and the cargo on board are in imminent danger and there is no reasonable opportunity to contact the Company in order to obtain their authority. The Command of the vessel shall so far as is safe and practicable should obtain the authority of the Company, as well as cargo owners, before agreeing to any proposed terms put forward by salvors.
Finally, it is important to note that most salvage agreements, including the LOF, require full co-operation between the crew of the salved vessel and the salvors. Although, there may be substantial tension between the two parties, the Master should ensure that crew fully assist and co-operate with the salvors.
The government of a country, whose interests are threatened, has a right to take action within its territorial waters in respect of a ship that has suffered a maritime casualty. In port or estuaries, the local port or harbour authority may have jurisdiction. The Master should comply with instructions given by the government or the authority, and a full report should be made to the owner or operator. If any such instructions are, in the professional judgement of the Master, inadvisable or dangerous, he should question them and, if appropriate, register a protest to the government or authority, in writing.
There are certain crucial items of evidence, which would be required in all situations involving salvage. Master should follow the procedure listed below:
Procedures
Ensure that an accurate record is kept of any conversations relating to a salvage agreement. If at all possible, where an agreement is reached by radio, an independent third party should be asked to take notes for future reference;
Ensure that a precise record is kept of the time of the commencement of salvage services, the times of any communications relating to salvage agreements, and time arrival of salvage vessels;
Delegate a record keeper or clerk whose task it is to fully and accurately record events in writing, by photographs, or any other available method;
Ensure that Deck, Engine, and Radio logbooks are accurate and current, and in particular the deck logs contain regular recordings of the vessel's position.
In addition to the above items, in the following situations where salvage services may be required, a record should be kept of the items listed below:
Main Engine/CPP/Bow Thruster Breakdown
The vessel's position, recorded at frequent intervals;

The extent of damage;
The prospects of repairing engine unassisted and the crew's ability to complete such repairs;
The prospects of repair at sea or in a port of refuge;
The wind direction and tidal or other currents;
If the vessel has to be towed, details of the tow, the distance towed, any difficulties on the tow, and the weather conditions during the tow; and
The identity of any alternative salvors.
Grounding
The nature of the bottom and the manner in which the vessel went aground;
The vessel's position and her heading when she grounded;
The prospects of re-floating the vessel unassisted;
Whether or not the vessel is being driven further aground;
Whether or not the vessel's auxiliaries and main engine are available for use;
Details of the pre-stranding draft of the vessel and the draft when she went aground with particular reference to tidal conditions;
Details of the vessel's movement fore and aft and port and starboard (movement may be detected by setting up two pendulums, one fore and aft and another athwart ship);
Whether or not the vessel is hogging or sagging;
The extent of damage to the vessel, if any;
Weather conditions including the wind direction;
Weights on board the vessel and where carried;
Condition and contents of tanks;
Details of other tugs or other vessels assisting to re-float the vessel and the length of time they were engaged in pulling the vessel; and
Details of lightering operations, including the number of gangs used, the names of lightering vessels, the vessel's draft on commencement and completion of lightering, and the amount of cargo unloaded;
In addition, Master should retain a copy of diver‘s reports on condition of the vessel's bottom.
Collision
The condition of the vessel and the extent of damage;
If there is an ingress of sea water, the areas of the vessel which were flooded, the attempts made to seal openings, whether or not the doors were water tight;
Whether or not the vessel's pumps, generators, and auxiliary machinery remains operable;
Whether or not there is a danger of the vessel sinking; and
The equipment used by salvors;
In addition, the Master should retain a copy of any reports made by surveyors or naval architects.
Fire
Where on the vessel the fire started and the extent of damage;
What combustible material is there on board the vessel which the fire may reach;
Attempts made by the crew to extinguish the fire including details of the use of foam, CO2 or portable pumps;

Whether or not there is a danger of explosion and whether or not the tanks are gas free or inerted;

Post-incident discussion should address how and which lessons can be learnt.
Note of Protest
Following a contingency on board the Master should note a protest in the circumstances enumerated below:
When there is damage to ship
When there is damage to cargo
When there is reason to believe that there is damage to ship or cargo.
Protest should be noted within 24 hours of arrival in port, and in case of cargo protests before breaking bulk. It will be necessary to extend protest when the full extent of damage is known.
Evidence
In the event of any emergency, it is essential to ensure that the records of the event are meticulously maintained in order to pursue claims settlement and safeguard the vessel‘s legal interest. The following documents constitute very important evidence:
Deck Log (with copies)

Engine Room Log (with copies)
Statements of Officers/Crew, as relevant

Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence | 
Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence
Definitions
Non-conformity
An observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfillment of a specified requirement.

Major Non-conformity
An identifiable deviation that poses a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship or a serious risk to the environment that requires immediate corrective action or the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the ISM Code.

Incident as per OHSAS 18001:2007
Work-related event(s) in which an injury or ill health (regardless of severity) or fatality occurred, or could have occurred.

An accident (OHSAS 18001:2007)
An incident which has given rise to injury, ill health or fatality.

Near Miss (OHSAS 18001:2007)
An incident where no injury, ill health, or fatality occurs may also be referred to as a ―near- miss‖, ―near-hit‖, ―close call‖ or ―dangerous occurrence‖
An emergency situation (OHSAS 18001:2007) – is a particular type of incident.

Hazardous Occurrence – is a situation, which could have led to an accident if it had developed further.

Accident
Incidents involving injury or damage to life, the environment, the ship or its cargo.

As per the marine Casualty Investigation code adopted by MSC.255 (84) the following shall be the contents for the terms and definitions described herein:

Marine Casualty
Means an event, or a sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following which has occurred directly in connection with the operations of a ship:
The death of, or serious injury to, a person;
The loss of a person from a ship;
The loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship;
material damage to a ship;
the stranding or disabling of a ship, or the involvement of a ship in a collision;
material damage to marine infrastructure external to a ship, that could seriously endanger the safety of the ship, another ship or an individual; or severe damage to the environment, or the potential for severe damage to the environment, brought about by the damage of a ship or ships. | Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence
Definitions
Non-conformity
An observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfillment of a specified requirement.

Major Non-conformity
An identifiable deviation that poses a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship or a serious risk to the environment that requires immediate corrective action or the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the ISM Code.

Incident as per OHSAS 18001:2007
Work-related event(s) in which an injury or ill health (regardless of severity) or fatality occurred, or could have occurred.

An accident (OHSAS 18001:2007)
An incident which has given rise to injury, ill health or fatality.

Near Miss (OHSAS 18001:2007)
An incident where no injury, ill health, or fatality occurs may also be referred to as a ―near- miss‖, ―near-hit‖, ―close call‖ or ―dangerous occurrence‖
An emergency situation (OHSAS 18001:2007) – is a particular type of incident.

Hazardous Occurrence – is a situation, which could have led to an accident if it had developed further.

Accident
Incidents involving injury or damage to life, the environment, the ship or its cargo.

Marine Casualty
Means an event, or a sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following which has occurred directly in connection with the operations of a ship:
The death of, or serious injury to, a person;
The loss of a person from a ship;

material damage to a ship;

As per the marine Casualty Investigation code adopted by MSC.255 (84) the following shall be the contents for the terms and definitions described herein:

Marine Casualty
Means an event, or a sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following which has occurred directly in connection with the operations of a ship:
The death of, or serious injury to, a person;
The loss of a person from a ship;
The loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship;
material damage to a ship;
the stranding or disabling of a ship, or the involvement of a ship in a collision;
material damage to marine infrastructure external to a ship, that could seriously endanger the safety of the ship, another ship or an individual; or severe damage to the environment, or the potential for severe damage to the environment, brought about by the damage of a ship or ships.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence | 
However, a marine casualty does not include a deliberate act or omission, with the intention to cause harm to the safety of a ship, an individual or the environment.
Serious casualty
Means a casualty which does not qualify as a ―very serious casualty‖ and which involves:
a fire, explosion, grounding, contact, heavy weather damage, ice damage, hull cracking or suspected hull defect, etc. resulting in:
structural damage rendering the ship unseaworthy, such as penetration of the hull underwater, immobilization of main engines, extensive accommodation damage etc.; or
pollution (regardless of quantity) and/or
a breakdown necessitating towage or shore assistance.
Very serious Marine casualty
Means a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship or a death or severe damage to the environment.

A marine incident
Means an event, or sequence of events, other than a marine casualty, which has occurred directly in connection with the operations of a ship that endangered, or, if not corrected, would endanger the safety of the ship, its occupants or any other person or the environment.

However, a marine incident does not include a deliberate act or omission, with the intention to cause harm to the safety of a ship, an individual or the environment.

A marine safety investigation
Means an investigation or inquiry (however referred to by a State), into a marine casualty or marine incident, conducted with the objective of preventing marine casualties and marine incidents in the future. The investigation includes the collection of, and analysis of, evidence, the identification of causal factors and the making of safety.

Marine Accident – means an accident which does not qualify as a very serious casualty or a serious casualty.

Causes
Means actions, omissions, events, existing or pre-existing conditions or a combination thereof, which lead to the casualty or incident.

A serious injury
Means an injury which is sustained by a person, resulting in incapacitation where the person is unable to function normally for more than 72 hours, commencing within seven days from the date when the injury was suffered.

Incident, which occurs off the ship but where the consequences appear on board at some later stage

Work Injury – Any sign or symptom of physical damage or impairment to any part of the body directly resulting from an incident, regardless of the length of time between the incident and the appearance of the injury.

Fatality – A death directly resulting from a work injury regardless of the length of time between the injury and death.

Permanent Total Disability (PTD) – Any work injury, which incapacitates a person permanently and results in termination of employment on medical grounds and precludes the individual from working either at sea or ashore.

Permanent Partial Disability (PPD) – Any work injury, which results in complete loss or permanent loss of use of any member or part of the body or any impairment of functions of parts of the body, regardless of any pre-existing disability of the injured member or impaired body function, that partially restricts or limits an individual‘s basis to work on a permanent basis at sea. Such an individual could be employed ashore but not at sea in line with industry guidelines.

Near Miss (An interpretation) – It‘s an event or sequence of events, which does not result in an accident; but which under slightly different conditions could have caused an accident.

Lost Workday Case (LWC) – An injury, which results in an individual being unable to carry out any of his duties or to return to work on a scheduled work shift on the day following the injury, unless caused by delays in getting medical treatment ashore.
An injury is classified as LWC, if the individual is discharged from the ship for medical treatment.

Restricted Work Case (RWC) – An injury, which results in an individual being unable to perform all normally assigned work functions during a scheduled work shift or being assigned to another job on a temporary or permanent basis on the day following the injury.

Medical Treatment Case (MTC) – Any work related loss of consciousness (unless due to ill health), injury or illness requiring more than first-aid treatment by a physician, dentist, surgeon or registered medical personnel.
Note: First aid cases have a different definition and should not be reported as MTC.

First-Aid Case (FAC) – Any one time treatment and subsequent observation or minor injuries such as bruises, scratches, cuts, burns, splinters etc. The first-aid may or may not be administered by a physician or registered professional. | This excludes:

Lost Time Injuries (LTIs) – A sum of Fatalities, Permanent Total Disabilities, Permanent Partial Disabilities and Lost Workday Cases.
LTIs = Fatalities + PTD + PPD + LWC
Total Recordable Cases (TRC) – A sum of all work-related fatalities, Lost Time Injuries, Restricted Work Injuries and Medical Treatment Injuries.
TRCs = LTIs + RWCs + MTCs.

Causal Factor – As per Casualty investigation code:
Causal factor means actions, omissions, events or conditions, without which:
The marine casualty or marine incident would not have occurred; or
Adverse consequences associated with the marine casualty or marine incident would probably not have occurred or have been as serious;
Another action, omission, event or condition, associated with an outcome in 1 OR 2, would probably not have occurred.
Structural/Machinery/Equipment/Outfitting problems, human errors and external factors that caused an incident, allowed an incident to occur or allowed the consequences of the incident to be worse than they might have been.

Notes:
For a typical incident, there are multiple causal factors.
Causal factors are identified during the first stage of the analysis/investigation.
Each causal factor is an event or condition for which steps should be taken to reduce or mitigate its occurrence.
For each causal factor, underlying causes will be identified and recommendations will be developed.

Human Errors – Performance of humans that deviates from the desired performance. Notes:
This definition is not a failure to perform as directed, but failure to perform as desired. An individual can follow the procedure precisely and still perform a human error, because the individual does not perform as desired (eg. there is a gap between actual and desired performance). In this situation, the procedure specifies the incorrect method for performing the task.
Human errors that are causal factors are might be performed by support level personnel on the vessel. Human errors performed by operational levels and management level are commonly classified as root causes.
Human Factors – Include fatigue, sleep deprivation, poor onboard communication, inadequate training, incompetence or inexperience, perceptual abilities, lack of teamwork, high workload, health, drugs and personal worries arising from domestic difficulties.

External Factor – issues outside the control of the organization. Examples include uncharted/unknown hazards to navigation, some sea or weather conditions, suicides or homicides and external events. | Lost Time Injuries (LTIs) – A sum of Fatalities, Permanent Total Disabilities, Permanent Partial Disabilities and Lost Workday Cases.

Total Recordable Cases (TRC) – A sum of all work-related fatalities, Lost Time Injuries, Restricted Work Injuries and Medical Treatment Injuries.
TRCs = LTIs + RWCs + MTCs.

Intermediate Cause – An underlying reason why a causal factor occurred, but it is not deep enough to be a root cause.
Note: Intermediate causes are underlying causes that link causal factors and items-of-note to root causes.
Structural/Machinery/Equipment/Outfitting Problems – Structural/Machinery/Equipment
/Outfitting performance that deviates from the desired performance of the item.

Note: The definition is not failure to perform as designed, but failure to perform as desired. This means that items can perform as designed and still fail or be degraded, because it fails to perform as desired (e., there is a gap between actual and desired performance). By defining failures in this way, structural/machinery/equipment/outfitting design issues can cause failures/degradations.

Root Cause – The cause that, if corrected, would prevent recurrence of this and similar occurrences. The root cause does not apply to this occurrence only, but has generic implications to a broad group of possible occurrences, and it is the most fundamental aspect of the cause that can logically be identified and corrected. There may be a series of causes that can be identified, one leading to another. This series should be pursued until the fundamental, correctable cause has been identified.

Root Cause Analysis (RCA) – An analysis that identifies the causal factors, intermediate causes and root causes of an incident and/or non-conformity and develops recommendations to address each level of analysis.

Personnel Injury Reporting Guidelines
The primary purpose of reporting Personnel Injury is to promote increased understanding and awareness of personnel safety through efficient and accurate reporting and recording of accidents.
The intent of reporting Personnel Injury is to provide a consistent method for collecting, classifying and reporting data on all personnel injuries occurring on board and continuous monitoring of such injuries in order to provide a measure of effectiveness of Safety Management System and to take appropriate measures with the objective of reducing the frequency of injuries to seafarers.
Documentary evidence relating to the accident, accident reports and follow up from Company shall be kept in relevant files in the department.

Safety Performance Measurement
Safety performance measurement shall be carried out onboard as per the following method:

Lost Time Injury Illness Frequency (LTIIF)
This is the number of Lost Time Injuries Illnesses per unit exposure hours. The most common unit in respect of LTIIF is one million man hours.

LTIIF = LTIIs x 	10,00,000

Safety Performance Measurement
Safety performance measurement shall be carried out onboard as per the following method:

Lost Time Injury Illness Frequency (LTIIF)
This is the number of Lost Time Injuries Illnesses per unit exposure hours. The most common unit in respect of LTIIF is one million man hours.

LTIIF = LTIIs x 	10,00,000	
Exposure Hours

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence | 
As an example, if the company had two lost time injuries and one lost time illness and during a year in which their fleet personnel had 50,00,000 exposure hours then their LTIIF would be calculated as follows:

LTIIF	=  3 x 10,00,000  = 0.60 50,00,000

Total Recordable Case Frequency (TRCF)
This is the number of TRCs (e. LTIIs + RWCs + MTCs) per unit exposure hours. The most common unit in respect of TRCF is 1 million man hours.

TRCF = (LTIIs + RWCs + MTCs) x 	10,00,000	
Exposure Hours

As an example, if a company had three LWCs, one PTD, one PPD, four RWCs and five MTCs during a year in which their fleet personnel had 5,000,000 exposure hours then their TRCF would be calculated as follows:

TRCF  =  (3 +1 + 1 + 4 + 5) x 10,00,000  =  2.8
50,00,000

Note: These frequencies can, by simple arithmetic, be expressed as a rate per any desired unit of exposure hours (2, 00,000 is commonly used in the United States).

Vessel to use Form: LTIIF & TRCF and the records are to be maintained in SMS File 316. The reports to be forwarded to Office on quarterly basis. | As an example, if the company had two lost time injuries and one lost time illness and during a year in which their fleet personnel had 50,00,000 exposure hours then their LTIIF would be calculated as follows:

Total Recordable Case Frequency (TRCF)
This is the number of TRCs (e. LTIIs + RWCs + MTCs) per unit exposure hours. The most common unit in respect of TRCF is 1 million man hours.

TRCF = (LTIIs + RWCs + MTCs) x 	10,00,000	
Exposure Hours

As an example, if a company had three LWCs, one PTD, one PPD, four RWCs and five MTCs during a year in which their fleet personnel had 5,000,000 exposure hours then their TRCF would be calculated as follows:

TRCF  =  (3 +1 + 1 + 4 + 5) x 10,00,000  =  2.8
50,00,000

Note: These frequencies can, by simple arithmetic, be expressed as a rate per any desired unit of exposure hours (2, 00,000 is commonly used in the United States).

Vessel to use Form: LTIIF & TRCF and the records are to be maintained in SMS File 316. The reports to be forwarded to Office on quarterly basis. | As an example, if the company had two lost time injuries and one lost time illness and during a year in which their fleet personnel had 50,00,000 exposure hours then their LTIIF would be calculated as follows:

LTIIF	=  3 x 10,00,000  = 0.60 50,00,000

Total Recordable Case Frequency (TRCF)
This is the number of TRCs (e. LTIIs + RWCs + MTCs) per unit exposure hours. The most common unit in respect of TRCF is 1 million man hours.

TRCF = (LTIIs + RWCs + MTCs) x 	10,00,000	
Exposure Hours

As an example, if a company had three LWCs, one PTD, one PPD, four RWCs and five MTCs during a year in which their fleet personnel had 5,000,000 exposure hours then their TRCF would be calculated as follows:

TRCF  =  (3 +1 + 1 + 4 + 5) x 10,00,000  =  2.8
50,00,000

Note: These frequencies can, by simple arithmetic, be expressed as a rate per any desired unit of exposure hours (2, 00,000 is commonly used in the United States).

Vessel to use Form: LTIIF & TRCF and the records are to be maintained in SMS File 316. The reports to be forwarded to Office on quarterly basis.

 | SHIPBOARD SMS MANUAL
Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence | 
Reporting
Company identifies the need of reporting Non-conformities, Accidents and Near Miss/ Hazardous Occurrences in order to analyse, investigate and effect improvement by implementing corrective action towards the objective of safety and environmental protection.

Non-conformity Reports
All non-conformities that arise shall be reported using Form: NCR001. Personnel are advised to read the foot-notes provided on Form: NCR001. Given below are examples of non- conformities:
failure to use permit to work system;
procedures or checklists documented in the SMS manual do not conform to the requirements of the specific ship;
non-compliance with mandatory rules and regulations;
failure to report accidents and hazardous occurrences;
failure to comply with specified requirement of SMS ashore may also be reported as non- conformities by persons identifying the same.
(above situations are given as examples only)

Master and Chief Engineer Officer shall ensure prompt reporting of non-conformities related to maintenance, equipment and technical systems, the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations. A separate non-conformity form need not be filled if such non-conformities are reported by Company‘s established procedure of reporting such as repair specification (defect list), dry dock defect list, emergency indent etc. Master shall ensure that a finite period of time is set for their rectification and implementation of corrective action.

Whenever a Non-conformity is identified by any shipboard personnel and is reported to the Master or the Safety Officer or the Departmental Head, a Non-conformity Report (NCR) shall be made by the Master on board the vessel, a copy of such report shall be sent by the Master to the concerned Superintendent and the concerned DO. If considered necessary, the superintendent may forward a copy of the NCR to the Safety Officer of the Operator for information. Handling of such NCRs will be as mentioned below.

Whenever a Non-conformity is identified within the Company and the Division, such non- conformity shall be reported in the non-conformity form by the concerned person and the report handed over to the Group Incharge and/or the Departmental Head. Handling of such NCRs will be as mentioned below: | Reporting

Non-conformity, Accident, Near Miss & Hazardous Occurrence | 
As regulatory requirement, the Company shall undertake investigation of near misses, since such investigation forms an integral component of continuous improvement in the Company‘s Safety Management System. The Company encourages ship staff to provide essential safety related information without fear of retribution. The Company shall undertake in depth investigation of only those near misses, which are likely to recur and/or which could have had severe consequences. The ultimate objective of near miss reporting and investigating is to identify areas of concern and implement appropriate corrective/preventive action to avoid future losses.

Master/Shipboard Safety Officer shall ensure prompt reporting of Accidents, Near Miss/ Hazardous Occurrence to the concerned Superintendent and DO, using either Form: AR001 or Form: NMHO001, as applicable. After proper analysis, Superintendent and/or Group I/C shall send necessary follow up and advice to the concerned ship as well as advise the ships under his charge. Concerned DO shall monitor same. If considered necessary, the superintendent may forward a copy of the report to the Safety Officer of the Operator for information.

When an accident (which involves personnel injury) occurs, priority shall be given to the safety of the injured and of those assisting them. Wherever immediate assistance is required, the Company should be informed immediately. Thereafter, the Safety Officer shall investigate the accident in the following manner:
Record the names and addresses of all those present in the vicinity of the event including non-crew members.
Note and mark the position of the injured and whether protective clothing was used. Take possession of any items, which may have relevance to the investigation.
Take photographs and draw sketches, as necessary.
Carry out more detailed examination at the scene of the event once the injured person(s) and bystanders have been removed, giving specific attention to any changes or any remaining hazards.

The following questionnaire may be used by the Safety Officer to investigate an accident:
What tools and protective equipment were used?
Who provided the tools and protective equipment?
What is the apparent condition of the equipment? (such as broken handrails, rungs etc., the location and extent of any damage)
What were the apparent effects of external factors on the condition of the equipment? (e.g. water or oil on the surface)
How was the equipment used?
Were there any ancillary safety equipment at the site of the event? (safety net, life buoy, lifeline, lighting);
What is the preliminary assessment on how the accident might have occurred?
What were the prevailing weather conditions?
Have all relevant distances been noted?
Safety Officer shall interview the witnesses as soon as possible. If for some reason it is not possible to interview a particular person, he shall be asked to send to Safety Officer his own | As regulatory requirement, the Company shall undertake investigation of near misses, since such investigation forms an integral component of continuous improvement in the Company‘s Safety Management System. Personnel Injury Reporting Guidelines
The primary purpose of reporting Personnel Injury is to promote increased understanding and awareness of personnel safety through efficient and accurate reporting and recording of accidents.
The intent of reporting Personnel Injury is to provide a consistent method for collecting, classifying and reporting data on all personnel injuries occurring on board and continuous monitoring of such injuries in order to provide a measure of effectiveness of Safety Management System and to take appropriate measures with the objective of reducing the frequency of injuries to seafarers. | detailed account of the incident. 9.3	Analysis of Accident, Near Miss/Hazardous Occurrence Reports
The Company‘s Safety Management System recognizes the need of reporting, investigating, and analyzing accidents and Near Misses/Hazardous Occurrences on each vessel.
This section applies to procedures for investigation and analysis of accidents, near misses/ hazardous occurrences reported by each vessel to the Company.
The objective of investigation and analysis, accidents and hazardous occurrences shall be to prevent similar casualties in the future. Investigations shall identify circumstances of the casualty under investigation and establish causes and contributing factors, by gathering and analyzing information. Ideally, it is not the purpose of such investigations to determine liability, or apportion blame. However, the investigating team should not refrain from assigning the fault and fully reporting the causes.
Not all near misses/hazardous occurrences will require a full investigation. An in-depth investigation is required for those near misses/hazardous occurrences, which are likely to recur and/or which could have had severe consequences. Near Miss to be reported in the prescribed format (Form: NMHO001) and should be discussed in ship‘s SHEC meeting as soon as possible to determine onboard safety themes, corrective actions and education/training to prevent recurrence and the near miss report (Form: NMHO001) to be forwarded to the Company.
Analysis of reports assists in reviewing SMS procedures and thereby revising such procedures, where necessary.
For the purpose of investigation and analysis, all the incidents are categorized as detailed below: | 9.3	Analysis of Accident, Near Miss/Hazardous Occurrence Reports

Not all near misses/hazardous occurrences will require a full investigation. An in-depth investigation is required for those near misses/hazardous occurrences, which are likely to recur and/or which could have had severe consequences. Near Miss to be reported in the prescribed format (Form: NMHO001) and should be discussed in ship‘s SHEC meeting as soon as possible to determine onboard safety themes, corrective actions and education/training to prevent recurrence and the near miss report (Form: NMHO001) to be forwarded to the Company.
Analysis of reports assists in reviewing SMS procedures and thereby revising such procedures, where necessary.
For the purpose of investigation and analysis, all the incidents are categorized as detailed below: | 9.3	Analysis of Accident, Near Miss/Hazardous Occurrence Reports
The Company‘s Safety Management System recognizes the need of reporting, investigating, and analyzing accidents and Near Misses/Hazardous Occurrences on each vessel.
This section applies to procedures for investigation and analysis of accidents, near misses/ hazardous occurrences reported by each vessel to the Company.
The objective of investigation and analysis, accidents and hazardous occurrences shall be to prevent similar casualties in the future. Investigations shall identify circumstances of the casualty under investigation and establish causes and contributing factors, by gathering and analyzing information. Ideally, it is not the purpose of such investigations to determine liability, or apportion blame. However, the investigating team should not refrain from assigning the fault and fully reporting the causes.
Not all near misses/hazardous occurrences will require a full investigation. An in-depth investigation is required for those near misses/hazardous occurrences, which are likely to recur and/or which could have had severe consequences. Near Miss to be reported in the prescribed format (Form: NMHO001) and should be discussed in ship‘s SHEC meeting as soon as possible to determine onboard safety themes, corrective actions and education/training to prevent recurrence and the near miss report (Form: NMHO001) to be forwarded to the Company.
Analysis of reports assists in reviewing SMS procedures and thereby revising such procedures, where necessary.
For the purpose of investigation and analysis, all the incidents are categorized as detailed below:
